issues.body:
## Summary

On OpenClaw 2026.10.8 (dc2523e), a NAS/Docker install spends **58.1 s of every startup** in `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync` — **96 % of `workspaceFactsMs` (60.2 s)**, inside `sidecars.model-runtime` (60.6 s). Startup already takes 157–245 s on this host, so this single stage is **24–39%** of total startup.

The cost is filesystem metadata operations (`stat` / manifest reads) over the whole plugin tree — 101 MB / 6 495 files / 603 directories, of which one plugin's `node_modules` holds 4 553 files. It re-runs on **every** startup, not once per install.

Cross-host comparison pins the mechanism: same build, same concurrency setting, only file count and filesystem differ — and the slowdown decomposes as **48× ≈ 7.3× (file count) × 6.5× (per-file cost)**. It is an I/O-count problem, not an algorithmic one.

## Minimal repro

1. Install a plugin with a large `node_modules` (the `feishu` plugin here contributes 4 553 files).
2. Apply the patch in [How to reproduce the instrumentation](#how-to-reproduce-the-instrumentation) and start the Gateway once. Record `runtimePluginMs`.
3. Disable that plugin, restart, record `runtimePluginMs` again.

The delta is that plugin's scan cost. On this host removing 6 small stock plugins (18 → 12 loaded, confirmed in the log) changed `model-runtime` by −1.6 % — the bulk is one plugin's dependency tree, not plugin count.

## Measured breakdown (via instrumentation patch)

The `onBuildStats` callback already computes 20 metrics, but routes them to `startupTrace.detail("sidecars.model-runtime-build", …)` → the diagnostic events channel, **not** the log file. That is why this was hard to see. Patching that one line to also `console.error(JSON.stringify(stats))` produced:

```
workspaceFactsMs               60247.4 ms   ← the whole phase
runtimePluginMs                58123.9 ms   ← 96 %, nested inside
agentFactsMs                    1316.7 ms
registryMs                       593.6 ms
staticProviderCatalogMs           28.4 ms
configuredProjectionMs            14.7 ms
ambientCredentialsMs               8.0 ms
pluginMetadataMs                   0.1 ms
catalogSourceMs                    0.0 ms
```

Total phase wall time `sidecars.model-runtime` = **60.6 s**, so `workspaceFactsMs` accounts for essentially all of it.

Scale metrics from the same payload:

```
agentCount=3  workspaceGroupCount=3  configuredFactsGroupCount=3
catalogSourceCount=0  credentialGroupCount=1  catalogGroupCount=0
runtimeRegistryCount=3  configuredRuntimeModelCount=21
generatedCatalogPluginCount=2  generatedCatalogReadCount=6
sourceConcurrencyLimit=2  fullCatalogConcurrencyLimit=1
```

## Where the time goes

Inside `prepareWorkspaceBuildGroup`, the `reportStage` labels map 1:1 onto those metrics:

| stage | metric | value |
|---|---|---:|
| `workspace plugins` | `runtimePluginMs` | 58 124 ms |
| `static provider catalog` | `staticProviderCatalogMs` | 28 ms |
| `ambient credentials` | `ambientCredentialsMs` | 8 ms |
| `agent facts` | `agentFactsMs` | 1 317 ms |
| `configured model projection` | `configuredProjectionMs` | 15 ms |

The `workspace plugins` stage's only `await` is `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync`, which goes through `createPluginCache` / `retainPluginCache` / `selectPluginMetadataSnapshot`.

> Scope caveat: `plugin-metadata-snapshot-*.mjs` itself contains only
> one `scan` call (with 14 `stat` and 45 `manifest` references). The
> 6,495-entry filesystem walk therefore happens **beneath** that call —
> inside `createPluginCache` / `selectPluginMetadataSnapshot` and their
> transitive helpers — not in this module. The 58 s is attributed to
> this stage by the `onBuildStats` instrumentation, which measures the
> whole `runtimePluginMs` span around the single `await`.

### Code locations

| what | path | line |
|---|---|---:|
| `prepareWorkspaceBuildGroup` | `dist/prepared-model-runtime.facts-*.mjs` | 400 |
| the `await` that owns the 58 s | `dist/prepared-model-runtime.facts-*.mjs` | 413 |
| `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync` | `dist/plugin-metadata-snapshot-*.mjs` | 550 |

```js
// dist/prepared-model-runtime.facts-*.mjs:413
await resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync(prepareOwnedPluginMetadataSnapshotParams(input, env));
```

## The tree being walked

```
~/.openclaw/npm/projects/    6495 files / 603 dirs / 101 MB
└─ feishu plugin              4553 files in node_modules (2 files are its own)
   @larksuiteoapi/node-sdk     7 files, 28.83 MB
   typebox                  1409 files
   zod                       840 files
   @openclaw/fs-safe          672 files
   protobufjs                 108 files
   @openclaw/fs-safe-*        8 platform variants, ~24 MB
```

## The two instances are a natural A/B

Same OpenClaw version (2026.10.8 / dc2523e), same code path, same
`fullCatalogConcurrencyLimit` (= 1), same `MAX_CONCURRENT_MODEL_RUNTIME_AGENT_SOURCE_BUILDS`.
Only two variables differ: plugin-tree size and filesystem.

| | Comparison host (bare metal, local SSD) | This host (Docker on Synology NAS) |
|---|---|---|
| `runtimePluginMs` | **1,209 ms** | **58,124 ms** (48×) |
| plugin-tree files | **885** = `extensions/` 849 + `npm/projects/` 36 | **6,495** = `npm/projects/` only |
| plugin-tree size | 7.2 MB | 101 MB |
| per-file cost | **1.37 ms** | **8.95 ms** (6.5×) |

Scope note: the two columns are **not** counted identically. The 885
figure includes `extensions/`; the 6,495 figure does not. This host's
`extensions/` tree was not counted, so both the 7.3× file-count ratio
and the 6.5× per-file ratio are **lower bounds** for the true gap.

Decomposition (conservative, given the scope note above):

    48× total ≈ 7.3× more files × 6.5× higher per-file cost

The first factor is ordinary data volume. The second is filesystem:
Docker overlay2 + NAS spindle/network storage makes each `stat`
substantially more expensive. This also explains why the host's ~100%
SQLite page cache does not help — `stat` does not go through it.

Note the fix target is *operation count*, not *operation scheduling*.

## What does not explain it (ruled out)

Single-variable experiments, each verified with a restart. Format: *hypothesis → how it was tested → result*.

1. Hollow `node-llama-cpp` install / provider pointing at a dead host → removed plugin + provider + aliases + install dir + install record → **−2 %** (62.9 s vs 64.4 s)
2. Plugin *count* → disabled 6 unused plugins, 18 → 12 loaded (confirmed in log) → **−1.6 %**
3. DB size → checked what the phase reads → `memory_embedding_cache` / `memory_index_chunks` / `embedding` referenced **0 times**
4. Memory / CPU → `mem_limit` 3 g→5 g, `cpu_shares` 512→4096 → `eventLoopUtilization` 0.997→0.999, **unchanged**
5. Disk I/O on the DB → page cache 100 % resident, `diskBytes=0` → **only covers SQLite**, not the plugin tree
6. External-service probe timeouts → 72 × 5 s `generativelanguage.googleapis.com` timeouts/day → **zero** fall inside the `model-runtime` window (first is 11 s after it ends)

Disabling 6 plugins changed nothing because those were small stock plugins; the bulk is one plugin's `node_modules`.

## Why this matters

- The scan runs on **every** startup, not once per install.
- On containers and NAS/NFS hosts the per-`stat` cost is amplified, so the effect is far larger than the tree-size ratio suggests.
- The metrics that reveal it already exist but never reach the log (see last section).

## Suggested directions (in priority order)

1. **Bounded, manifest-first lookup (largest win).** Check for `openclaw.plugin.json` at the known layouts — the package root, and `node_modules/<pkg>/` directly under each plugin root — and fall back to a full walk only when nothing is found. This preserves support for arbitrary-depth installs while removing the walk from the common case.
2. **Cache the metadata snapshot**, keyed on `pluginGeneration` or directory mtime, so startup does not re-scan an unchanged tree. Pushes steady-state operation count toward 0. A cold install or upgrade would still scan once.
3. **Parallelism — consider last, and probably not at all on network filesystems.** Little's law predicts it will not help:

   ```
   throughput = concurrency / latency_per_operation
   ```

   On NAS / overlay2 the per-operation latency **already includes queueing**. Raise concurrency → queue deepens → latency rises with it → throughput stays flat → total time does not drop. The bottleneck is the metadata path, not the workers feeding it.

   **A measurable guard for anyone tempted to try it:** after raising concurrency, if `runtimePluginMs / fileCount` (cost per file) **rises instead of falling**, the metadata path is saturated and concurrency is a negative optimization. This holds for NAS, containers, and network filesystems generally.

The fix target is *operation count*, not *operation scheduling* — see the per-file cost table above.

## How to reproduce the instrumentation

Patch `onBuildStats` in `dist/server-startup-post-attach-*.mjs` to also print (comma operator, one line, original trace unchanged):

```js
onBuildStats: (stats) => (console.error("MODELRUNTIME_BUILD_STATS " + JSON.stringify(stats)), params.startupTrace?.detail("sidecars.model-runtime-build", [ /* unchanged */ ]))
```

One startup then prints all 20 values to stderr.

## Observability gap (this cost is currently invisible)

`onBuildStats` computes all 20 metrics and then discards them into `startupTrace.detail`, which reaches the diagnostic events channel and never the log file. So a phase can burn 58 s of every startup and leave no trace in any log the operator can read.

**Suggestion:** emit these at debug level by default, or behind a verbose flag. They already exist — surfacing them would make the next occurrence diagnosable without patching the bundle. This issue took a plugin-tree audit and a bundle patch to attribute; with the numbers in the log it would have been one `grep`.

## Environment

- Gateway 2026.10.8 (dc2523e), Linux x64, Node 24.22.1, **Docker on Synology NAS**
- Plugin tree `~/.openclaw/npm/projects/`: 101 MB / 6 495 files / 603 dirs
- 3 agents, 12 plugins enabled, 21 configured runtime models
- Container: 5 GiB memory, 4 cores, no cgroup CPU limit
- Comparison instance (different host, same version): 885-file / 7.2 MB tree, `runtimePluginMs` 1 209 ms

issues.body:
﻿## Summary

On OpenClaw 2026.11.6, valid external native plugins can fail during Gateway startup with:

`Error: Plugin preparation callback timed out`

The timeout is hardcoded to 15 seconds in `dist/plugins/plugin-generation-preparation.worker.js` (`performance.now() + 15e3`). On Windows, a plugin whose module preparation itself is fast can still exceed the host callback window. When that happens the plugin never reaches `register()`, so its services and Gateway methods are unavailable.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.11.6 (06afb10)
- Windows 11
- Runtime: bundled Node 24.22.3
- Plugin: local source plugin loaded through `plugins.load.paths`

## Evidence

Startup trace from the same Gateway start:

```text
knowledge-proposals ... loadMs=15507.5 modulePreparationMs=345.2 loadFailedCount=1.0 workersStarted=1 workersStarted=1 workerScripts=plugin-generation-preparation.worker.js:1
local-bge-service ... loadMs=15553.9 modulePreparationMs=347.0 loadFailedCount=0.0 registerMs=0.4
```

Both plugins are local source plugins. `local-bge-service` finishes just over 15 seconds and succeeds; `knowledge-proposals` finishes just under/around the boundary and fails. Its Gateway method is then reported as `unknown method: knowledge-proposals.status`.

`plugins doctor` reports only the load timeout; `plugins lint` reports zero compatibility warnings; there are no missing dependencies or manifest errors. Setting `activation.onStartup: false` and loading the plugin after startup still hits the same 15 second timeout, so this is not only startup contention. Moving tests/docs out of the plugin root and lazy-loading a native SQLite import did not change the failure.

The same 15 second boundary also makes `local-bge-service` borderline; without the extra margin it can fail depending on machine load.

## Request

Please make the plugin preparation callback timeout configurable, for example:

- environment variable: `OPENCLAW_PLUGIN_PREPARATION_TIMEOUT_MS`
- or config: `plugins.preparationTimeoutMs`
- default remains 15s, but allow 60s/120s
- log the actual wait duration and preparation phase on timeout
- optional per-plugin override, or no hard cap for explicitly trusted local plugins

A better long-term fix would make the callback path asynchronous so a busy Gateway main thread cannot fail an otherwise valid plugin.

## Workaround

Locally raising the hardcoded value from `15e3` to `60e3` in `plugin-generation-preparation.worker.js` is being tested. It requires a full process restart (an in-process Gateway restart does not reload the worker), and it is overwritten by upgrades.

## Related

#174681 — plugin preparation blocking the Gateway main thread; this is the other side of the same loader design.

issues.body:
### Bug type
Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker
No

### Summary
When the Gateway service starts through a `gateway install --wrapper` script stored inside the OpenClaw state directory, the Mac app ends its update flow in "Gateway update needs help: The installed Gateway service command could not be inspected", and Retry never clears it, although the Gateway is healthy.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Install the CLI with npm and create an executable wrapper script at `~/.openclaw/service-env/my-wrapper.sh` that runs the working npm-installed CLI by its absolute path and forwards `"$@"`.
2. Register it: `openclaw gateway install --force --wrapper ~/.openclaw/service-env/my-wrapper.sh`. The LaunchAgent then runs `/bin/sh <env-wrapper.sh> <env-file> ~/.openclaw/service-env/my-wrapper.sh gateway --port 18789`.
3. Keep the default profile, the default CLI install policy (`exact`) and local connection mode.
4. Update the Mac app through Sparkle and let it relaunch.

### Expected behavior
The app treats this Gateway as externally managed and finishes the update without a recovery window. That is what happens with the same wrapper stored outside the state directory and the pending post-update record cleared: after moving it to another folder and running `gateway install --force --wrapper <new path>`, the app launched normally. The docs examples store wrappers in `~/.local/bin` (docs/cli/gateway/service.md, "Install with a wrapper").

### Actual behavior
The app opens "Gateway update needs help / Gateway verification failed" with:

> The installed Gateway service command could not be inspected.
> Repair this Mac app's managed installation, then retry recovery.

Retry shows the same window again, and it came back on every relaunch I observed. At the same time, `openclaw gateway status --deep` reports the Gateway running, connectivity ok, and CLI and Gateway versions matching.

### OpenClaw version
OpenClaw.app 2026.11.5 (first seen on 2026.10.10); CLI and Gateway 2026.11.6

### Operating system
macOS 27 (Apple silicon)

### Install method
Mac app + npm global CLI (Node 24 through nvm), Gateway as a LaunchAgent with a --wrapper script

### Model
Not applicable: the Mac app's post-update check, with no model call involved

### Provider / routing chain
Not applicable

### Logs
```shell
# LaunchAgent ProgramArguments (home directory shortened to ~)
/bin/sh
~/.openclaw/service-env/ai.openclaw.gateway-env-wrapper.sh
~/.openclaw/service-env/ai.openclaw.gateway.env
~/.openclaw/service-env/openclaw-nvm-node-wrapper.sh
gateway
--port
18789
```

### Impact and severity
- Affected: Mac app users whose Gateway LaunchAgent starts through a `--wrapper` script stored under the state directory. I observed it with the default profile (`~/.openclaw`).
- Severity: blocks the app's post-update flow. The window offers only a repair that cannot succeed.
- Frequency: every relaunch I observed after an update, until the wrapper was moved and the pending record cleared.
- Consequence: the user sees a "needs help" error for a healthy Gateway and has no way to clear it from the app.

### Additional information
Workaround: move the wrapper outside the state directory (for example `~/.local/libexec/openclaw/`), run `openclaw gateway install --force --wrapper <new path>`, then clear the pending post-update record with `defaults delete ai.openclaw.mac openclaw.postAppUpdateReceipt` and relaunch the app.

Cause, from reading `apps/macos` on main: two checks disagree about the same LaunchAgent.
- `CLIInstallPrompter.launchAgentUsesManagedCLI` counts any executable under the state directory as app-managed, except `tools/node/`. An operator wrapper there passes, so `PostUpdateController.ownsManagedRuntime` is true.
- `GatewayLaunchAgentManager.installedServiceCLI` only parses `node|bun <entrypoint> gateway`, so for `<wrapper> gateway ...` it returns nil.
- `resolveGatewayAction` then returns `.managedRuntimeUnavailable`, which is the dead-end window.
- That window also marks the stored update record as incomplete. So it returns on later launches, and the flag carries into the next app update. Once the service is seen as external, an incomplete record leads to "The Gateway could not be checked" instead, the state described in #169919.

Related: #169919. A fix with a test is ready, and I'll link the PR here.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

### Summary

After a config hot reload that touches a plugin, none of my plugin slash commands work on Telegram any more: they answer "This command is no longer available after the plugin registry changed. Please try again." every time, until I restart the Gateway. The repro steps and diagnosis below were put together with an AI assistant; they match what I see, but please verify.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run the Gateway with Telegram connected and a plugin that registers a chat command (I use my own `/claude_login`; the stock `/dreaming` goes the same way).
2. Change `plugins.entries.<any plugin>` so a hot reload applies (log: `config hot reload applied (... plugins.entries.ollama ...)`).
3. Send the command in a Telegram DM.

### Expected behavior

The command runs, as it does when sent from the Control UI or another chat after the same reload.

### Actual behavior

`⚠️ This command is no longer available after the plugin registry changed. Please try again.` on every try. The reload does not restart Telegram (one `[telegram] [default] starting account` line at boot, none after it), so the state does not clear by itself.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.10 (7dc3350). The same code is in v2026.11.3 and main (81ca4f4).

### Operating system

Ubuntu on WSL2 (Linux 6.6)

### Install method

npm global

### Model

n/a (slash command, no model call)

### Provider / routing chain

n/a

### Logs

```shell
Nov 11 22:39:37 [telegram] [default] starting account (reason: startup)
Nov 12 04:41:26 [reload] config hot reload applied (agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, plugins.entries.ollama, models.providers.ollama)
Nov 15 13:33:59 [telegram] [diag] isolated polling worker update received updateId=933428464
Nov 15 13:33:59 [telegram] text delivery ok chat=<dm>   <- the "no longer available" reply
```

### Impact and severity

Every plugin-registered command on Telegram, for the rest of the Gateway's life after any plugin-affecting reload. Always (every attempt). Workaround: restart the Gateway.

### Additional information

`registerTelegramNativeCommands` builds the plugin command candidates once, at provider start (`extensions/telegram/src/bot-native-commands.ts:80`, `listNativeCandidates("telegram")`), and registers a `bot.command` handler per command that reuses that candidate. `bot-native-command-plugins.ts:94` dispatches through the captured `candidate.prepareDispatch`, which is bound to the registry of that moment. After the reload retires that registry, `executePluginCommandDispatch` returns the retired reply (`plugin-command-runtime.ts`, `isPluginRegistryRetired(selected.registry)`).

Suggested fix: in `executeTelegramPluginCommand`, look the candidate up again by name from `createPluginCommandRuntime()` at execution time (and fall back to the captured one if it is gone). I'm applying it as a local patch and will report back.

Same class of bug, already closed: #125275 (session tool catalog pinned at creation) and #77254 (Discord adapter lost after a registry reload).

I never checked an older version, so I can't say whether this ever worked.

Thanks!

issues.body:
### Summary

Tell `agent_end` hooks when a durable context engine already owns the finished attempt, by passing `ctx.contextEngineTurn = { logicalTurnId, enginePluginId? }`.

### Problem to solve

A plugin that provides a durable context engine (`commitTurn`) often also registers an `agent_end` hook as the fallback that captures turns the engine does not own (degraded leases, native Codex, CLI runners). Today the hook context does not say whether the finished attempt was engine-owned.

So the plugin either captures engine-owned turns twice (once in `agent_end`, once in `commitTurn`) or guesses ownership from its own state. That guess goes wrong when a lease degrades mid-run, because the host's ownership decision is not visible to the hook.

### Proposed solution

When the embedded runner finishes an engine-owned attempt (the engine supports durable turn advancement, the lease is not degraded, and the user turn has an admission receipt), pass

```ts
ctx.contextEngineTurn = { logicalTurnId: string; enginePluginId?: string }
```

to `agent_end`. `enginePluginId` is set for plugin-owned engines.

Advertise this as the `hostRequirements` capability `agent-end-context-engine-turn-v1` for `agent-run`, so an engine can require it and be refused on hosts that do not provide it.

No new API. Attempts the engine does not own carry nothing, so existing hooks see no change. The field assigns capture responsibility only; it does not claim that retention has completed.

### Alternatives considered

- **Infer ownership in the plugin from its own lease state.** Wrong when the host degrades the lease mid-run; the plugin cannot see that decision.
- **Capture everything in `agent_end` and dedupe in the engine.** The hook has no key to dedupe on. `logicalTurnId` is exactly the missing key.
- **Drop the `agent_end` fallback.** Loses turns on runners the engine does not own.

### Impact

- Affected: plugins that provide a context engine with `commitTurn` and also capture turns in `agent_end` (memory and retention plugins).
- Severity: data quality. Duplicate captures, or gaps when the plugin's guess is wrong.
- Frequency: the duplicate-or-guess choice applies to every engine-owned turn; wrong guesses happen on mid-run lease degradation.
- Consequence: duplicated or missing turn records, and host-state guessing code in each plugin.

### Evidence/examples

Reference implementation, two commits on top of main (+265/-1, 9 files including `docs/concepts/context-engine.md`), with tests for the hook context, attempt finalization and capability advertisement:

https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/compare/main...vernmic:openclaw:promote/context-engine-agent-end-turn

- `feat(agents): carry context-engine turn identity into agent_end hooks`
- `feat(context-engine): advertise agent-end-context-engine-turn-v1`

We have run this in production on a fork since 2026-11-15 with a memory plugin's context engine.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself

### Additional information

Happy to open the branch as a PR if the contract is acceptable. Backward compatible: unowned attempts and hosts without the capability behave as today.

issues.body:
## Summary

In a Docker deployment where the state directory is a persistent host volume, a
hard kill of the gateway leaves a lock file behind whose liveness check can
never fail again. Every subsequent start is rejected with
`failed to acquire gateway state ownership`, and the gateway never comes back
without manual intervention.

The reason is that the lock records a **container-internal PID** in a file that
**outlives the container**.

## Environment

- OpenClaw **2026.9.8**
- Docker on Linux, started by systemd with `Restart=always`
- State on a persistent host volume: `--volume <hostdir>:/home/node/.openclaw`
- Container runs `--read-only` with `--tmpfs /tmp` and `XDG_CACHE_HOME=/tmp`

## What happened

The container's main process was killed (systemd reported
`Main process exited, code=exited, status=137/n/a`) while a shutdown was in
progress. From then on, every start failed:

```
Gateway failed to start: failed to acquire gateway state ownership
  | Another Gateway owner lease is still active for this state directory
systemd[1]: openclaw.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
```

With `Restart=always`, this becomes a loop: five starts in thirty minutes, and
between attempts no container exists at all, so `docker inspect` answers
`no such object`. Nothing recovers on its own.

## Cause

Two lock files in the state directory held this:

```
<state>/tmp/openclaw-1000/gateway.state.lock
<state>/tmp/openclaw-1000/state.<hash>.lock

{
  "pid": 27,
  "ownerId": "<uuid>",
  "createdAt": "...",
  "configPath": "/home/node/.openclaw/openclaw.json",
  ...
}
```

PID 27 is a **container-internal** PID. The files, however, live on the
persistent host volume and survive the container. A newly started container has
a fresh PID namespace, so checking whether PID 27 is alive says nothing about
the previous owner — and the lock is treated as still held, indefinitely.

Note the asymmetry: the SQLite-level lease **does** carry an expiry and
recovers on its own, for example

```
[state/lease] Waiting for state lease core:mcp-oauth/<name> held by <uuid>;
current lease expires at 2026-10-21T19:06:04.859Z.
```

The **file** locks carry no expiry and no heartbeat, so only they deadlock.

## Workaround

Stop the unit, confirm no container or process remains, delete the two lock
files, start again. The gateway then comes up normally.

## Suggested fix

Any one of these would remove the deadlock:

1. Record an owner identity that is comparable across container restarts — boot
   id plus container/cgroup id — instead of a bare PID, and treat a lock whose
   identity cannot be matched as stale rather than as held.
2. Give the file lock the same expiry/heartbeat the SQLite lease already has.
3. Place the lock in a volatile location. The container already mounts `/tmp` as
   tmpfs and points `XDG_CACHE_HOME` there, so a lock under the state directory
   is the one piece of this that is unnecessarily persistent.

A PID alone cannot identify an owner across a namespace boundary. A closed
report, #149429, hit the same class of problem on the WSL2 side for browser
control, which suggests the owner-verification pattern is worth looking at
beyond this one call site.

issues.body:
## Problem

On OpenClaw 2026.9.8, a normally recorded **community** ClawHub plugin can receive `plugin.trust.reason: "provenance-invalid"` in plugin inspection. The [plugin documentation](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/plugin) recommends reinstalling from the official source for that reason.

This conflates two different states: an installation that **does not claim official trust** and an installation whose **claimed official provenance is inconsistent**. Reinstalling a community listing cannot make it an official-catalog plugin.

## Source-level reproduction

In an isolated fixture, provide a plugin candidate and matching install path with a recorded ClawHub install whose `clawhubUrl` is `https://clawhub.ai`, `clawhubChannel` is `community`, and package identity is consistent. Ensure the package is not in the official plugin catalog.

[`resolvePluginTrust`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fc23bc864e4553c2d215e479eeec47b67a0bf943/src/plugins/installed-plugin-record-match.ts#L81-L145) rejects official trust, then falls through to `provenance-invalid`. The [official-install predicate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fc23bc864e4553c2d215e479eeec47b67a0bf943/src/plugins/official-external-install-records.ts#L91-L145) correctly requires official catalog identity and provenance. **The trust decision is correct; its diagnostic classification and remedy are not.**

## Expected behavior

Inspection should explain that a valid community installation is **not eligible for trusted-official capabilities**, without suggesting that its files or install provenance are corrupt or that reinstalling the same listing will help. An inconsistent claim of official provenance should retain a distinct invalid-provenance diagnostic.

## Why this matters

The current advice sends operators through disruptive reinstall and registry-refresh attempts that cannot change catalog eligibility. It also makes a routine security boundary look like package corruption. A precise diagnosis helps operators distinguish “plugin installed, but not official” from an actual install-record problem, while preserving the existing refusal of privileged APIs.

## Suggested scope

Add a cause-specific inspection reason or equivalent actionable message for a consistently recorded community ClawHub install. Update the reason-to-remedy guidance. **Do not change official-catalog eligibility, grant community plugins trusted APIs, or treat artifact hashes as proof of official status.**

## Acceptance criteria

- A valid community ClawHub fixture remains untrusted, but inspection identifies its expected non-official status and does not recommend reinstalling the same listing.
- A genuinely conflicting or partial *official* install record still reports an invalid/missing-provenance reason with appropriate recovery guidance.
- Existing trusted-official and missing/path-mismatched record cases retain their behavior.
- Regression tests cover both the classification and its user-facing remedy.

Related but distinct: [#76433](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/76433) asks whether community plugins should gain host-managed state access; [#138774](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/138774) concerns an allegedly official plugin missing official trust. This issue requests **diagnostic accuracy only**.

### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On 2026.11.6, reading a compressed session archive (`*.jsonl.zst`) fails with `ERR_BUFFER_TOO_LARGE` whenever the plain transcript is bigger than the compressed file plus 1 MiB; #192743 already fixes this on main, but no stable release carries it.

### Steps to reproduce

1. On 2026.11.6, archive a session whose transcript is about 3,000 records (several MB of plain JSONL).
2. Read its history.
3. Result: `ERR_BUFFER_TOO_LARGE`.

### Expected behavior

The archive reads, as the same fixture does on 2026.11.4.

### Actual behavior

The read fails with `ERR_BUFFER_TOO_LARGE` ("Session archive … exceeds N decompressed bytes; the archive is unchanged. Export it as uncompressed JSONL to read it."). That covers archived history, CLI history, transcript and usage reads, and the memory session indexer.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.6

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux x86_64)

### Install method

npm (pinned dependency)

### Model

Not model-specific (archive read, no inference)

### Provider / routing chain

None (local archive read)

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell
Session archive … exceeds N decompressed bytes; the archive is unchanged. Export it as uncompressed JSONL to read it.
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

2026.11.6, `src/config/sessions/archive-compression.ts`, `readSessionArchiveContentSync`:

```ts
const maxOutputLength = expectedBytes ?? stored.length + 1024 * 1024;
```

Writers pass `expectedBytes`. Readers don't, so they get the fixed +1 MiB budget. The cap came in with #190690 (Nov 1).

#192743 ("read compressed archives as streams instead of refusing expansion", merged Nov 4) replaces the cap with a streaming decode and a 4 GiB ceiling. Its description measures the impact: on team-metal, 9,461 of 16,806 archives (56%) were refused. #193548 (Nov 5) follows it up. Both are in v2026.11.10-beta.1 and missing from v2026.11.6, which is the current npm `latest`.

garrytan/alphaclaw#470 had to cut its live test fixture (`tests/live/openclaw-archive-read-cache.e2e.test.js`) from 3,000 to 1,000 records to pass on 2026.11.6.

### Impact and severity

A stable user who upgrades from 2026.11.4 loses read access to long archived sessions until the next stable release. That was 56% of archives on team-metal, per #192743.

### Additional information

Ask: a 2026.11.6.x patch with #192743 and #193548, or the next stable release that carries them.

Last known good: 2026.11.4. #200232 hit the same error on 2026.11.5-beta.3 and was closed as already fixed on main, which is true; this issue asks only for a stable release that carries the fix.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

With a local reasoning model routed through LiteLLM using `openai-completions`, OpenClaw 2026.6.11 can reduce the configured output budget from 6000 to `max_completion_tokens: 1`, after which the embedded agent ends with `stopReason=length` and produces no usable response.

### Steps to reproduce


1. Run OpenClaw 2026.6.11 in Docker with a local reasoning model behind LiteLLM and llama.cpp using the `openai-completions` API.
2. Configure the OpenClaw model with `contextWindow: 30000` and `maxTokens: 6000`.
3. Start a new direct embedded-agent session and set thinking to `medium`.
4. Send a normal request or a request requiring a tool call.
5. Capture the request from OpenClaw to LiteLLM and observe `max_completion_tokens: 1`.
6. Observe the gateway log reporting `stopReason=length`, `payloads=0`, and no usable agent response.

### Expected behavior

The request should retain the configured output budget. In the same environment, after bypassing the secondary proxy-specific clamp, four captured agent requests contained `max_completion_tokens: 6000` and the agent completed the previously failing multi-turn and tool-call workflows.

### Actual behavior

OpenClaw sends `max_completion_tokens: 1`. The local reasoning model begins generating reasoning content but immediately reaches the output limit. The user receives `Agent couldn't generate a response. Please try again.` and the gateway records an incomplete turn with `stopReason=length`.

### OpenClaw version

2026.6.11

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (OpenClaw/LiteLLM Docker host); Windows 11 llama.cpp backend

### Install method

Docker; custom image derived from the official OpenClaw image

### Model

litellm/openclaw-local -> gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw embedded agent -> LiteLLM -> llama.cpp OpenAI-compatible server -> local Gemma 4

### Additional provider/model setup details

OpenClaw provider API: `openai-completions`.

Redacted effective model configuration:

```json
{
  "id": "openclaw-local",
  "reasoning": true,
  "input": ["text"],
  "contextWindow": 30000,
  "maxTokens": 6000
}
```

The llama.cpp server reports an actual context window of 32768. OpenClaw compaction reserve is 6000. The failure was reproduced in new sessions with little conversational history.

### Logs

```shell
[provider-transport-fetch] [model-fetch] start provider=litellm api=openai-completions model=openclaw-local method=POST url=http://litellm-gateway:4000/v1/chat/completions timeoutMs=180000 proxy=none policy=custom
[provider-transport-fetch] [model-fetch] response provider=litellm api=openai-completions model=openclaw-local status=200 elapsedMs=2859 contentType=text/event-stream; charset=utf-8
[agent/embedded] incomplete turn detected: provider=litellm/openclaw-local stopReason=length hasLastAssistant=yes hasCurrentAttemptAssistant=yes payloads=0 tools=0 replaySafe=yes compactions=0 reasoningRetries=0/2 emptyRetries=0/1 missingAssistantRetries=0/1 — surfacing error to user
[model-fallback/decision] model fallback decision: decision=candidate_failed requested=litellm/openclaw-local candidate=litellm/openclaw-local reason=format next=none detail=Agent couldn't generate a response. Please try again.


Captured request before the workaround:


"max_completion_tokens":1


Captured requests after bypassing the secondary LiteLLM proxy clamp:


"max_completion_tokens":6000
"max_completion_tokens":6000
"max_completion_tokens":6000
"max_completion_tokens":6000
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The behavior was traced to the OpenAI-completions custom transport. After resolving the configured maximum, it performs another clamp for explicit proxy-like endpoints:

```js
const estimatedInputTokens = estimateOpenAICompletionsInputTokens(params);
const remainingBudget = Math.max(
  1,
  effectiveContextTokens - estimatedInputTokens - 1
);

if (clampedMaxTokens > remainingBudget) {
  clampedMaxTokens = remainingBudget;
}
```

In this environment the transport's character-based estimate reduced the budget to one token even though the normal context precheck had accepted the request.

A temporary provider-specific diagnostic workaround changed the condition from:

```js
if (compatDetection.capabilities.usesExplicitProxyLikeEndpoint && ...)
```

to:

```js
if (model.provider !== "litellm" &&
    compatDetection.capabilities.usesExplicitProxyLikeEndpoint && ...)
```

No model, LiteLLM, llama.cpp, prompt, or hardware changes were made in the A/B comparison. The configured value then reached LiteLLM as `6000`, and the affected agent workflows completed.

### Impact and severity

Affected: Embedded OpenClaw agents using local reasoning models through LiteLLM/OpenAI-compatible proxy routing.

Severity: High; it blocks ordinary replies and tool execution.

Frequency: Reproduced repeatedly across multiple new sessions before the workaround, often within one or two messages.

Consequence: The agent surfaces a generic generation error and cannot reliably complete normal multi-turn work.

### Additional information

The narrow `model.provider !== "litellm"` check is only a local diagnostic workaround, not the proposed general fix.

Suggested upstream behavior:

1. Reuse the context precheck token estimate instead of performing a second incompatible character-based estimate in the transport.
2. Do not silently issue a one-token agent request when the estimated remaining budget is exhausted.
3. Trigger compaction or return a clear context-budget error when the remaining completion budget is below a practical minimum.
4. Add a regression test for a local reasoning model routed through a LiteLLM/OpenAI-compatible proxy with a large system prompt and tool schemas.

No last-known-good OpenClaw version was tested. A separate auto-compaction recovery issue was observed but is intentionally excluded from this report.

issues.body:
# Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash). Not known to be a regression: measured only on 2026.9.6; we did not test an earlier version.

# Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

The `agent_end` plugin hook fires once per **model attempt**, not once per run. When an attempt fails with a retryable provider error (HTTP 429), the embedded runner rotates the auth profile or falls back to another model and keeps going under the **same `runId`**, but every plugin has already received `agent_end` with `success: false`. `PluginHookAgentEndEvent` carries no field that distinguishes an intermediate attempt from the terminal end of the run, so a plugin that acts on `agent_end` (closing work, reporting failure, releasing claims) acts on a run that is still alive.

The emission is inside `completeEmbeddedAttemptAfterTurn` (installed bundle `dist/builtin-openclaw-*.mjs`), which runs at the end of each `runEmbeddedAttempt`:

```js
// async function completeEmbeddedAttemptAfterTurn(input, settled, prompt)
if (attempt.operation !== "settled-tool-finalization" && attempt.sessionPersistence !== "detached" && !beforeAgentFinalizeRevisionReason) {
	const lifecycleForAgentEnd = projectAgentRunAttemptTerminal(executionState.terminal);
	const agentEndError = promptError && !lifecycleForAgentEnd.aborted ? formatErrorMessage(promptError) : void 0;
	...
	runAgentEndSideEffects({
		...
		event: {
			messages: projectNestedToolActivityForHooks(messagesSnapshot, nestedToolActivities ?? []),
			success: !lifecycleForAgentEnd.aborted && !promptError,
			error: agentEndError,
			durationMs: Date.now() - promptStartedAt
		},
		...
	});
}
```

The failover decision (`embedded run failover decision: ... decision=rotate_profile|fallback_model`) is taken **after** this point by the outer run loop, so the hook cannot know whether another attempt follows. The hook contract:

```ts
type PluginHookAgentEndEvent = {
  runId?: string;
  messages: unknown[];
  success: boolean;
  error?: string;
  durationMs?: number;
};
```

has no `final` / `willRetry` / `attempt` field. `success: true` is always terminal in practice; `success: false` is ambiguous.

A second, smaller defect on the same path: `durationMs` is `Date.now() - promptStartedAt` of the attempt, so on a run with N attempts no hook event ever reports the run's duration.

Related but distinct: #132721 (Codex harness `agent_end` omits structured abort metadata). That one is about a terminal abort lacking classification; this one is about non-terminal attempts being reported as terminal.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Register a plugin with an `agent_end` hook that logs `runId`, `success`, `error`.
2. Configure an Anthropic agent with two auth profiles (or a model fallback chain).
3. Start a turn while the first profile is rate-limited (429).
4. The runner rotates profile / falls back and the turn completes normally.
5. Inspect the hook log: `agent_end` with `success: false` arrived for the 429 attempt before the run actually ended.

## Expected behavior

Either `agent_end` fires once per run, after the failover loop has settled; or the event carries enough to tell the two apart, e.g. `final: boolean` (or `willRetry: boolean`) plus `attempt` index, with `durationMs` measured from run start on the final event.

## Actual behavior

Gateway journal, OpenClaw 2026.9.6, 2026-10-03 (America/Sao_Paulo), `journalctl --user -u openclaw-gateway`. 45 `embedded run agent end ... isError=true ... 429` lines that day. Four runs that **continued and finished normally** after the failed attempt:

```
15:56:56.490 [agent/embedded] embedded run agent end: runId=f38395ea-0306-478b-aa6e-b098a6b3db37 isError=true model=claude-sonnet-5-5 provider=anthropic error=⚠️ API rate limit reached. Please try again later. rawError=429: {"error":{"message":"This request would exceed your account's rate limit. ...","type":"rate_limit_error"},...}
15:56:56.607 [agent/embedded] embedded run failover decision: runId=f38395ea-... stage=assistant decision=rotate_profile reason=rate_limit attempt=1 retry=0 rotations=0
15:57:57.174 [agents/agent-command] [agent] run f38395ea-0306-478b-aa6e-b098a6b3db37 ended with stopReason=stop

17:22:57.548 embedded run agent end: runId=a2e8aa39-8768-411d-9a4d-8220bef928f4 isError=true model=claude-sonnet-5-5 ... 429
17:22:57.662 embedded run failover decision: runId=a2e8aa39-... decision=rotate_profile reason=rate_limit attempt=1
17:23:16.740 [agent] run a2e8aa39-8768-411d-9a4d-8220bef928f4 ended with stopReason=stop

17:26:10.091 embedded run agent end: runId=3d7ce67c-72b7-48b8-86e5-87269cea3b7a isError=true ... 429
17:26:10.201 embedded run failover decision: runId=3d7ce67c-... decision=rotate_profile reason=rate_limit attempt=1
17:27:29.265 [agent] run 3d7ce67c-72b7-48b8-86e5-87269cea3b7a ended with stopReason=stop

17:46:36.123 embedded run agent end: runId=09ac3887-6658-4c8f-b082-44f385cd6f79 isError=true ... 429
17:46:36.239 embedded run failover decision: runId=09ac3887-... decision=rotate_profile reason=rate_limit attempt=1
17:54:20.573 [agent] run 09ac3887-6658-4c8f-b082-44f385cd6f79 ended with stopReason=stop
```

The 09ac3887 run lasted 7 m 44 s after the first `agent_end`. One run shows the multiplicity directly — four failed-attempt ends under one `runId` in 5 s, before the real terminal failure:

```
17:16:43.342 embedded run agent end: runId=1da22a00-1959-464e-9916-e1ecf6d02e54 isError=true model=claude-sonnet-5-5 ... 429
17:16:43.465 embedded run failover decision: runId=1da22a00-... decision=rotate_profile reason=rate_limit attempt=1
17:16:44.494 embedded run agent end: runId=1da22a00-... isError=true model=claude-sonnet-5-5 ... 429
17:16:44.581 embedded run failover decision: runId=1da22a00-... decision=fallback_model reason=rate_limit attempt=2
17:16:46.234 embedded run agent end: runId=1da22a00-... isError=true model=claude-haiku-4-5 ... 429
17:16:46.348 embedded run failover decision: runId=1da22a00-... decision=rotate_profile reason=rate_limit attempt=1
17:16:48.298 embedded run agent end: runId=1da22a00-... isError=true model=claude-haiku-4-5 ... 429
17:16:48.371 embedded run failover decision: runId=1da22a00-... decision=fallback_model reason=rate_limit attempt=2
17:16:48.443 [ws] ⇄ res ✗ agent errorCode=UNAVAILABLE errorMessage=All models failed (2): ...
```

Only the fourth of those is the run's end; a plugin sees four identical `success: false` events and cannot tell which.

Plugin-side consequence: our ticket-dispatch plugin treated the first `success: false` `agent_end` of these runs as the end of the agent's turn, while each agent went on to finish the work and report the ticket afterwards.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.6 (`build-info.json` commit `eb377ac59e6c9fd6c7705028034812becf00271b`)
- Linux 7.0.14 (Proxmox LXC), Node 24.21.0
- npm global install, systemd user Gateway
- Models: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5 with fallback anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5; 2 Anthropic auth profiles

## Provider / routing chain

Gateway -> embedded agent runner (`runEmbeddedAttempt`) -> Anthropic Messages API; on 429 the outer loop rotates auth profile, then falls back model.

## Additional setup details

Local plugins: `backlog-v2` (ticket dispatch; consumes `agent_end` to close the ticket a session was working on), `nexus-context` (context engine). No dist patches touch the agent-end path. Our mitigation, in plugin code: on `success: false`, query the run registry for the session and ignore the event while the session's run is still live. That is a liveness poll standing in for a field the event should carry, and it races with registry teardown.

## Impact and severity

Any plugin that treats `agent_end` as "the run is over" misbehaves exactly when the provider is rate-limiting, which is when operators are least looking. For us: 4 runs on 2026-10-03 were treated as ended by the plugin while they were still working; it surfaced only when the agents' reports arrived after the plugin had already acted, and was diagnosed from the journal. 45 failed-attempt `agent_end` lines in one day on a single gateway means every such plugin is exposed daily.

**Version:** 2026.9.4 (3a9d69d), official container image, Linux arm64, self-hosted.

**Symptom:** `view_image` on a HEIC file logs

```
view_image failed: Image processor unavailable for jpeg encoding; tried: photon, imagemagick, graphicsmagick, ffmpeg
```

**Workaround:** install ImageMagick with HEIC support in the container. The same test then ends at ~0.66 GB with all images converted.

**Possibly related:** #131492.

issues.body:
## Summary

When a model calls a tool by a name that is not a real tool (for example a Tool Search catalog id used as if it were a function name), the failure is recorded as the run's `lastToolError` under that wrong name. If the model then recovers by calling the correct entry point and finishes with an intentional `NO_REPLY`, the earlier error is never cleared and the run is reported as failed. Scheduled (cron) runs then send an "automation failed" notice although the work completed.

## Observed

OpenClaw 2026.9.7, Linux, gateway in a container, isolated cron runs, a stdio/HTTP MCP server exposed through Tool Search.

- In 5 cron runs over one afternoon, one hosted model emitted 18 calls whose function name was the catalog id of an MCP tool instead of calling the Tool Search call tool with `{id, args}`. Each such call returned `Tool ... not found`.
- In every one of those runs the same search succeeded a moment later through the proper call tool, the agent finished its work, and the final reply was the declared `NO_REPLY`.
- The runs were still marked failed, with the first tool error as the run error. The next scheduled run was fine each time. Other models on the same jobs did not produce the bad name, so this is a model-quality problem, but the run outcome is decided by OpenClaw.

## Where I think it comes from (from reading current `main`, not yet reproduced with a test)

- `src/agents/tool-terminal-outcome.ts`: a failed observation sets `lastToolError`; it is only cleared (`else if` branch) when a later observation has the same normalized `toolName` and is not a failure. A recovery through a different tool (here the Tool Search call tool) never matches, so the error stays.
- `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/settled-turn-finalization.ts`: `preserveOriginalTerminal` is true whenever `initial.attempt.lastToolError` is set, and its comment says that intentional silence does not replace a tool error. So the leftover error wins over `NO_REPLY`.
- `embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.replay-safety.test.ts` already models this case ("unknown-tool fallback", `executionStarted=false`), so the failure is known to be pre-dispatch and side-effect free.

## Possible fix

A tool failure with `executionStarted === false` for a name that is not a registered tool is not a failed action. Either do not record it as `lastToolError`, or let any later successful tool call clear a pre-dispatch (`executionStarted === false`, non-mutating) error. Mutating errors would keep today's behavior.

I am happy to send a PR with a regression test if this direction fits; I wanted to check first because the current behavior looks deliberate for real tool failures.

## Not verified

- Not reproduced on current `main` with a unit test yet; the above is from logs of 2026.9.7 and reading `main`.
- Which model produced the bad names is deliberately left out; I do not think it matters for the lifecycle question.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Summary

Setup provisions an enabled **Proactive check** (`createDefaultProactiveJob`, `src/cron/default-proactive-job.ts`):
every 30 minutes, an agent turn in the owner agent's main session, `skipIfScratchEmpty: true`,
`delivery: { mode: "announce", target: "owner" }`. On a Gateway with no channel that can reach the owner
(Control UI / API only), every run still sends the whole main-session prompt to the model and then records
`Owner delivery unavailable (no-route)`. The default job has no scratch, and missing scratch is not "empty",
so the skip never applies. The work is thrown away every time.

On a hosted model this is a steady token cost. On a local server it is worse: each run is a full prefill of a
prompt that grows with the main conversation, it holds one of the server's few parallel slots, and it evicts the
cached prompt of whatever conversation was using that slot. `idleOnly` only sees OpenClaw's own activity.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Fresh setup with any model and no channels (`channels` empty, no `commands.ownerAllowFrom`).
2. Use the main session from the Control UI for a while.
3. `openclaw automations list --all` after a few hours.

### Expected behavior

With no owner route and no scratch checklist, the default check does not call the model (as the legacy heartbeat
did: `heartbeat skipped: no-route`, under a second, no model request).

### Actual behavior

Measured on one Gateway (2026.11.3 source build, fa155ff; the job definition and scratch check are unchanged on
main 3f078860b54) with a local llama.cpp server (2 slots of 65,536 tokens), over 6 days:

- 307 runs, one every 1,800 s; every run `lastDeliveryStatus: not-delivered`,
  `Owner delivery unavailable (no-route); configure an authorized owner DM or edit this automation's delivery`.
- 344 model requests from the job, median prompt 51,212 tokens, 57 above 60,000: 62% of all prompt tokens the
  server processed, about 22 minutes of GPU time a day.
- The same install on 2026.11.2 (legacy heartbeat) skipped every run with `heartbeat skipped: no-route` in under a second.

### Possible directions (maintainer choice)

1. Before execution, skip an owner-targeted run when the owner route does not resolve and there is no scratch
   or pending notice for that occurrence (record it as skipped with the reason), i.e. restore the old no-route
   skip for `delivery.target: "owner"` only.
2. At setup, provision the default job disabled when no owner route resolves, and have `doctor` suggest enabling
   it once one exists.
3. Let local providers use the existing `resolveProactiveCadenceMs` hook (only Anthropic implements it) for a
   longer default cadence.

Related: #134994 (retirement design), #201282 (draft that removes `idleOnly`/`skipIfScratchEmpty` and lets the
check overlap foreground work, which would make this more expensive on local servers), #197938.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.3 (source, fa155ff); behavior confirmed in source on main 3f078860b54

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04 (aarch64)

### Install method

Source checkout (`node openclaw.mjs gateway`)

### Model

Local llama.cpp server, OpenAI-compatible (`api: "openai-completions"`), 74B model

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> custom openai-completions provider on loopback

issues.body:
## Summary

Phone (Voice Call realtime), meeting (Google Meet / Teams / Zoom / Slack huddle) and FaceTime voice consults fail on agents whose model runs on a CLI runtime such as Claude CLI. Typed messages and Discord voice in the same agent work.

The shared helper `consultRealtimeVoiceAgent` (`src/talk/agent-consult-runtime.ts`) ends in `runEmbeddedAgent` with an explicit provider/model. The embedded runner calls the provider API directly and never selects the agent's runtime, so a subscription-only Claude CLI setup fails with `No API key found for provider "anthropic"` (or an auth error if a stale key exists). Discord voice works because it runs a normal agent turn through `runtime.agent.runCommandFromIngress`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an agent with `agents.defaults.models["anthropic/<model>"].agentRuntime = { id: "claude-cli" }` and only a Claude CLI login.
2. Enable Voice Call realtime with the default `openclaw_agent_consult` tool (no `responseModel`).
3. Call in and ask something that triggers a consult.

## Expected behavior

The consult runs on the agent's own runtime (Claude CLI), like a typed message.

## Actual behavior

The consult runs on the embedded runner against the Anthropic API and fails; the caller hears an error. The Claude CLI is never invoked.

## Scope

Callers of the shared helper: `extensions/voice-call/src/runtime.ts`, `src/meeting-bot/agent-consult.ts`, `extensions/facetime/src/talk-consult-controller.ts`. Talk's Gateway path is covered separately by #161885 / #164229 / #199378. The Voice Call classic (non-realtime) responder is #188440.

Related: #188440, #161885, #164229, #199378, closed #191683 (earlier voice-call-only attempt).

issues.body:
### Summary

`browser.tabCleanup.idleMinutes` and `browser.tabCleanup.maxTabsPerSession` are hardcoded (120 and 8) and rejected by the config schema, which leaves an operator running one shared headless Chrome for many concurrent agent sessions with no way to tune tab retention short of patching constants and rebuilding.

### Problem to solve

On a gateway that serves several agents (19 on ours) through one Chrome instance, finished tabs sit for the full 120-minute idle window while their renderer processes hold memory. On a 13Gi container we measured 26 chrome processes at about 4.4 GiB RSS, most of them idle affiliate and sign-in pages from different agents waiting out the timer. The only remedy today is `openclaw browser stop` from outside the process, which kills any in-flight browser task for every agent at once.

At `v2026.9.1`:

- `extensions/browser/src/browser/config.ts` `resolveBrowserTabCleanupConfig` reads only `enabled` from config and returns `DEFAULT_BROWSER_TAB_CLEANUP_IDLE_MINUTES` / `..._MAX_TABS_PER_SESSION` / `..._SWEEP_MINUTES` for the rest.
- `extensions/browser/src/browser/constants.ts` sets those to 120 / 8 / 5.
- `src/config/zod-schema.root-shape.ts` declares `tabCleanup` as `z.strictObject({ enabled: z.boolean().optional() })`, so setting the other keys fails validation.

### Proposed solution

Reinstate `browser.tabCleanup.idleMinutes` and `browser.tabCleanup.maxTabsPerSession` as optional, validated keys with the current values as defaults and sane bounds (for example 1 to 1440 minutes, 1 to 64 tabs). `sweepMinutes` can stay fixed.

### Alternatives considered

- Restarting the browser from a sidecar on a memory threshold (what we do now). It works but is blunt: every agent loses its browser mid-task.
- A gateway-level env var instead of a config key. Equivalent for us, but the config key is where `enabled` already lives.
- Patching the constants in a fork. Not sustainable across releases.

### Impact

Operators running multi-agent gateways (one Chrome shared by many sessions). Single-agent local setups are unaffected by the defaults either way.

### Evidence/examples

These keys were accepted and read by the runtime after #74577 was closed (April 2026) and were removed again in #111382 (July 2026) as tuning knobs with no meaningful product choice. For a single user that is a fair call. On a shared gateway the idle window is a capacity setting, not a micro-knob: it decides how much renderer memory the deployment must reserve per agent.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, if maintainers agree with the direction.

issues.body:
# Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash). Whether it is a regression is unknown: no earlier version was tested.

# Beta release blocker

No

# Summary

When the stuck-session watchdog kills a cron run because a tool call is blocked waiting for an approval that can never arrive (isolated cron session, no interactive approver), the classification it acted on is discarded at the `abort()` call. The run history keeps the cause-free literal `cron isolated agent run aborted`, and on a chat route the failure alert degrades further, to `Check automation history for details.`

The information exists at abort time and is thrown away one layer above the formatter, so no amount of cron-side formatting can recover it.

**1. Recovery knows the cause.** `resolveSessionAttentionClassification` classifies exactly this state (`src/logging/diagnostic-session-attention.ts`):

```ts
    if (
      params.activity.activeWorkKind === "tool_call" &&
      (params.activity.activeToolAgeMs ?? 0) > params.staleMs &&
      lastProgressAgeMs > params.staleMs
    ) {
      return {
        eventType: "session.stalled",
        reason: "blocked_tool_call",
        classification: "blocked_tool_call",
        activeWorkKind: params.activity.activeWorkKind,
        recoveryEligible: false,
      };
    }
```

`isBlockedToolCallRecoveryEligible` (`src/logging/diagnostic.ts`) then admits that classification for recovery, and the activity snapshot in scope carries the active tool identity (`activeToolName` / `activeToolCallId`), already used in the recovery warn line.

**2. The abort drops it.** `recoverStuckDiagnosticSession` passes a reason (`src/logging/diagnostic-stuck-session-recovery.runtime.ts:274`):

```ts
      const result = await abortAndDrainEmbeddedAgentRun({
        sessionId: activeSessionId,
        sessionKey: params.sessionKey,
        settleMs: STUCK_SESSION_ABORT_SETTLE_MS,
        forceClear: true,
        reason: "stuck_recovery",
      });
```

`abortAndDrainEmbeddedAgentRun` accepts `reason?: string` and uses it for staleness bookkeeping, but calls the abort with the session id alone (`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/runs.ts:1292`, shipped as `dist/runs-DkiZS9mO.js:607`):

```js
		let aborted = abortEmbeddedAgentRun(params.sessionId) || expiredReplyRun;
```

`abortEmbeddedAgentRun` aborts with `opts?.reason`, which is `undefined` on that overload (`dist/runs-DkiZS9mO.js:379`):

```js
			handle.abort(opts?.reason);
```

The single-session overload cannot carry one at all — its signature is `abortEmbeddedAgentRun(sessionId: string): boolean`, and the `reason` parameter exists only on the `sessionId: undefined` overload, typed `reason?: "restart"`. So the classification and the tool identity never reach the `AbortSignal`.

**3. The operator gets a string with no cause.** With nothing attached, cron's finalizer falls to its literal (`src/cron/isolated-agent/run-finalize.ts:309`, shipped as `dist/isolated-agent-BbrXa1yO.js:279`):

```js
	if (finalRunResult.meta?.aborted === true && !cronPayloadOutcome.hasFatalErrorPayload) {
		const error = normalizeOptionalString(finalRunResult.meta.error?.message) ?? "cron isolated agent run aborted";
```

**4. On a chat route the alert does not even carry that string.** `emitFailureAlert` picks the detail lines by route (`src/cron/service/failure-alerts.ts:326-332`): a webhook route prints `Last error: cron isolated agent run aborted`, while every chat route goes through `cronFailureDetailLines(errorReason, failureNotificationDetail)` (`src/cron/failure-notification-text.ts:18`). For this failure both inputs are empty — `errorReason` is `resolveCronRunErrorReason("cron isolated agent run aborted")`, which finds no `FailoverReason` (`src/cron/run-error-reason.ts`), and `failureNotificationDetail` only describes command/script payload failures, not an `agentTurn` one. So the notification body is the generic constant:

```ts
const GENERIC_FAILURE_DETAIL = "Check automation history for details.";
```

An operator watching the alert channel is told a named job failed and nothing else, while the cause was in the gateway's own diagnostics before the abort.

**A second, narrower gap on the same theme.** The immediate (non-hang) form of the same denial is also unclassifiable downstream. `deniedReason` for these is free text — `"allowlist-miss"` (`src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts:1288`) and `"approval-timeout: allowlist-miss"` (`:627`) — while `resolveEmbeddedRunFailureSignal` only recognizes `FAILURE_SIGNAL_CODES = ["SYSTEM_RUN_DENIED", "INVALID_REQUEST"]` (`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/failure-signal.ts:14`), read off `result.details.errorCode` / `result.errorCode` by `extractToolErrorCode` (`src/agents/embedded-agent-tool-results.ts:445`). Those codes are produced by the approval-binding sites (`src/infra/system-run-approval-binding.ts`, `bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts:933`), not by the allowlist-miss path — so the coded failure-signal route that does surface a real reason never fires for the common denial.

# Steps to reproduce

1. Give an agent an enforced exec allowlist (`exec-approvals.json`, `security: "allowlist"`) whose default `askFallback` is `allowlist`, i.e. an unlisted command asks for approval.
2. Schedule a cron job for that agent with `sessionTarget: isolated` — no interactive approver exists in the run.
3. Have the job's prompt call `exec` with a command outside the allowlist.
4. Let the run sit until the stuck-session watchdog fires, and read the cron failure alert / run history entry.

# Expected behavior

The failure carries the cause the watchdog already classified: the blocking condition and the command it fired on, e.g. `blocked_tool_call: exec <command>`. Any other abort cause gets its own reason string instead of being flattened into the same text.

# Actual behavior

The run dies at ~150s and reports a cause-free string. Verbatim, from two of our incidents (gateway diagnostics and the cron run history):

```
11:01:23  stalled session  reason=blocked_tool_call  activeTool=exec  (no progress)
11:02:53  recovery abort_embedded_run → run aborted: "cron isolated agent run aborted" (152s)
```

The internal diagnostic names the cause (`reason=blocked_tool_call`, `activeTool=exec`) 90 seconds before the abort; the operator-facing failure never mentions it. Both of our incidents (2026-07-02 and 2026-07-05, same agent, different root command) were diagnosed only by reading the gateway journal by hand — the second one after the generic message had masked the real cause for weeks.

Scope of what was observed versus read: the `cron isolated agent run aborted` text and the diagnostic lines above are verbatim from those two incidents. The chat-route notification body (`Check automation history for details.`) is read from the code path in point 4 — we armed chat-route failure alerts fleet-wide only on 2026-09-04 and no failure of this class has fired since.

# Environment

- openclaw `2026.8.1 (ea80657)`, npm global install (`~/.local/lib/node_modules/openclaw`)
- Linux 6.17.2-1-pve x64, Node v22.23.2
- Verified unchanged on `main` at `d2a674a6c85` (paths and quotes above are from `main`; the two `dist/` quotes are from the installed 2026.8.1 bundle)
- Model-independent: the defect is in the abort/finalize plumbing, not in a provider path. Our affected runs were on `anthropic/claude-opus-5` and the `claude-cli` backend.

# Provider / routing chain

cron scheduler → `runCronAgentTurn` (isolated session) → embedded agent runner → `exec` tool → gateway exec-approval host → allowlist gate with no approver → stuck-session watchdog → `recoverStuckDiagnosticSession` → `abortAndDrainEmbeddedAgentRun` → cron `run-finalize` → `emitFailureAlert`.

# Additional setup details

Local customizations disclosed so they can be ruled out: one first-party plugin (`nexus-context`, prompt/context injection only — it does not touch cron, exec approvals or the embedded runner), per-agent enforced exec allowlists, and agent commands wrapped in shell scripts under `~/.local/bin`. No dist patch is applied for this defect; the quoted bundle lines are stock 2026.8.1.

# Impact and severity

- Every cron failure of this class reaches the operator with no cause. We armed `cron.failureAlert` on a chat route fleet-wide on 2026-09-04, across 31 scheduled jobs, so the generic body is now the default shape of a failure notification here.
- Time-to-notice is the cost: the alert fires immediately but says nothing actionable, so diagnosis requires reading the gateway journal for the `blocked_tool_call` line. In our second incident that gap ran for weeks of daily failures on a job that silently produced nothing.
- Each affected run also burns its full stall window (~150s of model/tool time) before dying.

# Fix shape

Thread the classification and the active tool/command from `recoverStuckDiagnosticSession` through `abortAndDrainEmbeddedAgentRun` → `abortEmbeddedAgentRun` → `handle.abort(reason)` as a real reason object (the single-session overload needs to accept one), and let cron's `resolveCronAbortReasonText` / `run-finalize` surface it as its own string rather than the generic aborted literal. A watchdog abort would then also have a classification to put on the chat route, which today can only print a cause it recognizes as a `FailoverReason`. Separately, attach a structured `errorCode` to allowlist-miss and approval-timeout exec denials so `resolveEmbeddedRunFailureSignal` can classify the immediate form too.

issues.body:
**Environment**
- OpenClaw 2026.8.1-beta.3 (5831b80); first observed on 2026.6.10
- OL9 ARM64, rootful Podman Quadlets; Mattermost + Telegram channels

**Symptom**
The scheduler has no end conditions. `openclaw cron add --help` / `cron edit --help` expose no until / max-runs / expire flag (re-checked on 2026.8.1-beta.3, 2026-08-26), so every recurring job runs until someone disables it. Job `state` carries `lastRunAtMs` / `nextRunAtMs` / `lastRunStatus` and *consecutive* error/skip counters, but **no cumulative run count**, so "stop after N runs" cannot be enforced externally either without keeping a counter elsewhere.

**Why it matters**
"Ends after N occurrences / ends on a date" is standard recurrence vocabulary and the natural shape for finite delegated work ("check this daily for two weeks", "remind me 5 times"). Without it, bounded chores become unbounded standing jobs that need manual cleanup.

**Proposed direction**
(a) `--until <ISO>` and `--max-runs <N>` on `cron add` / `cron edit`, plus a `state.runCount` counter; at the bound the job **disables** (not deletes) so the audit trail survives. (b) Failing that, just `state.runCount` — external tooling can then enforce bounds cheaply.

**Workaround we're using locally**
A sidecar sweep that counts fires from the tasks ledger and disables the job at the bound.

## Current scope — 2026-10-21

The original report below is historical; the later [author correction](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/120385#issuecomment-5223526688) supersedes its claim that the cron allowlist was ruled out. The original scheduled-job failure was caused by finite core-only `toolsAllow` data suppressing bundle MCP. The suspected identity-binding commit was exonerated for that case.

The separate generated-media continuation mechanism identified in the [October19 follow-up](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/120385#issuecomment-6267849914) is addressed upstream by merged [#174696](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/174696), commit [749464ce0a56](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/749464ce0a56c75d8b2ef9b4fa2caf745a8bc549). The completion now uses ordinary requester tools instead of forcing restart-safe tools. This does not explain the distinct 65-tool capture or prove all catalog reductions fixed.

Remaining scope: unexplained reductions need paired activation/final-catalog diagnostics on an updated build; cron outcome classification and configuration-warning requests remain distinct. #121796 added catalog-miss diagnostics, not universal failure classification; warning work is tracked by #130073. The merged media PR also explicitly records remaining first-completion prompt-cache misses, so normal tools do not imply full cache equivalence.

Our currently running Gateway is older than this merge; this update is based on current source and the upstream author's published proof, not a new live reproduction here. Keeping this broader issue open.

<!-- grynn-author-scope:120385:2026-10-21 -->

## Historical report (retained verbatim)

### What happened

Code Mode (`exec` bridge) builds an **incomplete tool catalog** for some execution contexts. Observed on one gateway over ~36h:

| Execution context | Catalog size | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| Interactive turn (main agent session) | 86 | openclaw 48 + mcp 38 |
| Scheduled cron/automation run | **47** | openclaw only, **0 MCP** |
| Internal pre-compaction memory-flush turn | **~40** | partial openclaw only — `openclaw:core:exec` itself missing |
| Some interactive turns, same session minutes apart | 75 | openclaw **37** + mcp 38 |

Guest code then fails mid-run:

- Scheduled run (cron session `295bed73`, 2026-08-07): `Unknown tool id: MCP.ibkr.get_account_positions. Did you mean: automations, browser, get_goal?`
- Memory-flush turns (repeatedly): `Error: Unknown tool id: openclaw:core:exec. Did you mean: read, write? at settle (openclaw-code-mode:controller.js:125:49)`
- New variant on a reduced-catalog turn: `Tool "openclaw:core:write" returned details that do not match its declared outputSchema` — the bridge rejected a core tool's own successful return (the file write did land on disk); `failurePhase:"bridge"`, repair disallowed.

Cron surfaces all of this only as **`⚠️ 🛠️ Exec failed`** — run history/diagnostics contain no guest error, so for two days this looked like model/prompt flakiness instead of a tool-surface regression.

### Impact

- On this gateway 3 of 28 automation jobs call MCP tools from Code Mode; **exactly those 3 fail on consecutive days** while the 25 non-MCP jobs keep passing. The same job bodies succeed when run interactively.
- Internal flush turns intermittently drop to a read/write-only surface and error out.
- 8 bridge failures logged in ~36h across the two failure modes.

### Timeline / suspect commit

- Last clean scheduled run of the canary job: `2026-08-05T22:19Z`. First failure: `2026-08-06T22:06Z`. Still failing after updating to `c25671cf275`.
- `d863dd5f5ec` ("refactor(agents): bind tool policy to exact execution identity", present in the running build) matches the observed mechanism — catalog contents vary by execution identity (interactive vs scheduled vs flush vs subagent) — **but** the first failure predates that commit's author date, so either an earlier commit opened the regression window (`2026-08-05T22:19Z → 2026-08-06T22:06Z`) or there are two contributors. Needs a bisect by someone who knows the intended identity-binding semantics.

### Ruled out

- **Job `toolsAllow`:** backed up and cleared the failing job's allowlist (normalizes to `["*"]` per `src/cron/tools-allow.ts`) → identical failure. An allowlist can only narrow a catalog that was already built; the MCP side is never registered for the scheduled identity in the first place.
- **Model/provider:** reproduces via `openclaw cron run <id>` independent of model.
- **MCP server health:** the same streamable-HTTP MCP server answers normally on interactive turns seconds later.

### Repro sketch

1. Configure any MCP server plus an automation whose prompt calls one of its tools via Code Mode.
2. Run the body interactively: journal logs `code-mode: cataloged 86 tools`, call succeeds.
3. Trigger via scheduler or `openclaw cron run <id>`: journal logs `code-mode: cataloged 47 tools`, guest gets `Unknown tool id: MCP.<server>.<tool>`, run ends `error: ⚠️ 🛠️ Exec failed` with no underlying error in diagnostics.

### Environment

OpenClaw 2026.7.2-beta.6 @ `c25671cf275` · Linux x64 (PVE host) · node v22.23.1 · gateway under systemd user unit · one MCP server (official IBKR hosted MCP via local streamable-HTTP proxy)

### Possibly related

#85030 (MCP tools not injected into `sessions_spawn` subagent sessions) looks like the same family — execution-identity-scoped tool surface dropping MCP registration — but this report covers **cron/scheduled runs and internal memory-flush turns of the main agent**, plus the `outputSchema`-rejection variant hitting a core tool.

### Asks

1. Scheduled/flush (and subagent) execution identities should build the same Code Mode catalog as interactive turns — or the reduction should be explicit, documented, and reflected in the quick index the guest is shown.
2. Cron run diagnostics should surface the real guest error (`Unknown tool id: …`) instead of a bare `⚠️ 🛠️ Exec failed`.
3. Explain/fix the `outputSchema` rejection of `openclaw:core:write`'s legitimate return on reduced-catalog turns.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Foreground `exec` strips the end of a unified diff returned to Code Mode, so Git rejects the returned patch.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a Gateway with Code Mode enabled and open an agent chat.
2. Ask the agent to run this Code Mode cell.

```js
const patch = ["diff --git a/probe b/probe", "--- a/probe", "+++ b/probe", "@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@", "-before", "+after", " ", ""].join(String.fromCharCode(10));
const cmd = "printf '%s' ";
const a = await exec({command: cmd + "'" + patch + "'"});
const control = await exec({command: cmd + "'" + patch + "' | git apply --numstat"});
const roundtrip = await exec({command: cmd + "'" + a.aggregated + "' | git apply --numstat"});
return {
  expectedTail: patch.slice(-8),
  actualTail: a.aggregated.slice(-8),
  expectedLength: patch.length,
  actualLength: a.aggregated.length,
  control: { exitCode: control.exitCode, output: control.aggregated },
  roundtrip: { exitCode: roundtrip.exitCode, output: roundtrip.aggregated }
};
```

### Expected behavior

The structured result retains all 84 bytes, including the final blank context line. Both `git apply --numstat` commands exit 0 and print `1  1  probe` with tab separators.

### Actual behavior

The live Gateway returned 81 bytes. The original patch parsed with exit 0. The patch returned by `exec` failed with exit 128 and `error: corrupt patch at <stdin>:6`.

`2026.11.5-0eb1fa3f7471-2026-11-20T01-48-37.899Z`

issues.body:
## Bug

On OpenClaw 2026.11.3, a gateway `agent` request from a CLI-mode client with an unknown `sessionId` and `createSessionIfMissing: false` receives positive acceptance instead of rejection. A caller cannot atomically require an existing session: `expectedExistingSessionId` is reserved for backend callers.

## Reproduction

1. Start with an isolated state store containing an agent and one known session.
2. Submit an `agent` request as a client with `connect.client.mode = "cli"`, using `{agentId, sessionId: "missing", createSessionIfMissing: false, message: "fixture", idempotencyKey: "missing-run", deliver: false}`.
3. Observe the gateway turn service admission response. The isolated fixture stopped immediately at positive acceptance before a model turn. A known session was also resolved successfully; the missing ID did not resolve in the session lookup.
4. Adding `expectedExistingSessionId` to the CLI request is rejected as reserved for backend callers.

**Expected:** reject the missing session without creating it when `createSessionIfMissing` is false, or provide a supported CLI-safe atomic existing-session constraint.

**Actual:** admission reports success. A pre-submit session probe cannot close the race if a session is deleted or reset between the probe and submission. This report establishes acceptance, not completion of a model turn.

Environment: OpenClaw 2026.11.3, Node 24.19.0, macOS.
