### Bug type

Crash (process/app exits or hangs)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The macOS Gateway exited after a Worker in the bundled Bun runtime hit `panic: unreachable: Alloc(AllocError)` while populating a directory cache during module resolution.

### Steps to reproduce

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Expected behavior

The Gateway keeps serving the Dashboard during normal operation, as it did before the incident and again after the Gateway was restarted.

### Actual behavior

Observed once on November 20, 2026. The Bun Worker raised `SIGABRT`, the Gateway process exited, and the local Dashboard could no longer connect until the Gateway was restarted. I have no reliable reproduction steps.

### OpenClaw version

`2026.11.5 (76cbb32)`

### Operating system

macOS 27.2 (`26B123`), Apple Silicon (`arm64`)

### Install method

Official OpenClaw macOS app with the bundled Gateway and Bun runtime.

### Model

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Provider / routing chain

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Logs

```text
Bun Canary v1.4.4-canary.1 (191755ec1) macOS Silicon
panic: unreachable: Alloc(AllocError)

macOS crash report: EXC_CRASH (SIGABRT), faulting thread: Worker

Selected symbolized frames, ordered from caller to panic:
Bun__resolveSync
  VirtualMachine::__resolve
    Resolver::resolve_without_symlinks
      node_package_scope_error_for_directory
        Resolver::dir_info_cached_miss
          Result::expect (inlined at src/resolver/resolver.rs:5135)
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The UUID of the official debug symbols matched the crashed Bun executable. Symbolication and disassembly locate the failure at `DirEntry::add_entry_with_store(...).expect("unreachable")`. The call returned `Alloc(AllocError)` and `expect` panicked.

- [Bundled Bun source at the failing call site](https://github.com/openclaw/bun/blob/191755ec115ece3dd642eba3cb0143cecb5e5d7a/src/resolver/resolver.rs#L5121-L5135)
- [Directory-entry insertion helper](https://github.com/openclaw/bun/blob/191755ec115ece3dd642eba3cb0143cecb5e5d7a/src/resolver/fs.rs#L482-L553)

### Impact and severity

One local Gateway became unavailable and had to be restarted before the Dashboard could reconnect. One incident was observed.

### Additional information

issues.body:
### Summary

Startup got materially **slower** after upgrading from 2026.9.9 to 2026.10.1 on the same Windows host: `gateway ready` went from a ~410 s baseline mean (489 s measured T0→ready) to **~1030 s**, reproducible across two consecutive hot boots. A previously invisible phase, `sidecars.control-ui-assets`, now spans **~477 s** per boot.

The release notes say startup with installed plugins was improved ("large plugins start without multi-minute stalls"), so this may be a local interaction or a regression — either way the numbers below are from a clean, disk-uncontended run.

### Environment

- Windows 11, Node v24.18.0 (nvm), `npm i -g openclaw@latest` → 2026.10.1 (e178c39)
- Gateway: scheduled task, loopback+token, heartbeat off, 13 non-bundled+bundled plugins enabled (acpx ~655 MB capture, tavily, tencent-weixin, ollama, memory-wiki, workboard, cua-computer, browser …)
- `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_STARTUP_TRACE=1` in the launcher; T0 = `schtasks /Run`; ready = first `gateway ready` log line after T0
- After the upgrade: install unified with `gateway install --force`, plugin generations refreshed (tavily 2026.10.1, weixin 2.4.10), asset cache rebuilt once on boot 1

### Measurements (same host, same config)

| # | scenario | port listen | T0 → ready | top phases (duration / total) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | first boot after upgrade | 432 s | **914 s** | runtime.post-attach 453 s, plugins.runtime-post-bind 421 s, config.snapshot.auto-enable 299 s, secret-preflight 73 s |
| 2 | hot reboot | 504 s | **1028 s** | sidecars.control-ui-assets 480 s, plugins.runtime-post-bind 458 s, auto-enable 335 s, secret-preflight 70 s |
| 3 | hot reboot, disk uncontended | 528 s | **1039 s** | sidecars.control-ui-assets 477 s, plugins.runtime-post-bind 456 s, auto-enable 374 s, secret-preflight 69 s |

For comparison, the same trace on **2026.9.9** (same host/config, 2026-10-08) had `ready` at ~308–410 s of phases and `sidecars.control-ui-assets` did not appear in the top-12 phases at all (<1.1 s).

### What control-ui-assets is doing

- `eventLoopMax=0.0ms` for the whole 477 s — pure wait, no CPU.
- The state-side asset cache (`~/.openclaw/cache/control-ui-assets`, 67 MB / 1039 files) was fully rebuilt on boot 1 (files stamped at ready time), but boots 2 and 3 did **not** rewrite it — yet still spent ~477 s in this sidecar.
- Both installs ship `dist/control-ui` (~53 MB), so the assets are present; something in verification/copy is waiting.
- `sidecars.total` reports only ~20 s of actual work while `sidecars.control-ui-assets` reports a 477 s span — suggesting the phase duration includes waiting on dependencies rather than doing work.

### Exclusions measured on this host (so these are NOT the time)

- Disk uncontended on boot 3: 97 GB free; the old 252 GB `plugin-captures` accumulation is gone (now 2 dirs / 3.3 GB).
- Capture reuse is working: boot 3 created exactly **one** new capture dir, 32 s — so `plugins.runtime-post-bind` at 456 s is not raw copying.
- Provider endpoints, file enumeration, and reindex locks were measured earlier and are seconds-scale (see #160959 comments by me on 2026-10-08).
- `config.snapshot.auto-enable` remains unpatched (was 237 s on 2026.9.9, now 374 s) — tracked under this issue.

### Health after boot 3

models.list 19 entries (incl. custom `opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor`), primary model unchanged, 13/13 plugins loaded, zero ERROR lines during boot. The gateway works — it is just ~2.5x slower to become usable.

### Ask

1. Is `sidecars.control-ui-assets` expected to block `ready` for ~8 minutes? What is it waiting on (the 20 s of work inside a 477 s span)?
2. Please capture a startup trace on 2026.10.1 with installed plugins on Windows to confirm/reject the regression vs 2026.9.9.
3. Happy to run `OPENCLAW_DIAGNOSTICS_EVENT_LOOP=1` + timeline, `NODE_DEBUG_NATIVE=COMPILE_CACHE`, or any env-gated probe you provide and post the output.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Crash (process/app exits or hangs)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

`openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive` ran for more than 15 minutes with no output and never reached the database repair it was run for. The doctor process and its single child `openclaw` worker sat idle (0% / ~1% CPU). The child held a freshly created `tmp/plugin-captures/<uuid>/owner.sqlite` (0 bytes) plus a 512-byte `owner.sqlite-journal`. Unlike #174842, there was no busy loop and no repeated log line, and a plain SIGTERM stopped it.

The run was prompted by the quarantine message from #176220 ("Run openclaw doctor --fix for explicit repair"), so the documented recovery path was a dead end here.

### Steps to reproduce

Seen in six runs on 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-20 (table in the first comment below). The steps describe run 5.

1. OpenClaw 2026.10.3 on macOS, gateway running under launchd. The main agent DB is quarantined because of the SQLite 3.54 FTS5 issue (#176220); the gateway is up but answers requests with `SqliteIntegrityError`.
2. Run `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive`, with stdout piped and no TTY.
3. After about 10 minutes, a new `tmp/plugin-captures/<uuid>/` directory appears (`captures/`, `native/`, `owner.sqlite`, `owner.sqlite-journal`). The worker holds the two `owner.*` files open and does nothing else.
4. At about the same time, the gateway receives SIGTERM via launchd and shuts down cleanly. Run 4 printed "Stopped the managed Gateway for Doctor repair.", so Doctor itself stops the Gateway.
5. No further progress. After 15+ minutes, `kill <doctor pid> <worker pid>` (SIGTERM); the command exits 0.

### Expected behavior

Doctor either gets to the agent-database integrity step or fails with a bounded timeout that names the stage it is stuck in.

### Actual behavior

- No output at all for the whole run.
- `ps` showed the doctor process at `S`, 0.0% CPU, and the child at `Ss`, ~1% CPU.
- A `sample` of the child showed the main thread in the libuv loop, in `uv__io_poll` → `uv__async_io` → `uv__work_done`, i.e. waiting on a threadpool result.
- The quarantine row was still present afterwards, and the agent DB was untouched.
- The gateway stayed down for about 15 minutes after the 11:15 SIGTERM, until it was restarted.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.3 (59cb447)

### Operating system

macOS 27.0.1, arm64 (Mac mini)

### Install method

npm global under Homebrew Node 26.12.0 (`/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/openclaw`), gateway as a launchd LaunchAgent, macOS app installed

### Model

n/a (CLI / Doctor)

### Provider / routing chain

n/a

### Logs

```shell
# gateway.log (local time, CEST), during the doctor run
11:05:00 … 11:15:42  [plugins] workboard external change check failed: SqliteWorkerError: … is quarantined …   (once per second)
11:15:45.844 [admission] closed: stop (SIGTERM)
11:15:45.858 [gateway] shutdown budget at shutdown: … source=launchd gui/501/ai.openclaw.gateway exit timeout=20000ms
11:15:47.423 [shutdown] completed cleanly in 1051ms

# process state at ~11:21 (doctor started ~11:05)
  PID  %CPU STAT ELAPSED
  665   0,0 S      15:24   node /opt/homebrew/bin/openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive
  673   1,0 Ss     15:24   openclaw (child worker)

# open SQLite files of the child
tmp/plugin-captures/3f962f95-…/owner.sqlite          (0 bytes)
tmp/plugin-captures/3f962f95-…/owner.sqlite-journal  (512 bytes)
```

### Impact and severity

- Blocks the documented recovery path for a quarantined agent DB: the quarantine message points to `doctor --fix`, which never reached the repair.
- Leaves the gateway stopped for as long as Doctor hangs. Doctor stops the Gateway itself (see step 4).
- Frequency: six runs on the same install; none completed the repair.

### Additional information

Possibly related to #174842 (Doctor hang with the Gateway running, 2026.10.4). The symptoms differ: idle rather than CPU-bound, no repeated snapshot log line, and SIGTERM worked. `owner.sqlite` has since been identified as the SQLite staging token, not a plugin-capture artefact, so the wait is in repair preparation, not plugin capture. The fixes mentioned in #174842 (SIGTERM deadlock, bounded admission wait) are not in 2026.10.3, so this may already be addressed on `main`. Happy to retest on the next release if someone can say which build to try.

The database itself was repaired manually with the workaround from #176220.

issues.body:
### Summary

Bring back the session menu entry that turned an existing session into a Workboard card, and let the chip in the session header open the linked card instead of only its board.

### Problem to solve

Since 2026.9.2 (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/138618) the Control UI has no **Add to Workboard** action. Before, it took one click on the button in the Chat header, or two in a session menu (open the menu, choose **Add to Workboard**). The card was created with title and notes from the session and opened.

Now each of these is a separate click or input:

1. Click **Workboard** in the sidebar (this leaves the conversation).
2. Click the target board.
3. Click **New card**.
4. Type the title (the title field has focus).
5. Click the **Notes** field.
6. Type or paste the notes. The removed action filled them from the recent user prompt and the latest assistant reply; without steps 5–6 the card has no notes.
7. Click the **Session** field.
8. Type part of the session name to filter the list.
9. Click the session.
10. Click **Create**.
11. Click the conversation in the sidebar to continue working in it.

That is at least 11 clicks and inputs instead of one or two (9 if the notes stay empty), and the user has to remember the session's name to find it in step 8.

The way back is longer too. The chip in the session header opens the card's board (`/workboard/<boardId>`), not the card. On a board with 137 cards that means: click the chip, click the board's search field, type part of the card title, click the card. Four actions instead of one or two (the same button or menu entry, now labelled **Open Workboard card**). The removed action changed its label to **Open Workboard card** once a card existed and opened the card details directly.

The capture code is still there, but nothing in the UI can run it:

- `workboard.cards.captureSession` is registered in `extensions/workboard/src/gateway.ts` (`operator.write`) and implemented in `extensions/workboard/src/store-core.ts`: it returns the active card for the session, restores an archived one, or creates one with a deterministic card id per session.
- No browser code calls it. The labels `sessionsView.addToWorkboard` and `sessionsView.openWorkboardCard` are still translated in `ui/src/i18n/locales/en-session-organization.ts` and in the Workboard plugin locales, but nothing renders them.
- `docs/plugins/workboard.md` still tells users to choose **Add to Workboard** in a session header or on the Sessions tab ("Session lifecycle sync", and step 2 of "Control UI workflow").

The only remaining way to reach the method is `openclaw gateway call workboard.cards.captureSession` with a JSON payload and the exact session key. The `workboard_create` agent tool has no session field (strict schema), and the request to add one (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/113991) was closed as not planned on 2026-10-24. So users cannot ask their agent to do it either: nothing in the UI or the docs tells them the method exists, and an agent only finds it by reading the plugin source.

### Proposed solution

1. Restore the capture entry in the session menus (sidebar session menu and the row menu `…` on the Sessions page). The Chat header button is not needed if that placement was the reason for removing it.
2. When the session already has an active linked card, the same entry reads **Open Workboard card** and opens the card details, as before 2026.9.2.
3. The session-header chip opens the linked card's details on its board, not only the board.
4. If capture stays out of the Control UI: update `docs/plugins/workboard.md` so it describes the **Session** field in **New card** / **Edit card** as the way to link an existing session.

@Patrick-Erichsen you removed the action in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/138618. The PR does not give a reason, and the 2026.9.2 release notes only say that no replacement capture workflow was added. Was the goal to remove session capture from the Control UI, or only the button from the Chat header? The answer decides between points 1–3 and point 4.

### Alternatives considered

- **New card** dialog with the **Session** field: works, but takes the 11 clicks and inputs above, or 9 with empty notes.
- `openclaw gateway call workboard.cards.captureSession`: works (see Evidence), but needs an undocumented method name and the session key. It is not a path users can discover.
- `workboard_create` agent tool: cannot link a session.

### Impact

- Affected: Control UI users who organize existing conversations as Workboard cards.
- Severity: slows a common workflow; no data loss.
- Frequency: every time a running conversation should become a card, and every time the user goes from the conversation back to its card.
- Consequence: 11 clicks and inputs instead of one or two per card (9 with empty notes), four instead of one or two on every way back, and users following the docs look for a menu entry that does not exist.

### Evidence/examples

- Removal: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/138618 (merged 2026-09-04, first release 2026.9.2) deleted `extensions/workboard/browser/session-action.ts`. It registered `capture-current-session` (Chat header) and `capture-session` (session menus); after capture it called `openCardDetails(...)` and opened the Workboard page, so the user landed on the new card.
- Release notes, `docs/releases/2026.9.2.md`: "Chat headers and session menus no longer offer Add to Workboard, and this change does not introduce a replacement capture workflow".
- `main` at `a78fe7aecc5` (2026-10-25): `extensions/workboard/browser/index.ts` registers one `session-header` accessory (`linked-card`) and no session action. `extensions/workboard/browser/session-accessory.tsx` navigates to `workboardPageTarget(workboardCardBoardId(card))`, whose path carries only the board id. The chip has behaved this way since it was added in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/134943.
- Live on 2026.10.5 (2026-10-25): the sidebar session menu and the Sessions page row menu have no Add to Workboard entry. A card linked through the **Session** field shows the chip in that session's header; clicking it opens `/workboard/default`, not the card.
- Live on 2026.10.5 (2026-10-25 23:32 UTC):

  ```bash
  openclaw gateway call workboard.cards.captureSession --json \
    --params '{"sessionKey":"agent:<agent>:dashboard:<id>","title":"…","boardId":"default","notes":"…"}'
  ```

  This created a card linked to the session; a second call returned the same card id. The chip appeared in the session header with the card title, its status followed the session (`todo` → `review` after the turn ended), and it disappeared without a page reload after `workboard.cards.archive`.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/113991 asked for `sessionKey` on `openclaw workboard create` and the `workboard_create` agent tool (agents and CLI). This issue is about the Control UI only.

issues.body:
### Summary

Make the Active Memory recall ceiling (`MAX_TIMEOUT_MS`, 120 000 ms) an operator setting instead of something only a dist patch can change, and make a running recall visible and skippable so a long wait does not look like a hung reply. This follows up #86065 with the measurements and the design its closing comment asked for.

### Problem to solve

#86065 was closed as not planned. Its closing comment named what would change the decision: "concrete proof of a product-safe design for longer recall waits, including user-visible progress/behavior that prevents the main reply from feeling hung, plus live local-model measurements showing the added budget is necessary and does not create worse latency reports."

**The ceiling cuts off slow recalls along with stuck ones.** On a local model, the 150 s budget (120 000 ms plus 30 000 ms setup grace) cannot tell a slow recall from a stuck one, so it stops both. In a week at the stock ceiling, 30% of our recalls hit it and returned nothing, after the turn had already waited the full 150 s. With the ceiling lifted, every recall that ran past 150 s completed (see Evidence).

**Only a dist patch can lift it.** At main @ 0c8d5740b167, in `extensions/active-memory`:

- The manifest caps `timeoutMs` at 120000 (`openclaw.plugin.json:118`). A larger value fails validation and the plugin does not load.
- `normalizePluginConfig()` clamps the value to `MAX_TIMEOUT_MS` (`config.ts:188-192`, `types.ts:21`).
- The `before_prompt_build` deadline is computed from the same constants (`index.ts:205-206`).
- Raising `hooks.timeouts.before_prompt_build` does not help, because recall's own watchdogs still use the clamped `timeoutMs`.

Our patch keeps `timeoutMs: 120000` in config so the plugin still loads, and swaps a hard-coded budget into the runtime. The config no longer says what the gateway does, and every update silently reverts the patch.

**A long recall looks hung today, at any ceiling.** Recall runs silently (`verboseLevel: "off"`, `silentExpected: true`, `recall-run.ts:296-300`) and reports no status to the turn waiting on it. While it runs:

- The Control UI shows "Preparing this turn…" (`preparing_context`) for the whole recall.
- Progress drafts have nothing to show.
- Typing indicators say nothing about what the turn is waiting on. Unmentioned groups (`message` typing mode) show nothing at all until the reply starts.
- With `messages.statusReactions.enabled`, WhatsApp's activity-mode reaction turns ⏳ at 10 s and ⚠️ at 30 s (`src/channels/status-reactions.ts:122-123`).
- The stall diagnostic reports the session as a stalled run (see Evidence).

### Proposed solution

1. **Ceiling in config, default unchanged.** Add `maxTimeoutMs`, defaulting to `120000` (today's `MAX_TIMEOUT_MS`).
   - The schema, the clamp and the hook deadline all read it. Nothing changes for anyone who leaves it unset.
   - To keep it deliberate, unlock it with a break-glass flag that the manifest declares in `configContracts.dangerousFlags`, for example `dangerouslyAllowLongRecall: true`. `openclaw doctor` then lists it with the other dangerous overrides. The docs should state that higher values delay the visible reply.
   - The upper bound is your call. On our data, 300 000 ms would have completed 14 of the 16 long recalls below. 600 000 ms, the existing limit for operator hook timeouts, would have completed 15. Both figures include the 30 s grace.
2. **Show recall while it runs.** Any of these:
   - **A. A recall phase.** Emit a `recalling_memory` run status to the parent run, the way the memory flush already emits `memory_flushing` (`src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-memory.ts:784-788`, shown as "Saving conversation memory…"). Show the elapsed time, for example "Recalling memory · 1:12". Count recall heartbeats as turn progress, so the status-reaction stall timers and the stall diagnostic stop treating a running recall as stuck.
   - **B. A progress-draft row.** Add a row like the new `model-wait` row on main (`src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-event-handler.ts:73-91`), for example "🧠 Recalling memory… 1m 12s", and clear it when the reply starts. Forwarding the recall run's own `waiting_for_model` status would also show when recall is queued for the model.
   - **C. A status reaction.** Show a recall emoji such as 🧠 instead of ⏳/⚠️ while recall runs.
3. **Let the user decide.** Any of these:
   - **D. Skip.** A "Skip memory" button where inline buttons exist, plus a command elsewhere. It ends recall and starts the reply at once, without memory. The result is the same as a timeout, but the user chooses it. Unlike `/stop`, it must not cancel the turn.
   - **E. Ask instead of dropping at a soft deadline.** At 120 s, post one notice ("Memory recall is taking longer than usual, still waiting", with Skip), then keep waiting up to `maxTimeoutMs`. Unattended turns such as cron and heartbeat keep the configured budget.
   - **F. Progress-idle budget.** Abort when the recall run shows no activity for N seconds, with `maxTimeoutMs` as the backstop, like the progress-idle semantics in #144327. A slow model that is still streaming keeps going, and a dead request is cut early. Time spent waiting for a model slot would have to count as waiting, not as idle.

The smallest set that meets the closing comment's bar is 1 + A + D. The other options can land separately.

### Alternatives considered

- **A hosted recall model**, the closing comment's first suggestion. It works: with the same Active Memory config on a hosted model, 26 of 26 recalls completed (p50 26 s, max 40 s). But every turn's recall context then leaves the machine, and keeping it local is the reason to run a local model.
- **Lighter recall** (`queryMode`, `thinking`, search limits). The operator here chose recall quality on purpose. The long recalls took a median of 217 s against a 150 s budget, so the trimming could not be marginal.
- **Disabling Active Memory** for slow models loses the feature.
- **Raising the constant**, as PR #87606 did (300 000 ms). It changes the budget but still gives the user nothing to look at during the wait.
- **Background continuation**: reply at the soft deadline, finish recall in the background, and attach the result to the next turn. This works on multi-slot backends. On a single-slot local server, the background recall competes with the reply for the slot.

### Impact

- Affected: local-model deployments (oMLX, LM Studio, vLLM, Ollama) that use Active Memory, especially with reasoning models or a single inference slot.
- Severity: on this host, 30% of turns waited 150 s and still lost their memory context.
- Frequency: every day with chat traffic. Timeouts cluster, in runs of up to 13.
- Consequence: replies without memory after the maximum wait, or a dist patch that every update reverts.

### Evidence/examples

All data comes from one host running 2026.10.5–2026.10.6. Active Memory settings: `mode: always`, `queryMode: full`, `promptStyle: recall-heavy`, `thinking: xhigh`. Recall uses the agent's own model, a local reasoning model served by oMLX (OpenAI-compatible, one inference slot). Counts come from the gateway log's `active-memory: … start` and `done status=…` lines.

| | Stock ceiling (120 000 + 30 000 ms) | Ceiling lifted (dist patch) | Hosted model, same config |
|---|---|---|---|
| Window | 7 days (Oct 16–23) | 10.5 h (Oct 23) | Oct 22–23 |
| Recalls | 360 | 46 | 26 |
| Completed | 212, all returned memory | 46, 45 returned memory | 26, all returned memory |
| Timed out | 107 (30%), all at 150.0–150.2 s, nothing returned | 0 | 0 |
| Failed (unrelated errors, Oct 16–18 only) | 41 | 0 | 0 |
| Completed: p50 / p90 / max | 63 / 113 / 148.5 s | 89 / 263 / 1097 s | 26 / 36 / 40 s |
| Mean pre-reply recall wait | 86 s | 150 s | 27 s |

- At the stock ceiling, the 107 timeouts held replies for 4.46 h in total and returned nothing. 17 of the completed recalls already needed the 30 s grace.
- With the ceiling lifted, 16 of 46 recalls (35%) ran past 150 s, close to the stock window's 30% timeout rate. Every one of them returned memory (813–996 chars). Their durations: 156, 156, 164, 164, 180, 194, 207, 213, 220, 232, 244, 263, 326, 330, 538 and 1097 s. On this host the timeouts were slow recalls, not stuck ones.
- The cost is real. The mean wait rose from 86 s to 150 s. One recall took 18 min while another chat's turn was using the single inference slot. The operator here prefers that to replies without memory. Still, 18 minutes of "Preparing this turn…" is exactly the "looks hung" case from the closing comment, which is why this proposal pairs the ceiling with visibility and Skip.
- OpenClaw's own diagnostics read that recall as a hang. During those 18 minutes the stall diagnostic logged the session 33 times, every 30 s from 125 s on: `reason=active_work_without_progress classification=stalled_agent_run activeWorkKind=embedded_run lastProgress=embedded_run:started`.
- The lifted window is a small sample (one host, 10.5 h). We are still collecting and can post a longer window.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

- Related: #86065 (closed as not planned, locked), PR #87606 (closed unmerged), #180978 (breaker; fixed by PR #181297, still open for the backoff policy), #72015 (foreground recall latency), #170661 (per-agent `timeoutMs`), #144327 (progress-idle timeouts).
- We can run any build or PR for this on the same host and post before/after numbers.

issues.title: [Feature]: Durable owner-native execution provenance for safe interruption recovery

labels.name: stale
labels.description: Marked as stale due to inactivity

labels.description: Issue quality rating does not apply to this item.

issues.body:
### Motivation

We are building an external Control Centre for long-running OpenClaw agent work. A future capability we would like to support is conservative interruption recovery: recognize work that is already complete, avoid duplicate consequential effects, resume only when mechanically safe, and ask for verification or human escalation when the outcome is unknown.

The difficult distinction is between:

1. authoritative evidence that an operation or effect happened;
2. observational or audit evidence that some state was later seen; and
3. an unknown outcome.

For safe retry, resume, or resend decisions, a model’s inference is not enough. The recovery policy needs an owner-native fact whose chain of custody begins at the component that actually owns the operation or effect. Missing evidence must remain unknown, and authority to perform a recovery action must remain separate from evidence that the action is appropriate.

This is a feature request for discussion, not a security report. OpenClaw’s current documented claims are narrower than the recovery capability we are exploring.

### What we tested

We built and adversarially tested several isolated designs:

- passive current-cut observation of native execution state;
- coherent SQLite/WAL observation and immutable native snapshots;
- explicit historical evidence that never claims currentness;
- immutable positive-event capture with a bounded, fail-open publisher; and
- durable delivery-operation modelling that separates work completion, external effect, delivery, authority, and custody.

The durable-operation concepts were useful, and the capture mechanics could be made nonblocking. The recurring blocker was provenance: a detached observer or immutable sink could preserve bytes, but could not prove that the authority owning the operation created the fact.

### Minimal counterexamples

These counterexamples arose in our own isolated prototypes and fixtures; neither involved OpenClaw's shipped code.

**Self-hashed serialized facts prove integrity, not origin.**

In one fixture, a valid-looking source-binding manifest and delivery-acknowledgement event were synthesized as ordinary serialized objects. Their schemas, canonical bytes, and self-hashes were correct. The reducer accepted them as a positive delivery fact even though no authoritative transaction or owner-native acknowledgement had occurred. Content addressing protected the supplied bytes but did not authenticate who was entitled to create them.

**A legitimate writer can attest to poisoned persisted state.**

In a second fixture, an alternate raw SQLite writer inserted authoritative-looking upstream operation state. A legitimate covered writer later consumed that row and emitted a genuine post-COMMIT fact. The receipt correctly proved what that writer had committed, but not that its causal input originated from the authority that owned the operation.

These cases matter because a false positive can suppress necessary recovery, while a false negative or inferred absence can trigger duplicate work, sends, or tool effects. A useful provenance boundary therefore has to cover the relevant chain of custody, not only the final projection or downstream commit.

### Relevant OpenClaw 2026.10.6 work

Our source reading of OpenClaw 2026.10.6 found what appears to be exactly the right kind of primitive at a scoped boundary: `sqlite-post-commit` together with worker-operation admission stages typed facts during an opted-in SQLite worker operation, exposes them only after commit, and discards staged publication on rollback. Because the live receipt is private to the boundary, ordinary serialized bytes cannot directly mint it.

That looks valuable for the writers that participate. Our reading also suggests that the exact domains needed by our experiment are not yet covered sufficiently:

- conversation/outbound delivery does not appear to expose durable owner-native provenance for operation creation, submission acceptance, and delivery acknowledgement;
- the adjacent subagent-completion receipt appears authentic in our reading but does not appear to establish the full work-completion/custody conjunction our policy requires; and
- generic mutating tool effects do not appear to expose a durable invocation-bound owner acknowledgement of “effect applied” versus “outcome unknown.”

We may have missed an existing owner-native mechanism and would welcome correction. We do not interpret the absence of these stronger semantics as a defect: OpenClaw’s operational recovery behavior appropriately treats uncertain outcomes conservatively, and the current committed-facts work appears intentionally scoped.

### Feature direction / question

Would OpenClaw be interested in evolving the existing committed-facts boundary into an optional durable provenance primitive for a small set of consequential operations?

The intended primitive would not need to prove complete execution history or current state; positive owner-native facts for selected consequential operations would already be useful.

### Alternatives considered

We considered leaving provenance entirely downstream and observational, but that cannot authenticate origin. Full writer confinement and database/ACL redesign could establish stronger guarantees but would be disproportionately invasive for the narrow use case. Always escalating every interrupted operation is safe, but discards useful positive evidence and leaves duplicate-effect prevention entirely manual. A scoped extension of the existing committed-facts boundary appears to be the smallest direction worth discussing, subject to maintainer views on core versus plugin scope.

Possible requirements for discussion:

- a fact can be created only by the authoritative owner path;
- publication occurs only after transaction commit or an equivalent owner acknowledgement;
- the fact binds operation/invocation identity, source/domain identity, and the exact effect or affected resource where applicable;
- alternate raw writers cannot manufacture equivalent authoritative evidence or poison inputs that a covered writer will attest without detection;
- missing evidence remains explicitly unknown and cannot be interpreted as non-occurrence;
- provenance survives serialization and restart where the recovery policy needs detached consumption;
- restore, replacement, rollback, incarnation, and replay semantics are explicit;
- an external observer is never on the native execution critical path; and
- provenance does not itself grant recovery authority.

Potential first domains might be outbound delivery, completion/custody transfer, and selected mutating tool effects. We are not proposing that every database mutation receive a signed event, nor prescribing cryptographic signing as the solution. Structural writer confinement, a private durable sink, authenticated receipts, or another core-native mechanism may fit OpenClaw better.

### Why this may be useful upstream

A small owner-native provenance primitive could support capabilities beyond our Control Centre:

- conservative crash and interruption recovery;
- duplicate-send and duplicate-effect prevention;
- clearer operator inspection of “completed,” “delivery uncertain,” and “effect unknown” states;
- safer long-running and autonomous agents;
- model-independent recovery policy; and
- a clean distinction between useful audit telemetry and authoritative receipts.

It could also let plugins and external control planes consume a deliberately narrow trusted interface without opening mutable native SQLite stores or inferring authority from projections.

### Questions for maintainers

1. Is durable execution provenance a direction already contemplated for the existing committed-facts/post-COMMIT boundary?
2. Is there an existing owner-native mechanism for conversation delivery, full work completion, or mutating tool effects that our source audit may have missed?
3. How do maintainers think about preventing a legitimate downstream writer from attesting to poisoned state introduced through an alternate or raw writer?
4. Would extending committed facts into a small set of consequential owner-native domains fit OpenClaw core architecture, or is this intentionally outside core scope and better handled by a plugin or external system?
5. Would maintainers prefer a narrower RFC/issue around outbound delivery provenance first?

We have reproducible adversarial fixtures and more detailed technical notes available if they would help, but have intentionally kept them out of this initial proposal.

issues.title: [Bug]: Control UI 2026.11.5 Sessions sidebar renders only agent headers - grouping defaults to 'category' with no exposed control

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Normal backlog priority with limited blast radius.

labels.name: impact:ux-friction
labels.description: User-facing flow adds avoidable confusion or support burden without fully blocking progress.

issues.body:
## Summary

On 2026.11.5 the Control UI **Sessions** sidebar renders only the agent headers (`RPK-16`, `QQ 潘多拉`) and **no session rows**, even with the owner filter set to **All owners** and **Status: All**. Clicking an agent row does nothing, and the console shows no functional error (only avatar 404/401 and performance violations).

The grouping mode is stored client-side (`openclaw:sidebar:sessions:grouping`) and **defaults to `category`**, but the Sessions filter panel exposes no control to change it. So a user whose sessions have no `category` cannot get a flat list through the UI at all.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| OpenClaw | `2026.11.5 (e13cf15)`, npm global |
| OS | Windows 11 `10.0.26300` |
| Node | v24.22.1 |
| Agents | 2 (`main`, `qq-lite`) |
| Sessions in store | 23 (`openclaw sessions list --json`) |

## Reproduction

1. Have a multi-agent install with sessions that have no `category`/section assignment.
2. Open the Control UI, Sessions view.
3. Set owner filter **All owners**, Status **All**, enable automation/system sessions.
4. Observe: only the 2 agent rows render; 23 sessions do not.

## Evidence

### 1) The server returns all 23 rows

```powershell
openclaw gateway call sessions.list --params '{"source":"agent-roster","rowMode":"sidebar","limit":100,"offset":0}' --json
```

```json
{ "count": 23, "totalCount": 23, "sessions": [ ... 23 items ... ], "owners": [ { "id": "gateway-owner", ... } ] }
```

The gateway log for the UI's own request agrees:

```
⇄ res ✓ sessions.list 1835ms source=agent-roster rowMode=sidebar limit=100 offset=0
  filterKind=includeGlobal+includeUnknown+configuredAgentsOnly+archived bytes=71619
{"operation":"sessions.list","selectedRowCount":48,"materializedRowCount":25,"handlerOutcome":"returned"}
```

### 2) Sidebar rows carry no `agentId`

`rowMode=sidebar` row fields:

```
key, kind, updatedAt, sessionId, rowMode, participants, expandedParticipants,
lastReadAt, lastInteractionAt, lastActivityAt, lifecycleRevision,
childSessions, sharedFacts
```

No `agentId`. The default CLI mode (`openclaw sessions list --json`) **does** include it (`"agentId": "main"`), so the client cannot group by agent from the payload alone.

### 3) The two visible rows are the agents, not sessions

```
openclaw agents list
- qq-lite (QQ 潘多拉（受限）)
- main (default) (RPK-16（潘多拉）)
```

These match the two sidebar rows exactly. Their subtitles are last-message previews, which makes them look like conversations.

### 4) Grouping defaults to `category` and has no UI control

In `dist/control-ui/assets/control-ui-boot-shared-*.js`:

```js
function Pme(e){return e===`none`||e===`person`||e===`project`?e:`category`}
function Fme(e,t={}){let n=t.grouping??`category` ...}
if (n===`none`){i.push(t);continue}
```

Storage keys present in the same bundle:

```
openclaw:sidebar:sessions:grouping
openclaw:sidebar:sessions:catalog-grouping
openclaw:sidebar:sessions:sort-mode
openclaw:sidebar:sessions:collapsed-sections
```

The **Display** section of the Sessions filter panel only offers: sort by, message preview, **+ New section**, session source. There is no grouping selector, although `docs/web/control-ui/sessions-and-sidebar.md` documents grouping as a Display setting.

### 5) Workaround that works

In the browser console:

```js
localStorage.setItem('openclaw:sidebar:sessions:grouping','none');
localStorage.removeItem('openclaw:sidebar:sessions:collapsed-sections');
location.reload();
```

After this, sessions list flat. This confirms the data and the render path are fine — only the default and the missing control are wrong.

## Expected behavior

One of:

- Default `grouping` to `none` (or to a mode that still lists sessions with no category), or
- Expose the grouping selector in the Sessions **Display** panel (matching the documented behavior), or
- Render the `ungrouped` bucket when it is non-empty rather than leaving only agent headers.

## Notes

- Related but distinct: #198515 (roster headers ignore "Last updated" sort), #196664 (group-first "All owners" view).
- Local dist patch used to confirm the cause (not a source proposal): changing the two `category` defaults to `none` in the bundle restores a flat list without any localStorage key.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

When a scheduled automation run calls `automations` `record_result` through the Tool Search dispatcher a second time with the same result, the run ends with a bare `⚠️ Tool Call failed` chat bubble. The bubble does not name the real tool and does not give a reason.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Use a Tool Search-enabled agent, where deferred tools are called through `dispatch_action`, and a recurring automation that resumes a session.
2. In the automation turn, the model calls `dispatch_action({ id: "automations", args: { action: "record_result", outcome: "no_change" } })`. The call succeeds.
3. In the same turn, the model makes the identical call again. It is rejected with `record_result already accepted for this automation run`.
4. The turn ends with no assistant text.

### Expected behavior

- Repeating the result that was already accepted changes nothing, so it should not be reported as a failure.
- Any failure notice that is shown should name the called tool (`Automations`), not the dispatcher (`Tool Call`). Tool Search chat rows already do this (#163829, #165095).

### Actual behavior

The automation completion posts a standalone assistant bubble that reads only `⚠️ Tool Call failed`. It has no tool name and no reason. Observed twice on 2026-11-19, in two wakes of the same automation, at 14:37 and 15:47 PST. The user could not tell that the failure was harmless, because the first result had already been saved.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.5 (3eee09d)

### Operating system

Linux 6.8 (Ubuntu)

### Install method

Source checkout

### Model

anthropic/claude-opus-5-5

### Provider / routing chain

clawrouter → anthropic

### Additional provider/model setup details

Not provider-specific.

### Logs

Session transcript, abbreviated:

```text
nested tool automations {"action":"record_result","outcome":"no_change"} -> {"ok":true,"outcome":"no_change"}
nested tool automations {"action":"record_result","outcome":"no_change"} -> isError: "record_result already accepted for this automation run"
toolResult dispatch_action -> {"status":"error","tool":"dispatch_action","error":"record_result already accepted for this automation run"}
assistant (model "automation-result"): "⚠️ Tool Call failed"
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Root cause at [`ede5c7d5fa5f`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/tree/ede5c7d5fa5f0da8ff6dfc71404b1c3d00839525):

1. **The duplicate is a hard error.** [`createAutomationResultRecorder`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/ede5c7d5fa5f0da8ff6dfc71404b1c3d00839525/src/infra/agent-run-registry.automation.ts#L117-L140) throws on any second `record_result`, even when it is identical to the accepted one.
2. **The run has no reply, so the guard warns.** The no-reply guard in [`payloads.ts`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/ede5c7d5fa5f0da8ff6dfc71404b1c3d00839525/src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/payloads.ts#L491-L502) calls `buildFailureWarning`. [`hasMeaningfulAutomationResult`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/ede5c7d5fa5f0da8ff6dfc71404b1c3d00839525/src/infra/agent-run-registry.automation.ts#L69-L74) excludes `no_change` on purpose, so the earlier recorded result does not count as a reply.
3. **The warning uses the dispatcher label.** [`buildFailureWarning`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/ede5c7d5fa5f0da8ff6dfc71404b1c3d00839525/src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/tool-error-warning.ts#L12-L91) resolves the label from the raw tool name, `dispatch_action`, and gets [`"Tool Call"`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/ede5c7d5fa5f0da8ff6dfc71404b1c3d00839525/src/agents/tool-display-config.ts#L212-L214). The failure summary does not keep which tool was called.
4. **The reason is hidden.** Error text appears only at `verboseLevel: "full"`. This is the deliberate default and is covered by existing tests.

### Introducing changes

- #137775 (2026-09-04) made the no-reply `⚠️ <tool> failed` guard unconditional.
- #163829 and #165095 (2026-10-02 and 2026-10-04) taught chat rows in the UI and native apps to show Tool Search calls as the called tool. They did not change the failure warning, which still shows the dispatcher label. That label has existed since Tool Search (#79823) and was carried over when the dispatcher was renamed to `dispatch_action` in #169552.
- #186652 (2026-10-28) deliberately keeps the warning for `no_change` automation runs. This is why the duplicate reaches the user in an unattended run.

Related: #160785 and #194437 show the same class of problem, where a rejected self-scoped automation call leaks a generic warning.

### Impact and severity

Low severity, but confusing. Unattended runs post an unexplained failure bubble even though nothing failed.

### Additional information

Proposed fix:

- Accept an identical repeat of the accepted result idempotently. A different second result is still rejected.
- Carry the called tool's name on the failure summary so the warning names `Automations`.

issues.body:
## Summary

Discord realtime voice (and Voice Call / Gateway relay) on GA OpenAI realtime models (`gpt-realtime-2.1`, `gpt-realtime-2.1-mini`, `gpt-realtime-2`) only works with an OpenAI Platform API key. An install signed in with ChatGPT (OpenClaw's `openai` OAuth profile) and no Platform key cannot use them: OpenAI is not offered as a configured realtime provider, and starting the bridge fails with "OpenAI Realtime voice requires an OpenAI Platform API key".

Browser Talk already runs these GA models on the same ChatGPT sign-in (#115623). The direct backend socket that Discord uses is the only GA route still limited to Platform keys.

## Why it can work now

#115211 removed an earlier OAuth fallback after a live check where the WebSocket answered "realtime conversation requires API key auth". A live check on 2026-11-20 shows the socket now accepts a ChatGPT sign-in when the request carries the account id:

- `wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?model=gpt-realtime-2.1` (no `call_id`), `Authorization: Bearer <ChatGPT access token>`, `chatgpt-account-id: <account>`, `originator: openclaw` → `101`, `session.created`, `session.update` accepted.
- A Discord-style session (server VAD with `create_response: false`, `silence_duration_ms`, `reasoning.effort`, the `openclaw_agent_consult` tool): real speech was transcribed exactly, a forced `tool_choice` produced `openclaw_agent_consult({"question":"What's on my calendar today?"})`, and the tool result was spoken back.
- Same results on `gpt-realtime-2.1-mini`.

## Proposal

Keep Platform auth first. When no Platform credential source is configured, let the direct GA socket to `api.openai.com` use the ChatGPT OAuth profile and send its `chatgpt-account-id`. A configured but unavailable Platform key keeps failing, custom `baseUrl` endpoints never receive the OAuth token, and GPT-Live keeps its own routes.

Related: #154468 (closed as stale, `needs-product-decision`), #115211, #115623.

issues.body:
### Summary

Automatically dismiss OpenClaw's already-delivered browser/PWA agent-completion notifications once their corresponding messages have loaded and actually been viewed in the foreground on that browser.

### Problem to solve

Using the Chrome-installed OpenClaw PWA on Android, I can open the app normally, switch between sessions and read the replies, yet still have roughly 10–20 completion notifications accumulated in the phone's notification shade. Reading the conversation and clearing its stale notifications become separate chores.

This is a user observation, not a fresh controlled reproduction. The installation was previously reported as OpenClaw 2026.11.5; its exact current version has not been reverified. This request concerns browser/PWA notifications, not the native Android application's notification system.

### Proposed solution

When a corresponding completion message is loaded and visibly presented in a foreground chat pane, close its already-delivered notification in that browser's service-worker registration.

- Cover ordinary app opening, session switching, and returning to the foreground/unlocking—not only notification clicks.
- Do not clear on navigation, session selection, history loading alone, hidden/prepared transcript rows, or merely having the app open.
- Preserve other sessions, off-screen/unseen messages, newer completions and other notification categories.
- Handle delayed push arrival and view-versus-push races without dismissing a newer unseen event.
- Restrict dismissal to notifications owned by this OpenClaw browser registration. No access to arbitrary phone notifications or promise of cross-device recall.

**Implementation possibilities to investigate (not an implemented or device-tested solution):**

1. **Page-driven exact-match dismissal.** After actual message visibility is confirmed, obtain the existing registration, enumerate its notifications with [`ServiceWorkerRegistration.getNotifications()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/ServiceWorkerRegistration/getNotifications), and call [`Notification.close()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Notification/close) only for conclusively matched completion events. MDN documents this scope and explicitly identifies already-read messaging notifications as a valid use of `close()`.
2. **Worker-coordinated reconciliation.** Send an exact seen-event acknowledgment from the foreground UI to the existing worker, which can reconcile outstanding notifications and late deliveries. This could address the race where enumeration finishes before a queued push appears; any retained acknowledgment state, lifetime and upgrade behavior need design and validation.

Current source offers useful starting points, but also an identity gap:

- [Gateway event push owner](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c9285dde971f6487e228aca1587d65fae90aa5de/src/gateway/event-web-push.ts#L84) builds completion tags as `openclaw-agent-finished-${runId}` and supplies a session navigation URL.
- [Service-worker push/click owner](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c9285dde971f6487e228aca1587d65fae90aa5de/ui/public/sw.js#L619) preserves the tag, but stores only `url` and `explicitUrl` in notification data; its click handler already closes the clicked notification.
- [Browser subscription runtime](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c9285dde971f6487e228aca1587d65fae90aa5de/ui/src/app/web-push.runtime.ts) already obtains the existing service-worker registration.
- Open PR #200911 has a [message-visibility hook](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/bd689fab92c1d8f282315b63dca93169b43186da/ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-mention-read.ts) that checks presented rows, foreground visibility, intersection and message/session/agent identity. That is useful related work, not a dependency or an already-shipped browser-notification solution.

Investigate whether persisted transcript messages can reliably map to the existing completion run tags. If not, propagate minimal unambiguous session + completion/message identity through the push payload and worker notification data. A session URL alone cannot distinguish older read completions from newer unseen ones. Prefer exact seen IDs; use a loaded/seen watermark only if authoritative ordering proves all covered messages were actually seen—loading history or viewing the newest message must not implicitly mark skipped messages read. Unknown/legacy identities should remain untouched rather than be broadly cleared.

### Alternatives considered

- Manually swipe notifications away: works, but repeats work after reading.
- Disable completion notifications: loses useful background alerts.
- Suppress future pushes while viewing a session: helpful, but does not remove earlier deliveries.
- Clear every notification for a session when opening it: risks losing newer or unseen events.
- A plugin: worth considering if appropriate UI/worker hooks exist, but this lifecycle spans the bundled transcript visibility and browser service-worker owners; no suitable plugin hook was established in this investigation.

### Impact

Affected: browser/PWA users who receive completion notifications and later read replies through normal app navigation.

Severity: recurring notification clutter and manual cleanup, not a reported workflow blocker. A batch of roughly 10–20 accumulated notifications was observed; frequency has not been measured. Stale alerts make genuinely unread work harder to identify.

### Evidence/examples

Related, not dependencies or proof of this solution:

- Merged #183535 suppresses future completion pushes to a device already viewing the session; it does not dismiss older deliveries.
- Open #200911 clears in-app mention entries after viewing their source messages and explicitly excludes browser/OS notification history.
- Open #133393 proposes focus-aware future delivery modes, rather than read-based removal of already-delivered notifications.
- #170854 / #170859 concern notification previews, a separate improvement.

Suggested validation for an eventual implementation: read A and retain B; preserve a newer unseen completion in A; delayed push after viewing; failed/partial history load; off-screen rows; session switching during asynchronous enumeration; foreground return/unlock; worker restart/update; missing legacy identity. Actual Chrome/Android PWA testing remains necessary.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes. We plan to develop a linked PR, with implementation and validation in an isolated checkout. No implementation has begun yet.

### Additional information

The source investigation above is pinned to `c9285dde971f6487e228aca1587d65fae90aa5de`; the related visibility hook is from the separately identified open PR head. API documentation and source inspection establish plausible implementation routes, not end-to-end proof. No code changes, builds or new device tests were performed.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The active-transcript byte count that `maxActiveTranscriptBytes` is compared against includes every `openclaw.system-prompt` checkpoint: the whole system prompt plus the tool surface (`tools`, `toolPolicy`, `publicationListing`). That entry isn't conversation, and compaction can't remove or shrink it, and a new one is written after each compaction because the tool pin is tied to `historyId`.

So on a setup with many tools the checkpoint alone uses a large share of the cap:
- Byte-triggered compaction fires while the actual conversation is still far below the cap.
- Right after a compaction the measured size is checkpoint + summary + kept tail, which can still be over the cap. `recordCompactionAccounting` then sets `transcriptByteCompactionLatch`, and every following turn posts the `context_bounded` notice ("Continuing with bounded recent context… resend any earlier details…") until the chat grows by another full cap.

Reported on a real setup with about 200 MCP tools: the checkpoint was about 150 KB, and two chats measured about 273 KB and 429 KB right after compaction against a 256 KB cap. Both latched and showed the notice on every reply.

### Steps to reproduce

Appended to `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-projection-facts.test.ts`, using that file's own `fixture`, `user` and `assistant`:

```ts
it("counts a system-prompt checkpoint as active transcript bytes", async () => {
  await withOpenClawTestState({ scenario: "minimal" }, async () => {
    const checkpoint = {
      type: "custom", id: "sp", parentId: "assistant",
      customType: "openclaw.system-prompt",
      data: { prefix: "x".repeat(150_000), routeKey: "r", historyId: "h" },
    };
    const f = fixture([user, assistant, checkpoint]);
    const result = readProjection(f.database, f.scope, (projection) =>
      readSessionTranscriptAccountingFromProjection(projection, { includeByteSize: true, includeUsage: false }),
    );
    console.log(result);
  });
});
```

Output on both refs: `{ kind: "value", value: { byteSize: 150339, eventCount: 3 } }`. The two conversation events are 198 bytes and the checkpoint is 150,141, so 99.9% of the measured "active transcript" is the saved prompt.

**Where it happens**

1. `persistSessionSystemPrompt` (`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/session-prompt-state.ts`) appends the `openclaw.system-prompt` custom entry with the prompt and tool surface.
2. `transcriptEventContextEligibility` (`src/config/sessions/session-transcript-projection-append.ts`) returns 1 for any entry that isn't a message with `excludeFromContext`, so the checkpoint row is `context_eligible = 1`.
3. `readVisibleTranscriptStats` sums `serialized_bytes` of context-eligible rows. `readCompactionTranscriptBytes` (`src/agents/compaction-transcript-bytes.ts`) uses that as compaction pressure, and corrects it only for expired Anthropic runtime context.
4. `runSessionCompactionIfNeeded` (`src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-memory.ts`) compares that with the cap before and after compaction, and sets the latch when the post-compaction size is still over it.

### Expected behavior

Compaction pressure should measure what compaction can actually shrink. One option is for `readCompactionTranscriptBytes`, which already exists to "correct compaction pressure without changing raw storage or acquisition accounting", to leave `openclaw.system-prompt` checkpoints out, the same way it leaves out expired runtime context. Raw storage accounting can stay as it is.

### Actual behavior

Measured active-transcript bytes include the `openclaw.system-prompt` checkpoint: in the repro above, 150,339 bytes are reported for 198 bytes of conversation. With the cap set, byte compaction fires early, and a freshly compacted chat can still measure over the cap, latch, and post the `context_bounded` notice before every reply.

### OpenClaw version

main 0eb1fa3f747 and 2026.11.6 (06afb10)

### Operating system

Linux (Ubuntu 24.04), source checkout

### Install method

source checkout, vitest

### Model

Not model-specific (byte accounting runs before the provider call)

### Provider / routing chain

Not provider-specific

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell

```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: any setup with `agents.defaults.compaction.maxActiveTranscriptBytes` set, more so with many tools
Severity: annoying (early compaction and a repeated warning, no data loss)
Frequency: every turn of a latched chat
Consequence: summaries run sooner than the cap intends; the user is told to resend earlier details on every reply

Workaround: Raise `maxActiveTranscriptBytes` well above the checkpoint size (for example 768 KB instead of 256 KB).

### Additional information

- #196475: the same latch, caused by image tool results that compaction can't shrink. Its expected-behavior note ("measure only bytes that are model-visible after the last compaction boundary") would cover this too.
- #196551 (open PR): ties the `context_bounded` notice to actual host omissions. It fixes the notice, but byte compaction would still fire early and the latch would still be set.
- #201384: notification policy for repeated bounded-context notices (needs a product decision).

issues.body:
**Version:** 2026.11.10-beta.1 (995f905), macOS 27.2 arm64, Node 26.13.0

**Symptom**
Scheduled agent turns on an OpenAI/Codex model fail before the run starts with:
`Cannot inspect Codex processes. Process identity is unavailable or invalid. Check /proc on Linux or native process inspection on macOS, then retry.`
This happens most often in the minutes around a Gateway restart (twice today, ~4 min after restart and during a deferred restart). Recurring jobs then wait for their next occurrence (only error backoff, no immediate retry), so a 2-hourly job is skipped for 2 hours.

**Cause (from dist source)**
`service-child-group-ownership` → `census()` lists every process on the host and filters with `hasReadableTopology`. If a listed process has `parentPid`/`processGroupId`/`state` undefined but `readProcessIdentity(pid)` still succeeds (a process that is mid-spawn or mid-exit), it throws `DarwinProcessInspectionError("unavailable")` instead of skipping that process. `readDarwinProcessTree` uses the unfiltered census, so one unrelated transient process anywhere on the machine aborts the Codex app-server start. Restarts spawn and reap many workers, which makes the race likely.

**Expected**
A transient, unrelated process with incomplete topology should be skipped (or the census retried once within the deadline), and only processes in the requested tree should be able to fail inspection.

**Related:** #138043 (concurrent starts exceeding the inspection deadline — a different failure reason, `deadline` vs `unavailable`).

**Workaround we use:** an external watcher re-runs idempotent jobs once after this specific error.

issues.body:
### Bug type
Regression / incomplete fix of #174089 (previously closed)

### Environment
- OpenClaw: **2026.11.5**
- macOS on Apple Silicon; case-insensitive filesystem
- Upgrade path: 2026.10.4 → 2026.11.5
- Five configured agents; Codex plugin installed but unavailable

### Summary
The previously reported `BA-EA` / `ba-ea` SQLite case-alias issue (#174089) remains observable after upgrading to 2026.11.5. OpenClaw Doctor now reports an **invalid update recovery database identity** for the BA-EA agent, while the Codex plugin's deferred state migration remains **pending**, preventing Codex-powered agents from running.

The connection between the recovery identity failure and Codex's pending migration is **suspected, not proven**.

### Confirmed evidence
1. On the macOS filesystem, `~/.openclaw/agents/BA-EA/` and `~/.openclaw/agents/ba-ea/` resolve to **the same directory inode (9032093)**.
2. The corresponding `openclaw-agent.sqlite` paths resolve to **the same file inode (9264648)**. These are aliases, not two separate databases.
3. Running `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive --full-integrity-check` reports:
   ```
   Pre-repair recovery copy was unavailable: Original update capture failed
   Invalid update recovery database identity: .../.openclaw/agents/BA-EA/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
   ```
4. The shared-state SQLite `migration_runs` record remains:
   ```
   deferred-plugin-migration:codex | pending | finished_at=NULL
   ```
5. Doctor continues to report `Plugin "codex" data/settings upgrade is unfinished` and `Plugin codex tool schemas were not inspected because registration failed`.
6. The five agent databases were detected at expected schema version 38 and earlier SQLite integrity checks passed. Existing state and backups have been preserved; no manual SQLite edits.

### Impact
Codex runtime remains unavailable, so configured Codex-powered agents cannot execute normally. Repeated Doctor repair attempts have not resolved the migration.

### Expected behavior
Migration/recovery should recognize case-insensitive filesystem aliases of the same physical SQLite database, or provide a supported recovery path without trapping an otherwise healthy agent installation in a pending migration state.

### Maintainer questions
- Does the fix associated with #174089 cover **update recovery database identity checks** in 2026.11.5, or only the earlier Telegram offset/session migration failure?
- Can the BA-EA recovery identity failure prevent completion of the deferred Codex migration, or are these independent problems?
- What is the safe, supported, non-destructive recovery procedure that preserves all agents, sessions, and credentials?

Related: #174089; possibly #201337.

I can provide sanitized Doctor output and run targeted read-only diagnostics if helpful.

issues.body:
### Summary

Pick a new progress label each time a status starts, like Claude Code's spinner words, instead of the same one for every turn in a conversation. Either pick at random from `streaming.progress.labels`, or let a plugin hook choose.

### Problem to solve

I gave my assistant on Matrix her own progress labels so her status messages feel like her:

```json5
{
  channels: {
    matrix: {
      streaming: {
        mode: "progress",
        progress: {
          label: "auto",
          labels: ["Divining", "Conjuring", "Squinting", "Scrying"],
        },
      },
    },
  },
}
```

Every turn in her room shows the same one. Earlier, with ten labels, I only ever saw one of those too.

The label is picked from a hash of a seed, and the chat channels seed with the account and conversation: Matrix uses the account and room, Discord and Slack the account and channel, Telegram the account, chat and topic. So the same room always lands on the same entry in the pool. In a room you use every day, a pool of four works like a single fixed label.

### Proposed solution

Either of these would work for me.

**1. Pick from the pool at random when a status starts.** Same config as above, no new key.

- The pick holds for every edit of that status (and across reconnects while it's up), so it doesn't flicker.
- The next status picks again. It can repeat; it just isn't locked to the room.
- No change when there's no custom pool (the built-in default stays plain `Working`, #107260), when `label` is a fixed string, or when it's `false`.

The docs already read this way: a custom pool is "picked at random/by seed" (`docs/concepts/progress-drafts.md`).

**2. A hook that picks the label before the status starts.** The plugin returns the label, or nothing to fall back to the config. That leaves the choice to whoever writes the plugin: a list of their own, something based on the time of day or the agent, or even asking a model.

```ts
api.on("progress_label", (event, ctx) => {
  // event: { channel, accountId, agentId, sessionKey, labels }
  const words = ["Divining", "Conjuring", "Squinting", "Scrying"];
  return { label: words[Math.floor(Math.random() * words.length)] };
});
```

(The hook name and fields are just an example.)

Why I think it's worth it:

- **It makes an existing setting pay off.** Setting a pool is already the opt-in. Today it mostly behaves like `label` set to one word.
- **It's shared.** Matrix, Discord, Telegram, Teams and Mattermost drafts all resolve the label through `resolveChannelProgressDraftLabel` in `src/channels/streaming.ts`, so either option is one change in one place. The label is resolved again on each render today, so the pick would need to be kept with the draft.
- **It works per agent.** Streaming settings are scoped per channel and per account, so two agents on their own bot accounts can each have their own pool, and a hook gets the agent in its context.
- **Nothing changes for anyone who doesn't use it.** No custom pool and no hook means today's behavior.

### Alternatives considered

- **A new opt-in key, e.g. `streaming.progress.labelRotation: "turn"`.** Keeps today's behavior as the default, but adds config for something the pool already expresses.
- **Set one fixed `streaming.progress.label`.** Works, but then the pool does nothing.
- **An existing hook.** I didn't find one for the label pick. `message_sending` and `reply_payload_sending` rewrite sends and reply payloads, not the label.
- **Have the agent's own model pick a word every turn.** Fun, but it spends tokens on every turn for a cosmetic label. With option 2, anyone who wants that can do it in their own plugin.

### Impact

- Affected: anyone with a custom `streaming.progress.labels` pool on a chat channel.
- Severity: low, cosmetic.
- Frequency: every turn.
- Consequence: the pool shows one entry per conversation, so the personality it's meant to add doesn't show up.

### Evidence/examples

- Seeds on main: Matrix `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/monitor/handler-draft-controller.ts` (`${accountId}:${roomId}`), Discord `message-handler.draft-preview.ts` (`${accountId}:${deliverChannelId}`), Slack `dispatch-progress.ts` (`${accountId}:${channel}`), Telegram `bot-message-dispatch-progress.ts` (account, chat, topic), Teams `reply-stream-controller.ts` ("Stable label rotation across reconnects, typically `${accountId}:${convId}`").
- `selectProgressLabel` (`src/shared/progress-labels.ts`) hashes the seed modulo the pool size.
- Slack's native cards and Feishu's cards build their titles another way, so they're out of scope.
- Related: #107111 picked a Control UI label per run, kept stable within the run. #107260 made `Working` the only built-in default and kept custom pools. #94850 kept themed labels out of the default.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

Separate from #132781 (using commentary as the progress headline).

issues.body:
### Summary

Realtime voice sessions never record the realtime provider's token usage, so session usage and cost reports leave out the realtime spend, which is usually the largest part of a voice session's bill.

### Problem

OpenAI Realtime sends `response.done` with `response.usage` for every response: input tokens split into text, audio and image, cached input tokens, and output tokens split into text and audio. The OpenAI realtime bridge (`extensions/openai/realtime-voice-bridge.ts`) reads only `status` and `status_details` from that event and drops `usage`. No other path records realtime usage.

As a result, `sessions.usage`, `usage.cost`, `/usage cost` and Control UI Usage show the agent consult turns behind a voice session but nothing for the realtime model itself. The realtime model is the part billed to the OpenAI API key, and audio tokens are priced several times higher than text.

Observed on a Discord voice setup (`gpt-realtime-2.1`, bidi mode): about 93 minutes of assistant speech and more than 100 consults over two days, with zero realtime usage recorded anywhere.

### Proposed fix

- Give realtime bridges a provider-neutral usage callback that reports, once per provider response, the billing provider and model, response id, outcome status, and the token split.
- The OpenAI bridge reads `response.usage` on every `response.done`, including cancelled responses and responses that finish on a connection already replaced by session rotation, because those are billed too.
- Core records each report in the voice session's transcript as a hidden, usage-only assistant row under the provider and realtime model. The response id is the idempotency key, so retries and replays cannot double-count. Session usage and cost reports then show a realtime model row next to the consult model.
- Wire it into Discord voice, the Talk gateway relay, Control UI Talk with Gateway control, and Voice Call.

### Out of scope / follow-ups

- **Audio pricing:** the model price table has only text/cache rates, and no realtime model has a catalog price, so realtime rows show tokens but stay unpriced. Pricing audio correctly needs audio input/output rates in the shared cost model.
- **Azure OpenAI realtime:** it bills outside the OpenAI catalog, so labelling its usage `openai` would be wrong.
- **GPT-Live** (quicksilver wire) does not report usage.
- **Meeting bot:** its only session is a consult subagent session that may not exist yet.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Summary

In v2026.10.10, a normal Codex session can continue receiving automatic “Advance the active goal” inputs while waiting for explicit human authorization, but cannot report a stopping Goal status: the Codex dynamic-tool filter excludes the Core Goal tools while native Codex Goals are disabled.

### Version / environment

- OpenClaw: 2026.10.10; Codex plugin: 2026.10.10.
- Linux, npm installation, local Codex harness, WebChat.
- Observed November 4, 2026.
- No private transcript, configuration dump, or account/session identifiers included.

### Reproduction

1. Use a local Codex session with the normal native tool surface and an active OpenClaw Goal.
2. Reach work that requires explicit human authorization before the next effect (for example, a browser configuration change). Leave that authorization pending.
3. The assistant asks for authorization and ends the turn without performing the effect.
4. Observe repeated automatic Goal-continuation inputs and repeated waiting replies, with no progress.
5. Inspect the actual model-callable tool catalog, including deferred tools: `get_goal`, `create_goal`, and `update_goal` are absent, although Goal context instructs the model to use `update_goal`.

The repeated waiting replies were reported by the operator. The affected session's full history was not independently inspected because session-tree visibility rejected access. The tool-catalog omission and the filter/runner mechanics below were independently checked; this is not a claim of a pristine end-to-end reproduction on current main.

### Expected behavior

The model must have a policy-permitted status path to the **Core Goal store used by the continuation runner**. Once an explicit-human-decision wait is recorded, preserve the unfinished Goal and suppress unchanged automatic Goal wakeups, including stale queued nudges at admission, until an actual authorized decision/resume occurs. Automatic continuation must never count as authorization.

A structured `waiting_on_human` state or an equivalent durable blocker reason would make this unambiguous. This is an acceptance requirement, not a claim that this status already exists.

### Evidence / smallest failing transition

Release source:

- [`dynamic-tool-profile.ts` at v2026.10.10](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.10.10/extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-profile.ts) classifies `get_goal`, `create_goal`, and `update_goal` as `"goal"` replacements and excludes them unless the native surface is disabled.
- The installed corresponding `buildCodexRuntimeThreadConfig` explicitly sets `"features.goals": false`. Thus the excluded Core tools have no native Goal replacement in the observed model surface.
- Core constructs all three Goal tools, but its model-updatable status enum is only `["complete", "blocked"]`; `waiting_on_human` is not currently supported.
- In Core's `goal-continuation.ts`, `isGoalContinuationCurrent` requires the persisted Goal to be `active`. A prose waiting reply does not mutate that state. `isGoalContinuationOutcome` recognizes a deterministic approval-prompt signal, but an ordinary model-written authorization question does not itself provide a durable Goal status transition.

An isolated test of the installed pure filter reproduced omission of all three Goal tools on the normal native surface. Removing only the implicit Goal exclusion preserved explicit `codexDynamicToolsExclude` entries and shell filtering in the tested cases. This was an offline candidate test, not an applied fix or a live runtime canary.

### Upstream disposition / related work

Current main's `dynamic-tool-profile.ts` no longer lists the three Goal tools as native exclusions. The relevant change is already present in merged #175918 (`eec35949bda1f0bec80ea6a4c45e74ae25a3f4f5`); the release tag still contains the exclusion. Comparing that commit to v2026.10.10 reports diverged history, so this report does not claim the mainline fix is included in the latest release. Please consider the release/backport boundary as well as the human-wait behavior.

Related but not the same symptom: #177351 (continuation/recovery), #186928 (missing continuation after length termination). This report concerns unwanted continuation with no usable Goal status handoff, not failure to resume or output-limit handling.

### Suggested acceptance checks

- Normal local/worker Codex tool projection exposes the permitted Core Goal status tool even when native Codex Goals are disabled; explicit policy denials remain effective.
- An explicit approval wait can be recorded immediately and durably without marking the Goal complete, deleting it, or requiring repeated identical authorization requests.
- Turn settlement and admission both respect that wait, including a Goal nudge queued before the state change and after restart/reconnect.
- Missing/denied Goal status capability fails visibly without an endless unchanged-nudge loop or policy widening.
- A real authorized decision/resume can continue the same Goal; automated inputs, unrelated messages, and a rejected decision do not grant authorization.
