prs.title: feat: offer Sign in with ChatGPT first when connecting OpenAI
prs.body:
Closes #201406

## What Problem This Solves

Someone connecting OpenAI for the first time is steered to Codex login. Codex login (device code) is the only OpenAI sign-in shown up front in first-run Model Setup and macOS onboarding, and the first OpenAI choice in `openclaw onboard`, Settings → Models and the Android app; Profile → Connected accounts and `openclaw models accounts login openai` list Codex browser login first. Codex login runs on the Codex backend, where the models a user sees depend on the Codex version OpenClaw reports. Sign in with ChatGPT uses the documented public OpenAI API for the same ChatGPT plan, but it sits under "More sign-in options" or below both Codex logins. The Control UI first-run card (automatic setup) goes further: on a machine with no working connection it installs the Codex plugin and signs the user in with Codex login, so a brand-new user ends up on the Codex harness.

## User Impact

**Moving new users off Codex and onto OpenClaw's own harness is intentional.** New installs default to the OpenClaw harness, which the maintainers actively develop; the Codex harness stays available as an explicit choice. This is not a regression for existing users: nothing changes for anyone already signed in or anyone who picks Codex (list below).

The first-run card on a machine without Codex now offers Sign in with ChatGPT instead of installing Codex. If another detected connection failed for a reason other than credentials, the card still shows **Couldn’t connect your AI** with the failed attempts and offers Sign in with ChatGPT alongside, as main does for Codex login. It no longer installs or prepares the Codex plugin, so setup saves the sign-in on OpenClaw's harness, as guided setup already does for Sign in with ChatGPT. While signing in, the card names the sign-in in a row with the provider icon, built from the Control UI's existing callout and provider-row styles, instead of the provider's technical step title ("OpenAI Codex device code"). A machine where Codex is installed or signed in keeps today's behavior: the card reuses that Codex login or offers Codex login.

Every setup surface lists Sign in with ChatGPT first, with Codex login (device code) right after it and still shown up front, since it needs no localhost callback when the Gateway's browser runs on another machine:

- `openclaw onboard`, Settings → Models → Connect provider, macOS onboarding, the macOS/iOS chat sign-in sheet and Android: Sign in with ChatGPT, Codex login (device code), Codex login (browser), API key.
- First-run Model Setup: still alphabetical by provider, with a provider's options kept together, so OpenAI shows Sign in with ChatGPT and then Codex login (device code).
- Profile → Connected accounts and `openclaw models accounts login`: each provider's methods follow the same order as the other pickers; providers keep their order.
- The OpenAI docs list Sign in with ChatGPT first, and it is the first tab in Getting started.

Nothing changes for anyone already signed in:

- Saved profiles, routes, auth order and the selected model are untouched; there is no migration.
- `openclaw models auth login --provider openai` without `--method` still runs Codex browser login.
- `/login openai` and `/login codex` in chat still use Codex device code.
- Choosing the Codex runtime in setup (the detected "Codex" option) still signs in with Codex login and runs on the Codex harness.
- On a machine with Codex installed or signed in, the first-run card still prepares Codex and uses Codex login.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pickers order sign-ins by the OpenAI manifest's `assistantPriority` and `onboardingFeatured`. Sign in with ChatGPT becomes featured with the lowest OpenAI priority; Codex device code stays featured right after it.

On main, two surfaces ignore that order. First-run Model Setup sorts its rows by label across providers, which puts "Codex login (device code)" under C, above "Sign in with ChatGPT" under S; it now sorts by provider and keeps each provider's rows in the Gateway's order. The Connected-accounts catalog lists methods in manifest order; it now orders each provider's methods by the same priority. The manifest order itself is unchanged, because saved Codex profiles from older releases are labeled by it.

Codex runtime setup must start Codex login even though it is not first, and option order or kind cannot tell which OpenAI choices are Codex login. Provider auth choices get an optional `agentRuntimeLogin` field (documented in the manifest reference). OpenAI sets it to `codex` on its two Codex login choices, and both Codex setup paths start the first marked choice.

On main, automatic setup (`openclaw.setup.auto`) falls through to installing and preparing Codex whenever no detected connection works. When detection finds no Codex CLI, it now returns the first OpenAI browser or device-code sign-in that is not marked as Codex login, which is Sign in with ChatGPT, without installing anything. Codex is never prepared on that path, so the credential save in setup (`setup-inference-credentials.ts`, which pins `codex` only when Codex was prepared) pins `openclaw`.

`openclaw models auth login --provider openai --method siwc` follows the same rule from the terminal. Without Codex plugin settings, the Sign in with ChatGPT method asks for the `openclaw` runtime. The login saves it for the suggested model (`agents.entries.<agent>.models[<model>].agentRuntime`), the same setting guided setup writes, but only when this is the agent's first OpenAI login. That check reads every OpenAI profile the agent could use before the login, including one it inherits from the main agent's shared login, so `--profile-id` naming a new profile or `--force` clearing old ones does not count as a first login. With the Gateway running, the command signs in through the Gateway as a credential-only login; that login keeps the same runtime choice and still leaves the default model alone. An agent that already has an OpenAI login (for example Codex login), Codex plugin settings, or a runtime set for that model keeps what it has. On main this command writes no runtime setting, so the model runs on the Codex harness implicitly. The setting goes on the method's suggested model, so a different OpenAI model chosen later with `models set` keeps today's implicit runtime.

Checking a Sign in with ChatGPT login right after it is saved could fail with "OAuth token refresh failed for openai: Auth profile credential authority is unavailable; retry after owner recovery". The save is still being published to the Gateway's model catalog, and preparing the credential reader refuses reads during that window instead of waiting. Setup's connection check then failed and the default model was never set. Main has the same code path. The OAuth resolver now waits for that publication to settle and reads again (ending early if the request is cancelled), the same retry that API-key saves already use. A publication that ends without confirmation still fails closed.

A first setup could then roll itself back after a successful connection check, leaving no model, no runtime and no login. Setup writes `plugins.entries.openai`, so the Gateway replaces the loaded OpenAI plugin while applying it. Before that, the write activates the saved credential, and the model runtime refresh that activation starts holds the OpenAI plugin. The Gateway defers that automatic reload ("Plugin openai reload is waiting for retained work...") and retries it about a second later, but setup counted the deferral as a failure and restored everything. Main does the same: an OpenAI API-key first setup on main's build fails the same way. When there is no working connection to keep, setup now keeps the activated config for the Gateway's retry, as it already does when a Gateway restart is pending. Setups that replace a working connection, and automatic setup that needs the change applied at once, still restore on a deferral.

## Evidence

Isolated Gateways with empty state and no credentials in a macOS VM, main (`6018bc9`) against this PR.

**Control UI first-run card** (`/custodian?onboarding=1`, after clicking the card's sign-in button), main against `57f44dc`. Main starts Codex device code; this PR starts Sign in with ChatGPT. The device code on the left is from the guest and expired unused.

| main | this PR |
| --- | --- |
| ![First-run card on main: "Connect ChatGPT to get started" with the step title "OpenAI Codex device code" and a one-time code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/2abe67085e1f2c2079f5c1b13d6dc1d823b7a264/images/2026/11/7aa6ddf5-9367-4048-9571-79531366b0d4.png) | ![First-run card with this PR: a row with the ChatGPT icon and "Sign in with ChatGPT", then Open sign-in and Copy link](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/96345272a03712f944c5d7f09602f38ca1d4dd00/images/2026/11/38e7e291-074f-415e-97df-26f1689e1d5a.png) |

The pickers below were taken on `f5a3cd0`; the newest commit changes only automatic setup. Each pair uses the same page, viewport and crop. The Gateways sit behind a local identity proxy with a made-up person, so Profile → Connected accounts can render.

**First-run Model Setup** (`/settings/model-setup?firstRun=1`, the up-front sign-in section):

| main | this PR |
| --- | --- |
| ![First-run Model Setup on main: Codex login (device code) is the only OpenAI sign-in up front](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/d22b7301ca1143ec24db19f73a3a911704ce4e47/images/2026/11/dbe3a900-0e84-4269-828b-b78f57e9eb2f.png) | ![First-run Model Setup with this PR: Sign in with ChatGPT, then Codex login (device code)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/d22b7301ca1143ec24db19f73a3a911704ce4e47/images/2026/11/fc653aee-fd36-4322-8d29-469382155942.png) |

**Profile → Connected accounts → Add account → OpenAI → Sign-in method:**

| main | this PR |
| --- | --- |
| ![Connected accounts on main: Codex login (browser), Codex login (device code), Sign in with ChatGPT, OpenAI API Key](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/d22b7301ca1143ec24db19f73a3a911704ce4e47/images/2026/11/599d9c50-fa18-412a-8afa-d641ec7c69e1.png) | ![Connected accounts with this PR: Sign in with ChatGPT, Codex login (device code), Codex login (browser), OpenAI API Key](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/d22b7301ca1143ec24db19f73a3a911704ce4e47/images/2026/11/9e147ec1-c58d-4796-a02e-772130ba38e8.png) |

`openclaw models accounts login` reads the same catalog.

**Automatic setup on a fresh machine** (`openclaw.setup.auto` on an empty Gateway, then again after saving a made-up Sign in with ChatGPT login), main against `fe60c0b`:
- main: `needs-sign-in` with `openai-device-code` ("Codex login (device code)"), `installedPlugins: ["codex"]`, and the Codex plugin enabled with `appServer.homeScope: "agent"`.
- this PR: `needs-sign-in` with `openai-token-sharing` ("Sign in with ChatGPT"), `installedPlugins: []`, no Codex plugin entry in config.

**An existing user keeps their login and model.** A user of the latest release (2026.11.5) with a saved Codex login and `openai/gpt-6-astra` selected; then this PR's build runs `doctor --fix` and the Gateway on the same state. Before and after are identical:
- the saved Codex login profile;
- the selected model `openai/gpt-6-astra`;
- setup reports setup complete, with the current model and "Saved Codex login (browser) sign-in".

The login is made up (synthetic tokens), written through the release's own OAuth credential writer. This runs the new build on the old state, as an update does after installing, without packaging the build for `openclaw update`; this PR changes nothing in update or Doctor. The automatic-setup and existing-user runs used `e8e97dd`, which differs from this head only in sign-in ordering and Codex device code's featured flag.

**A first setup that the Gateway's reload defers** (isolated Gateway, `openclaw.setup.activate` with a made-up OpenAI API key against a local stand-in for the Responses API; this goes through the same activation step as Sign in with ChatGPT setup):
- main (`6018bc9`): the probe answers, the Gateway logs "config reload deferred: ... Plugin openai reload is waiting for retained work", and setup fails ("Activation failed and recovery could not complete"). prs.title: fix(worker): wait for queued cleanup before idle work
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A worker can report idle while admitted resource cleanup is still running. The runtime host uses that callback to schedule idle GC and compile-cache flushing. With multiple queued closes, the callback can run between closes or immediately after a task that a pending close must still follow.

## User Impact

Workers now publish idle only after the running task and every admitted resource close have settled. This prevents idle work from starting while cleanup still owns resources. Successful and failed closes retain their existing receipts and ordering; agent-deletion cleanup can still run beside execution.

This fixes an idle-publication boundary. It does not guarantee reclamation of all released memory, change GC thresholds, or claim a process-RSS improvement.

## Why This Change Was Made

`packages/worker-runtime/src/worker-task-server.ts` owns the task and close queues. Both completion paths already know `pendingResourceClosures`; both now require it to be zero before invoking the host's idle callback. The final close publishes eventual idle. Task completion does not await the close queue, because a close can itself be waiting for that task.

The existing synchronous-task ordering test now checks idle events. Two queue regressions cover a successful or rejecting first close followed by a pending second close. A real worker fixture admits both closes through native message ports, verifies that neither idle nor GC starts prematurely, then checks that the released payload can collect while a separate live payload survives.

Runtime change: net +3 lines, including the ownership comment. Tests and their fixture: net +193 lines. No new config, API, dependency, GC policy, or compatibility path. Changelog is release-generated under the repository's contribution rules.

## Evidence

- Frozen source base: `9745e409c50eb061ca204de6065775e1dc8f2ccd`.
- Candidate: `4321de59bb6699ff9d89c23422d6a16d4fcd4980`, tree `2e31dc10172c11f7faeabd21e25d77b762a3b23c`.
- Source review: the complete owner, caller, native-custody helper, snapshot-staging caller, and sibling tests were inspected. Local autoreview of the complete committed range (P0–P3) completed one pass with no findings. The shared local ClawSweeper runner was dirty and left untouched; this uses the documented fallback. The only subsequent change makes the runtime test's empty Node Worker transfer list explicit; it preserves the message and follows neighboring tests.
- Node 24.22.1 and pinned Bun `1.4.4-canary.1+191755ec1`: the original owner reproduced both queued-close failures and the real-worker premature-idle failure on each runtime. After restoring the candidate, all 19 tests across the package server, core adapter, and idle-GC unit/runtime files passed on each runtime, with no skips.
- Initial static proof passed formatting, line limits, core/package lint, all three type lanes, and production/full-tree unused-file scans. One runtime-test lint failure required a browser `targetOrigin`; the explicit empty Node Worker transfer list repairs that call. The initial build was withheld. The follow-up passed both runtime tests on Node and Bun, affected lint/types/formatting, and the full build with `OPENCLAW_RUN_NODE_SKIP_DTS_BUILD=0` (293.25 seconds, including 139.6 seconds for unified declarations). All 43 pinned inputs matched before and after; the remaining 17 tests per runtime retain their unchanged-input proof. No tests were skipped.
- A separate source-level reproduction using a real worker, real timers and GC on Node 26.7 showed the premature callback and confirmed its removal with the candidate. That instrumented synthetic retention observation is not pinned Node 24/Bun qualification, process-RSS measurement, or an acceptance benchmark.
- The build reported five Control UI budget advisories: largest CSS 58,604 B versus 58,315 B; total CSS gzip 339,040 B versus 337,312 B; total CSS raw 1,746,098 B versus 1,740,234 B; chat boot 21 requests versus 20 and 1,333,251 B gzip versus 1,332,637 B. Build exit was zero. This repair does not establish their attribution; no UI files changed.
- Exact-head CI passed: [run 44670833734](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44670833734), completed November 20, 2026 at 04:03:54 UTC on `4321de59bb6699ff9d89c23422d6a16d4fcd4980`. All 60 jobs completed: 31 passed and 29 were skipped; none failed. Focused proof and the required full build are also complete.

The growth-only GC policy can separately retain a previously live allocation released after a genuinely idle collection. That policy question remains outside this change; no generation fences or release hints are introduced here.

prs.title: fix: keep streamed acknowledgments visible while waiting
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A streamed acknowledgment can disappear when the agent delegates work and calls `sessions_yield({})` without a separate acknowledgment. The user sees the message briefly, then loses the explanation of what is still running.

## User Impact

Already-visible model-authored acknowledgments remain available while delegated work is pending. Empty yields and deliberate silence stay quiet; no canned waiting text is added. No configuration change or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reply runner asks the channel for eligible visible text at yield settlement. The shared progress compositor retains authored text alongside a confirmed transport snapshot; Discord, Telegram, and Slack confirm the rendered frame rather than treating a queued edit or callback as visible. Delayed startup, formatted/compacted preambles, and failed replacement edits retain the confirmed acknowledgment without promoting hidden reasoning. Explicit yield acknowledgments take precedence; existing final/cancel cleanup remains in charge. Telegram's partial-mode fallback also excludes tool-only drafts using its existing authorship flag.

Snapshot formatting moves to its existing owner to keep the compositor within the repository's line budget. The superseded callback-capture approach was removed during review.

## Evidence

- The original yield regression fails against the original payload owner and passes with the fix. At `e532ba582caa51365bf2ca6677fc5a83b408e552`, 473 focused tests across 9 files passed, as did the full package build and [CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44667807798).
- The [hosted review's Telegram tool-only finding](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202211#issuecomment-7029674061) was reproduced before repair: a tool-only partial draft incorrectly returned formatted tool telemetry. The correction reuses the existing tool-only flag after flushing. The HTTP suite now passes all 24 cases, including a tool-only negative control and a genuine authored-text positive control.
- At current head `23ddf8175ff8c7ba9820477ee45fd28fb1c4f7ff`, `pnpm build` passed, including declaration emission. Targeted lint, formatting, extension typechecking, and `git diff --check` passed for the correction. [Current-head CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44670247247) completed successfully, including `openclaw/ci-gate`.
- Fresh independent review of the Telegram correction found no substantive issues. It verified the tool-only flag transitions, genuine authored fallback, final/reset behavior, and regression coverage without rerunning completed checks.
- **Remaining live-proof gap:** the Discord QA doctor lacked authenticated Convex broker access. No live Discord/model or screenshot proof is claimed. This PR remains draft pending live verification; it has not been merged.

<details>
<summary>Verification details</summary>

Base: `3f078860b5498f9f2e6aa9d5f3f48ad8e18eeb0d`.

Initial-head focused results: streaming 58; commentary/continuation 29; runner 206; Discord REST/draft-final 45; Telegram HTTP 22; Slack native/fallback and draft-stream 113. The initial combined local test run was interrupted during the runner suite; unfinished suites were rerun separately to completion. No interrupted run is counted as passing.

The corrected Telegram suite ran through the production channel dispatch and an HTTP Bot API fixture: `pnpm test extensions/telegram/src/bot-message-dispatch.progress-lifecycle.telegram-http.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` (24 passed, 83 seconds wall time). It verifies authored-only retention and final cleanup; it does not exercise the live Telegram service. Hosted jobs cover multiple suites, so their timing is not represented as this file's standalone cost.

Both package builds exited 0. The first reported UI asset-budget warnings; no UI source was changed. The CI `build-artifacts` jobs were skipped, so build proof comes from the local package builds, not those jobs.

Independent local review cleared the prior transport-confirmation findings. The later hosted review found the Telegram tool-only case, now fixed, regression-tested, and independently reviewed at the current head.

The task-owned Testbox allocation `tbx_01m7vc7ry22b2t7nh71s4hc565` ([allocation workflow](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44660418126)) was stopped. No credential or permission changes, production restart, or live configuration edits were attempted. The live QA gap requires authenticated access to the existing Convex QA broker.

</details>

Reported and requested by @fuller-stack-dev.

prs.title: fix: bound background worktree deletion bursts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Retiring a managed checkout handed its whole renamed tree to one recursive delete. On shared storage, that metadata burst can delay unrelated database persistence despite a low-priority subprocess and once-per-minute admission. Orphan GC could also rename and recursively delete a tree while paced cleanup was pending.

## User Impact

Cleanup now limits unlink bursts and backs off on slow filesystem commits. Normal retirement and orphan recovery share the serialized deletion owner, including permission-repair retries. Snapshot preservation, live-run checks, owner custody, and Git checks remain intact. Background cleanup takes longer and uses more total CPU/allocation; foreground removal can still release the original checkout name promptly.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing child deletes at most **128 entries or 8 MiB apparent bytes**, then requests a **100 ms pause**. One indivisible oversized file occupies its own batch. It reuses the existing host-pressure probe between batches, including current/recent btrfs commit times, with five-second waits under pressure. The child has a separate 30-minute budget; foreground checkout timeouts are unchanged. A new SQLite telemetry channel or host-probe subsystem was unnecessary.

The 62k-file fixture completes in about 55 seconds with 489 pauses and 2.34 MB at most per ordinary burst. This makes the entry budget a practical starting point for background work; the 8 MiB guard also bounds larger-file mixtures. It is not a calibrated btrfs transaction or latency limit.

Snapshot inventory already runs in the Git worker. `snapshotMs` is asynchronous elapsed wall time; `isMainThread` identifies the logging owner. No duplicate snapshot worker was added. Cumulative MAIN CPU spans many callbacks and is distinct from uninterrupted blocking.

## Evidence

Five final-head A/B pairs ran serially, with A/A controls and host load recorded. Cleanup uses 62,000 generated files × 18,432 bytes plus directories; service removal uses 50,000 dependency files × 22,000 bytes plus 2,388 tracked files. Setup is outside timing. With five samples, nearest-rank p95 is the observed maximum; it is not a production tail estimate. MB is decimal, allocation is total V8 allocation including instrumentation, not retained memory.

| Metric | Before median (min–p95) | After median (min–p95) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cleanup wall, s | 2.66 (2.43–13.18) | 54.77 (54.33–56.06) |
| Cleanup CPU, s | 2.33 (2.19–11.83) | 4.80 (3.69–6.12) |
| V8 allocated, MB | 3.48 (3.25–3.74) | 188.62 (181.29–189.41) |
| Maximum entries/burst | 62,621 (62,621–62,621) | 128 (128–128) |
| Maximum apparent MB/burst | 1,142.78 (1,142.78–1,142.78) | 2.34 (2.34–2.34) |
| Pauses | 0 (0–0) | 489 (489–489) |

| Metric | Before median (min–p95) | After median (min–p95) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Removal wall, ms | 1,168.5 (1,108.5–1,501.4) | 1,111.3 (1,050.2–1,151.6) |
| Snapshot wall, ms | 526.6 (511.1–836.0) | 515.9 (480.3–539.0) |
| Total process CPU, ms | 940.8 (905.8–985.4) | 873.3 (854.2–918.1) |
| Cumulative MAIN CPU, ms | 86.8 (80.3–94.8) | 81.0 (79.0–86.1) |
| MAIN V8 allocated, MB | 38.47 (33.90–46.81) | 34.54 (29.20–38.44) |
| Maximum event-loop delay, ms | 12.20 (12.06–12.43) | 12.19 (12.04–12.75) |

All candidate cleanup runs made 489 scheduled pauses, with observed durations 99.12–102.39 ms (median 102.08 ms). No retired cleanup directory remained after the service processes settled. The extra total CPU and allocation buy bounded work and byte accounting; this is not a throughput improvement. Final-code profiling placed active cleanup samples mostly in unlink and snapshot inventory in the Git worker; a native sample of the cleanup child observed a 35.2 MB physical footprint.

An earlier loaded-host sample is retained in the local report: cleanup took 99.93 s / 44.86 s CPU, with host load rising sharply. Its service removal had 2.42 s snapshot wall time but only 16.91 ms maximum event-loop delay. It is not included in this fresh final-head series and is not hidden as a passing performance claim.

Sanitized actual final worker report excerpt (the committed driver asserts complete deletion before writing this):

```json
{
  "files": 62000,
  "fileBytes": 18432,
  "entryCount": 62621,
  "elapsedMs": 56061.000542,
  "cpuMs": 6119.198,
  "allocatedBytes": 187561880,
  "maxBatchEntries": 128,
  "maxBatchBytes": 2340864,
  "pauses": 489
}
```

```sh
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/retired-worktree-unlink-measure.ts --output "$PERF_ROOT/unlink-b"
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/worktree-removal-snapshot-measure.ts --files 50000 --file-bytes 22000 --tracked 2388 --output "$PERF_ROOT/main-b"
```

Repeat with fresh cleanup outputs and `--reuse-fixture --report <new-name>.json` for service measurements. Baselines use the original cleanup worker via `--worker <pinned-worker.ts>` and `OPENCLAW_BENCH_BASELINE_DIR` for the pinned removal/GC modules. All baseline files came from `1ade2b7a8899ea45934f93e7ede48443dff7d515`.

119 focused owner tests passed; a separate expanded GC/custody run passed 96 tests (these run counts overlap). The pacing regression fails on the original worker, and the held-open retirement/GC regression fails on the preceding PR head. Both pass with the fix. Coverage includes filesystem entry/byte counters, synthetic slow-commit holds, oversized-file batches, symlink targets, real compiled subprocess deletion, permission repair, live-run refusal, owner custody, pending slots, and #202122 scratch-only re-arming. Existing host-pressure tests prove current/recent slow btrfs commits trigger pressure with zero PSI.

The final full `pnpm check:changed` passed. Independent Codex autoreview is scoped-clean through P2; the subsequent test-only commit removes two redundant string conversions without changing behavior. All five final-head measurement pairs are complete and published above. The hosted Codex orphan-GC finding has a code/proof response and is resolved. No changed runtime module is imported by Control UI, so its browser-test boundary is not crossed.

This is APFS/macOS proof, not a Linux/btrfs latency experiment. Apparent bytes and entry counts do not bound physical delayed references or the size of a shared filesystem transaction. Pacing and the existing slow-commit brake mitigate bursts; they do not prove that the reported seven-second SQLite stall is eliminated. No live-service access, copied production data, configuration option, or schema change was used.

The separate generated SQLite file contains 5,000 session-shaped rows and occupies 37,621,940,224 bytes (35.04 GiB). It supplies passive storage scale on the same volume, not the production agent schema or an active 35 GiB database workload. No database commit-latency result is claimed.

Production delta: **+112/−29, net +83 lines** across three modules. Growth provides the bounded walker and one shared deletion queue; it removes the orphan recursive-delete bypass. There is no new cache, manager, schema, or public option.

## Inherited CI Failure

Final head `f19e348802aad625f0b43419aca879a164970fe7`, [CI run 44666643767](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44666643767), attempt 1: **41 passed, 27 skipped, 2 failed**. The only independent failure is `check-docs`; the other is its aggregate gate. `security-fast` passed.

All 18 release-note heading errors reproduce on exact CI main parent `c3d658254b0835eb1663067163adcde6b4620401`, with the same failing file/config as tested merge `756c046bbe58b208bafa8e2093d411e9d69590d8`. They were introduced by #201913 (`72702a3600f77f42f40b9387b3f353fa4a5fac1a`). Later #202186/#202192 edits only add a count paragraph. This is a **main regression requiring repair**, not noise. The user explicitly authorized the pinned-head inherited-failure exception; the native evidence retains this failed CI verdict.

prs.title: feat: dismiss browser completion notifications after viewing replies
prs.body:
Related: #202178

## What Problem This Solves

Browser/PWA completion notifications can remain in the notification shade after the corresponding replies have been opened and read. Repeated completions leave users manually dismissing notifications for work they have already seen.

## User Impact

This change is intended to dismiss a delivered completion notification after its exact final reply is loaded and visibly viewed in the foreground. It preserves other sessions, newer/unseen replies, and notifications without reliable message identity.

This is a draft awaiting execution proof. Existing notifications without the new descriptor remain untouched. Cleanup is local to the same browser/service-worker registration, not cross-device recall.

## Why This Change Was Made

The notification carries the authorized session, recipient and persisted final-response identity. The existing chat bubble supplies actual presentation/intersection evidence; the existing Web Push capability owns dismissal and a bounded in-memory seen-receipt cache. A service-worker hint after notification display reconciles pushes that arrive after a reply was viewed.

Admission is fenced against navigation, disconnection, profile/client replacement and teardown. Seen receipts are not durable: if every page closes before a delayed delivery, that notification waits until another actual view. No blanket session timestamp or notification-tag clearing is used.

## Evidence

- Static source review traced embedded/CLI final identity producers and reviewed ownership, retained-view and late-push boundaries. Follow-up static fixes fence lazy admission, client replacement and viewport exit.
- `git diff --check` passed on the retained implementation.
- Focused regression tests were authored but have **not run**. They cover exact versus newer/unrelated/legacy identity, recipient separation, post-display reconciliation, stale owner results and hidden/preview presentation.
- **Unrun:** focused tests, formatter/lint, type checks, `pnpm ui:build`, core build and real-browser notification proof. No phone/device test or current-installation reproduction is claimed.
- A secretless offline Node24.22.3/pnpm12.15.0 toolchain passed its smoke check, but the frozen offline dependency install stopped at `ERR_PNPM_NO_OFFLINE_META` for `@ampproject/remapping`. Required supply-chain metadata was unavailable; this is an infrastructure gap, not a product test failure. No supported secretless online provisioning or remote proof capacity was qualified.

Published as a draft under the repository's build-unavailable proof policy. Automatic CI skips drafts. Required builds, focused tests, type/lint/format checks and browser proof remain pending through a qualified secretless route bound to the exact PR head. A skipped job or workflow-ref SHA is not proof; do not mark ready until the required exact-head checks succeed. No maintainer-only CI dispatch is requested.

prs.title: fix(database-port): treat SQLite zero sequence high-water as uncalled
prs.body:
Closes #201573

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw database port --to postgres` aborts when an `AUTOINCREMENT` table has a `sqlite_sequence` row with `seq = 0` (an empty `audit_events`, for example). The port derived `{ value: "0", called: true }`, emitted `SELECT setval(seq, 0, true)`, and PostgreSQL rejected it with `value 0 is out of bounds for sequence (1..9223372036854775807)`. The CLI then reported only the misleading namespace-owner refusal.

## User Impact

An empty AUTOINCREMENT table no longer aborts the port. SQLite treats `seq = 0` like an absent row, so the destination keeps the uncalled shape (`setval(seq, 1, false)`) instead of an out-of-range value.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Treat a zero high-water (and a zero row maximum) as "never called" when reading a SQLite identity.
- Extract the per-identity SQLite allocation read and fact shaping into `port-allocation-fact.ts` so the worker stays within its line cap.
- Cover that reader in the existing narrow offline-port SQLite exception (`check-kysely-guardrails.mts`).
- Legacy values above zero and genuine row maximums keep the existing `called: true` behavior.

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/infra/database-engine/port.worker.allocations.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 2/2 passed: zero sequence yields `{ value: "1", called: false }`; a real high-water of 7 yields `{ value: "7", called: true }`.
- Red-on-base: reverting `port.worker.ts` makes the zero case fail with `expected { value: '0', called: true }`.

prs.title: feat(templates): sign in to ClawHub from a private draft
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Trying to review a private Template draft while signed out of ClawHub led to a `clawhub login` error. **Retry review** repeated it. Creators had to leave the conversation and sign in on the Gateway host.

## User Impact

The card starts with **Sign in to ClawHub**. Select **Sign in** to request a code without leaving the conversation. The code replaces the subtitle and the same button becomes **Copy & open ClawHub**. Select it, paste the code into ClawHub, and approve. Review resumes on the original unpublished draft. A blocked clipboard or popup offers manual recovery; cancellation or expiry leaves the draft private. **Preview** shows the files without publishing. Only **Publish** uploads the draft.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway binds the pending approval to the original person, registry, conversation and draft. It stores the verified credential in the existing private SQLite identity store for that person and registry; another administrator cannot borrow the host account. The card displays the short approval code, never the device credential or API token.

## Evidence

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3c1c0ce8-c4bd-423d-a12e-f38f633f2e46

[13.36-second before/after recording with compact Preview](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202013#issuecomment-7028869474). Before, ClawHub opened with an empty field and no code on the clipboard. After, the first click stays on the draft; the second copies the code and opens one approval tab. A keyboard paste fills the field. Approval opens exactly one review of the original unpublished draft. Opening and closing Preview sends neither chat nor a publish request. The card and button kept their dimensions and positions at 400, 820, 1280 and 1440 px.

The recording uses Chromium, a rebuilt Control UI and Gateway, the [pinned ClawHub approval component](https://github.com/openclaw/clawhub/blob/63a48631a855dfda27254b4a767962ca7a4ece8b/src/routes/cli/device.tsx), and a local fixture account and authorization backend—not a production sign-in. It shows tree `715f2b57bf28` before the upstream protocol merge.

On the current PR head `98bf708cbe59` (tree `c8956918ccff`), the same end-to-end test passed with freshly built UI and Gateway. It verified keyboard paste, one review of the original draft, read-only Preview, no chat or publication, and fixture teardown. The sign-in and review screenshots were pixel-identical to the earlier run, and the four-width layout measurements matched. Of the 40 PR paths, only the generated protocol predicates changed between those runs.

**Local validation:** The regenerated Gateway validators passed their canonical check, 58 targeted protocol/Gateway/credential tests passed, and `pnpm check:changed` passed against `66fc4d8848c5`. On the recorded tree, 59 focused UI/Settings tests and six compact-card Chromium cases passed. Its clean performance comparison measured CSS −9 bytes raw / +55 bytes gzip (64-byte allowance) and chat boot JavaScript −2 bytes gzip. No budgets changed.

**Earlier recordings:** [CSS repair](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202013#issuecomment-7028406678) · [Conflict repair](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202013#issuecomment-7027856897) · [Before conflict resolution](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202013#issuecomment-7027187181) · [Manual-entry version](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202013#issuecomment-7021694420) · [Original sign-in proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202013#issuecomment-7019878271).

prs.title: fix(auto-reply): carry provider-native chat id into session-event turns
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

#199701: while a backgrounded task runs, a human correction sent from the
same conversation sits queued (observed 95-153 seconds) and the running
assistant never receives it — it keeps acting on superseded instructions.
Steering was rejected with `tool_authority_mismatch` even with
collaborative steering enabled, and an `@mention` retry did not help.

Root cause: session-event turns (background completion finalization,
restart recovery, scheduled automation prompts) are injected through
`buildSessionEventContext`, which never set `MsgContext.ChatId`. Run
assembly copies `conversationId` from that field, so the
same-conversation authority projection compared against an empty
conversation id and rejected the correction. The reporter confirmed
supplying the matching conversation id re-enables the unchanged
authority snapshot.

## The Change

- Session-event targets retain the host-captured `nativeChannelId`
  alongside permission settings (`SessionEventTarget["settings"]`,
  destination settings, and the narrowing function — identity is a fact
  that follows current, never an intersected authority).
- The captured id is read through the canonical origin reader
  (`sessionDeliveryOrigin(entry)?.nativeChannelId` via
  `resolveSessionEventDestinationSettings`), not a route address.
- `buildSessionEventContext` populates `ChatId` from that captured id
  **only**: route addresses (`channel:<id>` for guild channels,
  `user:<id>` for DMs) are not the native conversation identity and do
  not substitute for it; the field stays absent when no identity was
  captured.
- Revocation, route, and thread checks are untouched: they read the same
  snapshot and now receive the identity they were already checking for.

## Evidence

- **Regression-first**: the ChatId case asserts the captured id flows
  through while a prefixed route address (`channel:<id>`) stays out of
  `ChatId` (it remains on `OriginatingTo`) and the field stays absent
  without a captured identity. First revision failed exactly as the
  projection would (`expected undefined to be '123456789012345678'`).
  Full file: **8/8** (capture case covers a real-shaped session entry — `delivery.origin.nativeChannelId` — through destination settings into context construction) (`session-event-context.test.ts`).
- **Sibling suites stay green**: session-event handoff, automation
  result, permissions, policy, config re-admission, and webchat-route
  files — **40/40**; authority and steering suites
  (`agent-runner-execution-message-authority`, `queue.authority`,
  `agent-runner-fallback-steering`) — **23/23**.
- Focused command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run
  src/auto-reply/reply/session-event-context.test.ts` on head
  `28790983e82` (Node 26, isolated worktree).
- **Isolated Gateway A/B, reviewed head:** At base `b601a4b206c` and head `a2dd7462a14`, the same synthetic channel ingress and scripted model exercised a background-exec completion followed by a same-conversation correction. The base rejected the correction with `tool_authority_mismatch` and deferred it as `followup`; the head dispatched it as `steer` and reported `active_run_injected`. The harness used a local `proof-channel` plugin and scripted model endpoint, not a real third-party channel or external model. Both runs used isolated state and loopback endpoints. See the [captured A/B output](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200345#issuecomment-6943968237).
- **Live Gateway trace through a real Telegram channel** (isolated profile,
  fix build; model endpoint held open so an inbound turn stays active):

  ```text
  [routing] resolveAgentRoute: channel=telegram accountId=core
            peer=direct:<tg-user-id> ...
  [model-fetch] start ... sessionKey="agent:main:telegram:core:direct:<tg-user-id>"
            runId="<run-uuid>" requestNumber=1
  [model-fetch] response ... status=200 contentType=text/event-stream ...
  [diagnostic] steering rejected; applying follow-up policy
            reason=requester-mismatch disposition=followup-policy
            channel=telegram sessionKey=agent:main:telegram:core:direct:<tg-user-id>
            activeRunId=<run-uuid>
  [diagnostic] message processed: channel=telegram
            chatId=telegram:<tg-user-id> ... outcome=completed
  ```

  This exercises the same authority-projection stack end to end on a real
  channel: inbound identity capture, an active run with the conversation
  session key, and a same-conversation correction reaching the steering
  decision. The correction shown is rejected one gate earlier
  (`requester-mismatch`: the active run was restored by gateway restart, so
  its requester origin differs from the live Telegram user) — the
  conversation-identity comparison this PR repairs sits one gate below that
  check, which requires requester origins to match first; reproducing that
  exact gate pair needs a Discord-style session where the background
  completion and the correction share one requester origin.

## Risk / compatibility

Additive field population on internal event turns only. The field's
consumers either want it present (authority projection, run assembly,
hook identity context) or treat it as optional template context. No
permission expansion: the id is the host-captured conversation identity
the session already stores, and the revocation and route/thread checks
are unchanged.

prs.title: fix(gateway): refresh native command channels when their registry is replaced
prs.body:
Root cause: src/gateway/server-plugin-reload-channels.ts:88 `collectTargets` restarts channels only when command entries change identity or the channel's own plugin changed. A reload of an unrelated plugin keeps the other plugins' command entries by identity, so no channel restarts. The old registry is still retired, and Telegram, Discord and Slack keep dispatching through native command candidates captured from it at account start.

Fixes #199612

Thanks @eliavb43 for the report and diagnosis, @jupiterkatz1989-coder for confirming it, and @555aaditya for the fix.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: after a config hot reload of any plugin, every plugin slash command on Telegram answers "⚠️ This command is no longer available after the plugin registry changed. Please try again." until the Gateway restarts. Discord and Slack native commands bind the same way.

## User Impact

User impact: plugin slash commands on native-command channels keep working after a plugin hot reload, including when the reloaded plugin is unrelated to the command.

## Why This Change Was Made

Telegram (`bot-native-commands.ts:80`), Discord (`provider.commands.ts:34`) and Slack (`slash.ts:919`) take native command candidates from `createPluginCommandRuntime().listNativeCandidates()` when an account starts. Each candidate is bound to that registry generation, and a dispatch from a retired generation returns the refusal above (`plugin-command-runtime.ts:149`). A plugin reload publishes a new registry and retires the old one, but `collectTargets` did not refresh channels when the command list kept its identity.

`collectTargets` now also targets channels with `capabilities.nativeCommands` that had a plugin command for that channel in the replaced registry. It uses the same `pluginCommandSupportsChannel` filter as `listNativeCandidates`. Those channels go through the existing reload stop, start and route-handoff path that command-list changes already use. Channels without native commands, or without plugin commands for that channel, keep running.

Update behavior: Gateway runtime only. No persisted state, config or schema change. It takes effect when the updated Gateway starts; the installed updater is not involved.

## Evidence

Live Telegram Test Server run (real QA user DM, TDLib records), built merge base `6341f93c9c` against this branch, same scenario: [proof comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/199743#issuecomment-7028740443).

- Base: `/p199612ping` answers `P199612_PONG`. After `plugins.entries.p199612-other.config.rev` changes (hot reload, no Telegram restart), it answers `⚠️ This command is no longer available after the plugin registry changed. Please try again.`
- This branch: Telegram restarts with `reason: plugin-reload` during the same reload, and `/p199612ping` keeps answering `P199612_PONG`.
- Control, same on both: disabling the plugin that owns `/p199612gone` removes the command. Its handler never runs, and the message goes to a normal agent turn.

Regression in `server-plugin-reload.recovery.test.ts`: an unrelated plugin reloads while a sibling owns a native-command channel with a retained command and a channel without native commands. It fails on the merge base (`expected [ 'plain', 'native' ] to deeply equal [ 'plain', 'native', 'native' ]`). On this branch it passes: only the native channel restarts, and its new candidate runs the command.

Merge danger: two-way door. A revert restores the old behavior, and nothing is persisted. Blast radius: on a plugin hot reload, channels with native commands and plugin commands (Telegram, Discord, Slack, Mattermost) now restart through the existing reload path. They already did this whenever the command list changed.

prs.title: feat: recover interrupted QuickJS cells after Gateway crashes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the Gateway dies while a Code Mode cell is awaiting a tool, the transcript can survive but the JavaScript continuation does not. Restart reconciliation cannot reliably finish the original program, even when its earlier tool results were already committed.

## User Impact

Persisted QuickJS cells can recover in a fresh VM: reuse committed replies, retry explicitly replay-safe pending calls, and finish the original tool result under the original requester's newly admitted authority. Node, incognito, and older unjournaled cells retain transcript-based reconciliation.

An external effect without a committed receipt is still uncertain, not exactly once. Recovery refuses unsafe pending effects and incompatible programs/catalogs/engines rather than silently repeating them. The additive agent-database migration is version 43 → 44. Limits are four unretired journals per session key, 256 calls per cell, and 4 MiB per encoded journal.

**Draft:** requested Crabbox proof, independent review, a real-model run, and latest-stable upgrade proof remain incomplete. Do not treat this as ready to merge.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing session worker owns the journal and transactions; the existing restart admission restores the requester, and the existing tool executor owns every dispatch. Ordered intent/result receipts reconstruct JavaScript locals and promise delivery in deterministic QuickJS without saving a native stack or adding another scheduler. Terminal results and buffered store writes commit together; authoritative transcript append retires the journal atomically, including completion through `wait`.

The smallest complete slice crosses storage, engine, and restart admission: a ledger alone would not restore the interrupted program. Simplification removed duplicate journal reads and the premature recovery hook; recovery now starts only after the subscribed executor is bound. Host dispatch and deterministic VM setup are extracted into coherent siblings rather than growing the already capped execution modules. No new dependency, configuration option, or production operation is included.

Requested by and co-authored with @fuller-stack-dev.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion with @fuller-stack-dev](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/11cd3553-8011-4c7a-979d-a3c7c1467a6b)

## Evidence

- **Real process kill/restart passed on commit 167dfdebdf3a1119606885b32c6eb5fccb676926.** An isolated Gateway commits A, blocks in B, receives SIGKILL, restarts on the same database, reuses A, retries replay-safe B, executes C once, and supplies the original completed tool result to the model loop. The provider and requester are synthetic; this does not claim a live-model run.
- Focused real QuickJS/SQLite tests passed for sequential/parallel replay, unsafe pending calls, catalog mismatch, local result handles, store projection, exact terminal-result reuse, and journal retirement through exec/wait. An elapsed-time regression was demonstrated red (30 ms timer advanced the virtual clock only 1 ms), then green with recorded wall-clock samples reused during replay.
- Requester recovery, existing restart admission, session-store and wait consumers, deterministic engine, execution preparation/cleanup, schema migration/rollback, and the 16-test prompt-prefix stability suite passed. Core typecheck, line-cap ratchet, formatting, four changed docs' MDX validation, Kysely, and PostgreSQL generated-artifact verification passed.
- **Crabbox blocked before allocation:** the configured ascii-box provider requires an organization for private visibility, and its read-only preflight reports missing `ASCII_BOX_API_KEY`. No remote test result or resource is claimed; no provider fallback or credential workaround was used.
- **Independent review incomplete:** local ClawSweeper is unavailable. Autoreview selected Codex / GPT-6.1 Sol, P0–P2, with the complete local change against `3f078860b5498f9f2e6aa9d5f3f48ad8e18eeb0d`, but refused before reviewer launch because its temporary-directory isolation requirement conflicts with this session's fixed workspace scratch policy. No clean review is claimed.
- **Lint blocked:** repository lint configuration cannot resolve `eslint-plugin-solid`. Shared dependencies were not modified. Latest-stable upgrade, live-model behavior, broader crash-window/queued-correction coverage, and exact-head CI remain pending.

<details>
<summary>Primary reproducible commands</summary>

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.e2e.config.ts test/gateway-code-mode-durable.e2e.test.ts --maxWorkers=1

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/code-mode-durable.integration.test.ts src/agents/code-mode-durable-recovery.test.ts src/config/sessions/code-mode-journal.test.ts src/state/openclaw-agent-code-mode-journal-migration.test.ts extensions/code-mode-quickjs/src/deterministic.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-execution-phase.test.ts --maxWorkers=1

node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json
```

</details>

- @fuller-stack-dev

prs.title: fix(voice): answer phone, meeting and FaceTime consults on Claude CLI agents
prs.body:
Closes #202208

Related: #188440, #161885, #164229, #199379, #199378; supersedes closed #191683.

## What Problem This Solves

On an agent whose model runs on Claude CLI (or another CLI runtime), a phone call (Voice Call realtime), a meeting bot (Google Meet, Teams, Zoom, Slack huddles) or a FaceTime call cannot get an answer from the agent: every consult fails with `No API key found for provider "anthropic"` or a sign-in error, and the caller hears an error. Typed messages and Discord voice to the same agent work.

## User Impact

User impact: phone, meeting and FaceTime voice consults run on the agent's own runtime, including Claude CLI and its configured fallbacks, like a typed message. Embedded-runtime agents keep working. Tool policy is unchanged: callers and meeting participants are guests, FaceTime owners stay owners, and a phone consult's `voice_call` can still only end the current call.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared helper `consultRealtimeVoiceAgent` always ended in `runEmbeddedAgent` with an explicit provider/model, which calls the provider API directly and never selects the agent's runtime. Discord voice works because it runs a normal agent turn through `runCommandFromIngress`.

- `consultRealtimeVoiceAgent` gains `runner: "agent-turn"`: after the helper prepares the consult session (fork from the requester, lineage, delivery fields, lifecycle admission), the consult runs as a turn of that session through `runCommandFromIngress` with `deliver: false`. Prompt building, timeout, cancellation, `onRunStarted`, speakable-text extraction and yield acknowledgements are unchanged. The default stays `embedded`, so Talk (which adapts embedded tool context and is being reworked in #164229 / #199379) and third-party SDK callers are untouched.
- Voice Call, meeting-bot and FaceTime opt in. Voice Call passes a model override only when `responseModel` is configured and a thinking override only when `realtime.consultThinkingLevel` is set; otherwise the session's own selection applies. Meeting consults no longer force thinking `high` (an explicit level the model does not support fails the turn); they use the session default.
- Plugin ingress (`runCommandFromIngress` wrapper): a plugin may omit `messageChannel` for a turn on its own surface. Owner authority still needs a bundled or trusted official plugin, and a named channel must still be the plugin's own. `toolBindings` are accepted only for tools the plugin declares in `contracts.tools`. **This widens the plugin ingress capability** (previously only channel plugins could admit turns); it stays narrower than `runEmbeddedAgent`, which any plugin can already call with an owner bit. Flagging for SDK/security owner review.
- The Claude CLI path carries `toolBindings` from the command attempt into the MCP loopback grant, as the embedded runner already does, so `voice_call` stays bound to the live call.
- Voice Call runs the consult in its service context so Gateway-dispatched tools such as `sessions_send` work from webhook handlers.

Not changed: the Voice Call classic (non-realtime) responder (#188440), Talk's Gateway consult path (#164229 / #199379), Discord voice. Passing the current conversation (provider/account/target) into plugin ingress turns is left to a separate change.

## Evidence

Isolated Gateway (QA gateway child, private state, mock voice provider, mock realtime bridge that calls `openclaw_agent_consult`), stub `claude` on `PATH` speaking stream-json and calling the real MCP loopback. No real model or provider credential.

| Scenario | Base `abd4b4fc6` | This branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude CLI agent, phone consult | embedded run → `anthropic` 401 / "Couldn't sign in to the AI service"; stub `claude` never got a turn | answered by `claude-cli` in 2.0–4.2 s; 0 "No API key" |
| `safe-read-only` tools on the CLI route | n/a | MCP tools exactly `memory_get, memory_search, read, voice_call, web_fetch`; `write` → "Tool not available"; `voice_call initiate_call` → "This realtime consult may only end_call." |
| `owner` tool policy, guest caller | n/a | `sessions_send` to another session accepted; owner-only `gateway` refused ("not started by the owner"); `voice_call` still end_call-only |
| Hangup during a running CLI turn | n/a | call finalized → turn aborted ~0.5 s later ("consult owner was cancelled"), no model fallback (`caller_signal_aborted`), `claude` got SIGTERM |

prs.title: fix(worktrees): keep completed chat sessions' worktrees for the idle window
prs.body:
Related: #202122

## What Problem This Solves

Reopening a completed chat could fail run preparation after idle cleanup removed its worktree only minutes after a reply. A terminal session status such as `done` describes the last run, while the conversation remains resumable.

## User Impact

Present, unarchived sessions keep their worktrees for seven days plus the existing stable delay of up to one hour after their latest activity, including completed, failed, killed, and timed-out runs. Already-removed worktrees remain restorable for 30 days through Settings > Worktrees (`worktrees.restore`). No schema or configuration change is needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

#202122 made terminal session owners immediately idle, bypassing the retention window. Idle cleanup now compares the later of registry activity and the owning session row's `lastInteractionAt`/`updatedAt` against the existing window and jitter. The existing worker owner census already reads these facts; GC consumes them without another query or new storage. Missing usable session timestamps fall back to registry activity.

Live or queued work remains protected, and archived or absent owners remain immediately eligible. Workboard retention, capacity eviction, scratch-clone reclamation, pack cleanup, nested-repository re-arming, and removal pacing keep their existing policies.

## Evidence

The regression runs real Git worktrees and persisted session rows through `ManagedWorktreeService.gc`. A completed chat with an interaction two hours ago retains its checkout despite a registry stamp older than seven days; the expired interaction is removed. Recent registry activity also retains the checkout. A recent archived owner is removed immediately, while live/queued work is protected. Interrupted/cancelled history still does not count as queued work. Existing census assertions were folded into this stronger boundary proof; net test lines versus the base are zero (63 added, 63 removed).

Red on base `9745e409c50eb061ca204de6065775e1dc8f2ccd`, before production edits:

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/worktrees/owner-protection.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
FAIL retains resumable finished owners through the idle window (recent interaction)
expected [ 'fixture-dashboard' ] to deeply equal []
Tests  1 failed | 18 passed (19)
Duration  47.41s
```

The scratch-clone regression also verifies that releasing a lease retains its freshly active checkout, then ages the synthetic registry row through the existing writer before proving cleanup and hardlink reclamation. This preserves the scratch policy without mocking worker lease clocks.

Green with the fix: all 19 owner-protection tests, 36 removal-budget tests, and 29 GC service tests passed (84 total). File wall times were 53.50 seconds for owner protection (including a cold worker compile), 70.98 seconds for removal budgets, and 59.17 seconds for GC services.

```text

Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  19 passed (19)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/worktrees/service.removal-budget.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  36 passed (36)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/worktrees/service.gc.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  29 passed (29)
```

`pnpm tsgo`, the agents-tools test typecheck, targeted type-aware oxlint on all five TypeScript files, formatting of all six changed files, the line-cap ratchet, and `git diff --check` passed. Codex-backed local autoreview of the final diff was scoped-clean through P2, with no actionable findings.

One preliminary run was invalidated by source edits during compiled-test execution and was rerun with fixed inputs. A clock-based scratch-fixture attempt correctly failed worker lease validation; the committed fixture ages its synthetic registry row instead. The optional standalone Markdown lint command was unavailable locally (`markdownlint-cli2` was not installed); formatting passed. CI timing and required checks remain to be observed on the exact pushed head.

No server, Gateway, or production host was contacted; proof uses isolated local fixtures.

prs.title: feat(gateway): make workspace file preview cap configurable
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Opening any workspace file larger than 256 KiB in the Control UI (workspace rail, chat file links, `sessions.files.get`, `agents.workspace.get`) degrades to a metadata-only entry or fails with `session_file_too_large`. Logs, CSV/JSON exports, lockfiles, and minified bundles routinely exceed the hardcoded `WORKSPACE_PREVIEW_MAX_BYTES = 256 * 1024` in `src/gateway/server-methods/workspace-fs.ts`, and there is no config to change it.

Closes #144881

## Why This Change Was Made

The cap's original rationale ("keeps file payloads comfortably under client WS limits") has drifted by two orders of magnitude: `MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` is now 25 MiB (raised for high-res canvas snapshots), leaving a 256 KiB read-only preview far below the transport it was sized against.

Instead of raising the default (which would change behavior for memory-constrained deployments), this adds `gateway.workspacePreviewMaxBytes` (1 byte–4 MiB, default 256 KiB — exactly today's behavior) and threads it through the consumers. The 4 MiB ceiling budgets the worst-case encoded frame: text can expand ~6x through JSON escaping (`\uXXXX` control characters) and binary 4/3x through base64, so a near-limit preview always fits under the 25 MiB WS payload limit.

Scope kept narrow: local workspace reads (`sessions.files.get`/`set`, `agents.workspace.get`) and stored repository artifact previews honor the configured cap; remote repository workspace previews (`repository.inspect`) keep the default cap and report it — no protocol change.

## User Impact

Operators working with large text files can raise the cap:

```json5
{ gateway: { workspacePreviewMaxBytes: 4194304 } } // 4 MiB
```

Default behavior is unchanged. Oversize errors (`session_file_too_large`) report the configured cap in `maxPreviewBytes`, so the UI can explain the effective limit. The key hot-applies per request (registered in `config-reload-plan.ts`) — verified live without a Gateway restart.

## Evidence

- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:core:test` — pass
- Touched suites pass with new cases for raised-cap preview, get → set → reopen round-trip above the default, oversize error reporting, and hot-reload plan assertions (`sessions-files.preview.test.ts`, `sessions-files.test.ts`, `workspace-fs.test.ts`, `config-reload.test.ts`)
- Config doc baseline regenerated; `config:docs:check` passes; oxfmt applied
- **Runtime proof on a running Gateway** (real WS transport via `callGatewayCli`): default 256 KiB rejection → in-place config edit hot-applied in both directions (`[reload] config hot reload applied`) → full 307,248-byte preview delivered → 300,000-byte above-default save → reopen hash matches the write. Full transcripts are in the comments below.
- Not run locally (CI covers): full `pnpm build` and the complete test suite

prs.title: improve(ci): avoid repeated package validation before FRV
prs.body:
Related: #201265 (earlier FRV fanout improvement; its savings are not counted here).

## What Problem This Solves

Full Release Validation waits for Package Acceptance to check out the repository, install validation dependencies, and fully inspect a package that its resolver has already inspected with the same qualification tooling. This repeat lies before the candidate Docker branch that was the longest path in the completed runs below.

## User Impact

No installed-product change. Release validation avoids one repeated full tarball check and its checkout/dependency setup, without removing a scenario, changing concurrency, or weakening package acceptance. The named integrity job still downloads the exact canonical artifact and rejects different or missing bytes before any acceptance transport runs.

**Expected full-FRV improvement is modeled, not measured:** approximately 2m27s and 2m09s against the two original traces below under unchanged scheduling and a one-second retained-hash allowance. Subsequent release-branch runs already contain this optimization; do not subtract those savings again from their baselines. This task dispatched no new FRV run.

## Why This Change Was Made

The resolver unconditionally runs the full tarball validator from captured qualification revision Q before emitting successful outputs. The dependent integrity job previously ran that same Q validator again against the same SHA-256. Keep the existing `needs` relationship, exact artifact/run download, digest check, job identity, timeout, summary and all four transport dependencies; delete only the duplicate checkout, dependency setup, checker call and checker-only timing setting.

This is deliberately narrower than removing imported-package validation: **Docker’s independent import checker is unchanged**, as are all source admission and C/Q identity checks. No new receipt, cache, bypass input, fallback or validation owner. The original integrity gate (52759294ca820d5498b1cde1536b892865d24dd4) protected acceptance from invalid/private package contents; the resolver already checked those contents at that revision, and remains the full-check owner.

## Evidence

- Real unchanged resolver CLI and full checker accept a valid synthetic package; a missing imported module, forbidden QA cargo, and malformed archive each fail before metadata/GitHub outputs. This exercises artifact-source resolution, not mocks; other sources retain the same unconditional convergence.
- Execute the actual retained workflow shell without repository/dependency setup: the resolver-approved archive passes; altered same-version bytes and a missing archive fail before an acceptance sentinel. The committed regression is red on the old workflow and green here.
- Original proof: **144 focused workflow cases and 3 real-checker cases passed**, including artifact identity, frozen admission, captured tooling, Docker reuse and dependency/timeout boundaries.
- November 20 integration at `10e1946735290daec2c53cb4f4ccf5fe94587a84`: **all 588 package-acceptance workflow tests passed** in 152.98s. Tooling typecheck, targeted lint, three-file format, actionlint/zizmor/workflow guards and PR-diff whitespace check passed. Frozen installation completed successfully. Original docs MDX/internal-link proof (16,760 checked, zero broken) is retained; this integration changes no PR documentation or production behavior.
- [Old CI 44533725841](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44533725841) had four stale workflow-contract assertions after authenticated receipt recovery #201814. All four reproduced locally. Integrated existing main repair `724de78fa44a328f3b1fa943f216774a87903c3b` (#201805), rather than weakening assertions; the complete affected suite now passes. The old failed CI remains prior-head evidence, not green acceptance for this head.
- Author simplification rechecked against main: exactly three files, workflow **+3/-18**, docs +2/-2, tests +45/-6. One compact executable transfer-boundary case; no production helper or duplicate validation policy. Independent local review is explicitly waived for this task; hosted ClawSweeper remains required.
- Hosted transport proof now exists on the release branch: [job 135686258927](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44558533228/job/135686258927) completed in **17s** (11s download, 1s hash), and [job 135968830511](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44639105831/job/135968830511) in **5s** (2s download, hash below timestamp resolution). Both execute the transfer-only integrity variant without checkout/setup/full revalidation. These are execution evidence, **not controlled before/after wall-time measurements**.
- ClawSweeper completed the original head with no findings on November 19 ([review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201840#issuecomment-7010979933)). Following main integration, new-head CI/review acceptance is pending; **not yet RFR**. No runtime/package code changes require a new product build.

### Critical-path timing (estimates, not A/B results)

| Completed diagnostic run | Measured redundant-job phases | Modeled additional full-FRV saving |

prs.title: fix(slack): stop untagged bot loops with opt-in explicit mentions
prs.body:
Related: #160750, #160752.

## What Problem This Solves

Operators cannot reject untagged bot thread replies without also making humans repeat mentions or changing existing bot handoffs on upgrade.

## User Impact

Slack operators can opt into `requireExplicitBotMention: true` alongside `allowBots: "mentions"` at the existing root/account/channel scopes. Strict mode rejects untagged bots that otherwise qualify through reply-to-bot or thread participation. Human follow-ups, explicit bot mentions, DMs, authorized commands, configured mention patterns, and `allowBots: true`/`false` retain their behavior.

Omitted or false preserves shipped implicit bot handoffs. This is an alternative to #160752's default change, not a downstream adoption decision. **Slack-owner acceptance of the new optional public setting remains required.**

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing bot-admission gate owns this choice. The unchanged mention classifier moves to the existing thread-mention sibling, keeping the oversized prepare module smaller. Existing no-restart reload metadata covers all four projections. No new admission mechanism, retroactive revocation, persistence schema, migration, private runtime patch, or distribution is added.

Integrated fixed official main `228b5e9e7df8b978a85a0f3f3aa249b705f383aa` with an ordinary merge to repair actual preparation-owner and generated-output conflicts. Main retains a single `prepareSlackMessage` owner; retired helper frames are not restored. Existing mention decision and unchanged source classification live together in the existing mention sibling to satisfy the shrink-only line-cap. Current canonical generators own the metadata/baselines. The schema regression uses main's direct `safeParse` assertions after its former test helpers were removed; all validity/default/type assertions remain.

<!-- forone-adoption-decision-20261102:start -->
## Adoption decision and fresh distribution evidence — 2026-11-02

The Slack-owner decision remains whether to expose the compatibility-preserving `requireExplicitBotMention` opt-in. The current submission section below owns the latest head and CI status; maintainer edits remain enabled. Owner acceptance is still outstanding.

The historical [advisory review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/177555#issuecomment-6274222081) reports no actionable findings and sufficient recorded isolated-Gateway output, and recommends accepting the opt-in. It does not record Slack-owner acceptance. Its two outstanding checklist entries both concern that same public-contract decision. The review is scoped to `39d01116dd2d5e01fa7f8ab50dbb1e44613a0e9a`; the earlier12-input comparison was bound to8fa0cc0d85711ab2ee19e488ec9e325309a476c2. That earlier integration retained11 byte-identical inputs; access-control documentation only adds accepted official Slack read-bound guidance. The strict opt-in authored delta and committed Gateway scenario are retained. The older proof retains its original head; that earlier head's CI supported its integration. No fresh live Slack run or current employee acceptance is claimed.

Recorded official distribution evidence confirms that the need remains after the implicit-thread silence repair: unmodified Core/Slack **2026.10.10-beta.5**, build `7e15622f37bd0ced194a3b0fccacb4ad6bc78d85`, still admits untagged bot messages through both `bot_thread_participant` and `reply_to_bot` in the isolated distributed-function/compiled-gate fixture. The same 20-case matrix passes 17, with these two strict-admission requirements and the separate optional-completion policy remaining. Package integrity and the scope are recorded in the [release follow-up](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/164877#issuecomment-6266458621). This is not a new live Slack incident or a claim that existing documented defaults were silently changed.

**Decision requested from the Slack owner:** accept or reject this optional public setting at the existing root/account/channel scopes. Omitted/false keeps existing implicit bot handoffs. With `allowBots: "mentions"` and the opt-in enabled, untagged bot activation is rejected while explicit bot requests, implicit human follow-ups, DMs, authorized commands, and existing sender restrictions retain their controls. This is the compatibility-preserving alternative to #160752's default change; no new default change is requested here.

This PR decides **admission**, not whether an already admitted explicit bot notification may finish empty. That latter product-policy question remains separate in #186514. A scoped acceptance/rejection of this opt-in is the missing adoption decision; existing code/proof work is not being represented as owner approval. No new review command or redundant behavior replay was added for this mechanical integration.
<!-- forone-stable-adoption-evidence-20261103:start -->
### 2026-11-03: the same admission requirement remains in stable2026.10.10

Official npm/latest Core/Slack **2026.10.10**, distributed Core build`7dc3350cb9f08fcf9a0af5c4845a20d5b2f1a8be`, was checked with the unchanged20-case synthetic matrix: **17PASS / 3FAIL**. The two untagged-bot admission cases (`bot_thread_participant` and `reply_to_bot`) still admit the bot under existing mentions-only behavior. The two implicit-thread optional/silent conditions from merged #164877 nowPASS in stable; the third remaining failure concerns #186514's separate explicit-bot completion policy.

The [stable distribution follow-up](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/164877#issuecomment-6266458621) fixes the verified immutable Core/Slack hashes and execution scope. This is actual distributed Core-function / verbatim compiled Slack-gate evidence, with unchanged cases/assertions and shipped package bytes. The existing native Gateway proof retains its original binding. This paragraph updates distribution evidence only; the current PR head and compatible opt-in proposal remain unchanged. Slack-owner acceptance or rejection remains unrecorded.
<!-- forone-stable-adoption-evidence-20261103:end -->
<!-- forone-adoption-decision-20261102:end -->

- Baseline `b8f91cb249b8c702cfc02befd6d2fb11215928f3` had five focused failures for strict bot admission/schema; legacy controls passed. The sole substantive failure is [the model-picker browser job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44665765068/job/136055320105): `keyCode229 ArrowUp` expected two model rows but found one after clicking the provider rail, before dispatching the keyboard event. Its aggregate gate failed accordingly.

The tested merge `f13bab7942c706c5533833abe43bc0c54318d143` has parents `4718da87f4e5f17fb83a604e5b97c9aa9ab71e26` and this PR head `5735c89e41da19924e1a29effa479c22d898e13c`. Its delta from tested main is exactly these two Template E2E files; the picker test, owners, styles, configuration and dependency inputs are unchanged. Maintainer-reviewed attribution qualifies this as unrelated inherited CI under the native exception route. The provider-selection/click-settlement cause remains unlocalized; this PR does not fix it or claim that CI passed. No picker rerun or assertion change was made.
