prs.title: fix: catch incompatible ownership before porting to SQLite
prs.body:
## Summary

### High Level TLDR

A move from PostgreSQL to SQLite could copy and verify the database before telling the operator that installation ownership makes the destination config invalid. The command and dry run now report the incompatible setting before copying. The operator chooses when to turn off installation ownership.

### What Problem This Solves

The late failure leaves an active recovery manifest, so the Gateway requires rollback before it can start again. The early refusal applies to both whole-installation and family ports.

## Root Cause

The config schema requires every configurable family to use PostgreSQL when `database.postgres.ownership` is `installation`. The port changes the selected engine and leaves the ownership setting as configured. Previously, strict config validation caught the conflict at publication, after the staged SQLite store had been verified. The command now checks the destination in its existing engine selection preflight and the operator guide explains the prerequisite.

## Real behavior proof

Ran the production database port CLI registration against a disposable PostgreSQL 18.7 server over a Unix socket. Seeded a shared-state store with a seven-byte blob and configured installation ownership.

- On main, `openclaw database port --to sqlite --dry-run` reported `Database port: preflight (postgres → sqlite); 1 database stores.` The real command exited 1 at `switch config` with `CONFIG_VALIDATION_FAILED`. The active manifest was `preparing` with a verified target. The source config and PostgreSQL anchor remained active.
- With the fix, `openclaw database port --to sqlite` and `openclaw database port --family state --to sqlite` each exited 1 with the ownership guidance. Both dry runs did the same. The config and anchor still selected PostgreSQL and the recovery directory was absent.
- Using the fixed command, `openclaw database port --rollback <manifest>` completed for the interrupted baseline operation and archived its active manifest. The original PostgreSQL config and installation ownership remained intact.
- With all writers stopped, set ownership to `state-directory` in the fresh fixture and reran `openclaw database port --to sqlite`. The command reported `Database port: complete (sqlite); 1 database stores.` The SQLite row matched the original blob and the operation archived its manifest.

Three timed dry runs after one warmup per build on the same host and workload took 35.33–45.61 s on main (median 44.65 s) and 11.64–19.38 s with the fix (median 14.56 s). These are source CLI invocations under shared host load. The before run inventories the source, while the after run refuses at config admission.

## What was not tested

No live Gateway, paid model calls, or production-size port. The disposable fixture covered one shared-state store. The interrupted-port proof covered rollback. No resume, cross-host lock failover, or older-release upgrade was verified.

## Verification

- `pnpm test src/commands/doctor-database-port.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`. Two new cases failed on main. All 9 passed on the candidate (60.04 s wall time).
- Targeted Oxlint with type checking, Oxfmt, the PostgreSQL guide MDX check, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Autoreview covered the candidate diff against `1fbcec108f4e4ed21c698d82e31e7ce23498b342` at P0–P2 and returned no actionable findings. The change adds one admission branch and two command cases. It uses the existing config and recovery contracts.
- The required CI gate passed on `79452f476694028c0fe338156a7bf39a94d379ba`, including PostgreSQL conformance. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44630101353
- Hosted review found no actionable issues on the same head. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202101#issuecomment-7024478684

prs.title: fix: let macOS launch with ready credentials when the PostgreSQL secret is unavailable
prs.body:
## Summary

### High Level TLDR

The macOS app could quit during launch when its bundled CLI could not resolve the Gateway's PostgreSQL connection secret. The CLI now prepares local runtime pins without looking up that secret when client credentials are ready.

## What Problem This Solves

A launch from the desktop can inherit a different environment from the Gateway service. If an env SecretRef is provided only to the service, the app's launch-time Doctor command fails and the app asks the user to recover already-usable credentials.

## User Impact

A profile with ready credentials can finish launch preparation even when the PostgreSQL secret is available only to the Gateway service. If the credential receipt needs recovery, the operator still needs access to the matching shared state store.

## Root Cause

`doctor --client-credentials --fix --non-interactive` asked for a fully resolved database selection before it checked whether credential work was needed. The PostgreSQL engine resolver threw on the missing environment variable. The real command returned exit 1 with `The CLI command failed.` on the baseline.

## Why This Change Was Made

The runtime pin owner only needs the configured shared-state engine to determine whether a legacy SQLite pin source exists. The ready path passes that engine to the existing pin owner under the service operation lock. Required credential recovery still resolves the database connection and runs through the existing Doctor maintenance path.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof

The regression boots a disposable PostgreSQL 17 fixture with ready local credentials. It replaces the config's connection string with an env SecretRef and withholds that variable from the built CLI subprocess. The app's exact `doctor --client-credentials --fix --non-interactive` command exits 0, completes the local pin receipt, and preserves the device identity. Replacing the anchor makes the credential receipt stale. The same Doctor path in JSON mode then exits 2 and reports `Configure a resolvable PostgreSQL DSN`.

```sh
node scripts/test-database-conformance.mjs --engine postgres --connection "$TEST_DSN" -- \
  src/commands/startup-client-credentials.postgres.test.ts \
  -t 'prepares native runtime pins' --maxWorkers=1
```

Before: `expected 1 to be +0`. After: `prepares native runtime pins without the PostgreSQL secret when credentials are ready` passed in 6.3 s.

### What was not tested

Signed macOS app launch, macOS launch latency, a latest-stable macOS app upgrade, and native exec approvals during a PostgreSQL outage were outside the Linux CLI proof. No paid model calls were used for the product test.

## Verification

- 99 tests passed in the focused credential, runtime pin, and CLI registration run. One legacy PostgreSQL migration test hit the disposable server's default lock table limit. The same test passed after matching the CI setting of `max_locks_per_transaction=512`.
- Targeted commands typecheck, lint on the four touched TypeScript files, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Autoreview found no actionable P0–P2 findings on the change from the pinned main revision. The simplification pass kept the existing pin migration, lock, and recovery owners. Production TypeScript changed by +37/-16 lines. The regression adds 35 lines to the existing subprocess suite.
- [GitHub CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44630209317) passed at `6a2dee198389520cccbab4dc50141820178fe9e5`, including all four PostgreSQL conformance shards and the PostgreSQL 16 smoke.
- [PostgreSQL conformance (3/4)](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44630209317/job/135935603578) recorded the built CLI regression as passing in 6.163 s.

prs.title: fix(talk): use PostgreSQL voice session indexes
prs.body:
## Summary

### High Level TLDR

Legacy voice-session lookup and stale-session recovery can use their existing partial indexes on PostgreSQL. This avoids scanning retained closed sessions as voice history grows.

## Root Cause

The PostgreSQL lookup filtered on `pg_input_is_valid` and a `jsonb` path. The generated indexes use `IS JSON` and typed `json` field extraction. PostgreSQL could infer neither the open-status predicate nor the indexed lookup keys from the runtime expressions. The lookup now uses the generated index expressions on PostgreSQL. The scope, timestamp cutoff, validation, and decoder stay in their existing worker.

## Real behavior proof

The agent-store conformance regression calls the production voice lookup with 3,000 rows, including 2,700 closed rows, plus malformed JSON. It checks the selected record and runs `EXPLAIN` on the worker's executed SQL, for legacy and stale lookup. The base used a sequential scan for legacy lookup and the general cache timestamp index for stale lookup. The fix selects `idx_agent_voice_session_open_scope` and `idx_agent_voice_session_open_updated`, respectively.

A second run called `lookupClientVoiceSessions` from the Talk caller through the PostgreSQL history worker. It reused the conformance fixture with a disposable shared-state store and captured the executed plans using PostgreSQL `auto_explain`. The record IDs below are synthetic.

```text
legacy [{"voiceSessionId":"1","sessionKey":"agent:voice-plans:target"}]
Index Scan using idx_agent_voice_session_open_scope on cache_entries
stale [{"voiceSessionId":"1","sessionKey":"agent:voice-plans:target"}]
Index Scan using idx_agent_voice_session_open_updated on cache_entries
1 passed
```

To repeat, copy the conformance fixture into an infra test and adjust its state imports. Open its disposable shared-state store first and await `lookupClientVoiceSessions(input)` for both inputs. Set `auto_explain.log_min_duration=0` on the disposable server and run the conformance command below against the copied test.

On Linux with PostgreSQL 17.12, a separate SQL benchmark used the generated cache-entry table and indexes with 10,000 retained records, 300 open. For each lookup and version, it ran 3 warmup queries and 30 measured `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON, TIMING OFF, BUFFERS)` queries on the same warmed fixture.

| Lookup | Baseline median | Fixed median | Shared buffer hits, before → after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Legacy by agent, session, and origin | 12.389 ms | 0.003 ms | 323 → 3 |
| Stale at timestamp 3,000, excluding one ID | 6.528 ms | 0.413 ms | 143 → 14 |

The timings cover database execution. Both versions returned the same counts for each query.

## What was not tested

Real-time audio, live providers, paid model calls, and a managed Gateway deployment. The local performance sample covers PostgreSQL 17 and synthetic data.

## Verification

```sh
node scripts/test-database-conformance.mjs --engine postgres --connection "$LOCAL_DSN" -- src/state/openclaw-agent-db.postgres.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 -t 'uses the partial indexes for PostgreSQL voice-session lookups'
```

- The focused regression is red on the base at the plan assertion. With the patch, the unfiltered PostgreSQL agent-owner file passes all 12 tests. The new case took 3.97 seconds.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/talk/client-voice-session-store.test.ts src/talk/client-voice-session.test.ts src/talk/client-voice-session.digest-retry.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` passed 42 tests.
- Targeted type-aware lint and type checking for both files, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed.

## Evidence

Local autoreview on the final diff from `1fbcec108f4e4ed21c698d82e31e7ce23498b342` to `78925d41370385af31eddfc19152b38d73574e6a` found no actionable P2 or higher issues. The local PostgreSQL run supplies the schema and planner proof.

prs.body:
Related: #200923

## What Problem This Solves

Automatic AI setup can ask you to sign in with ChatGPT when an already-detected local model failed for a different reason. The sign-in screen also hides the failed attempts, so the local server problem is easy to miss.

## User Impact

When an attempted connection fails for a non-credential reason, setup now says it could not connect and shows the recorded reason. ChatGPT sign-in remains available as an alternative. When only credentials are missing or expired, setup still asks you to sign in and now shows any recorded credential errors. Existing configured models and successful fallback selection are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The automatic setup owner already receives categorized activation failures. It now retains whether any failure was not authentication-related instead of treating an absent Codex login as the diagnosis for the whole run. This reuses the existing `unavailable`, `needs-sign-in`, `attempts`, and optional `signIn` fields; there is no schema, configuration, permission, or model-capacity policy change.

This is independent of #200923: no context-window floor from that unmerged PR is included. The current-main reproduction uses the existing local-provider HTTP error path.

## Evidence

- Reproduced before editing on current main `bde2e84084bffa49cad046351f7ddd739d26d9ea`: real isolated Gateway and `openclaw gateway call openclaw.setup.auto`, with a synthetic loopback llama-server. Discovery advertises a 32,768-token local model; the real completion request receives HTTP 503 `insufficient_memory`. Setup returns `needs-sign-in` despite a non-authentication attempt failure. No real account or model inference was used.
- New owner regressions fail on the base for the intended status mismatch (3 failed, 19 existing tests passed), then all 22 pass with the fix. They cover local capacity-shaped rejection, timeout, mixed credentials/capacity, and retain existing missing/expired credential behavior. Base wall time 48.02 s; patched wall time 43.01 s (mostly worker preparation). CI seconds not yet available.
- Browser E2E: **8/8 pass** in Chromium 156.0.8078.4 (25.05 s), covering visible non-auth and credential errors, actual recovery-button requests, successful alternatives, dismissal, and native/web recovery. Matching before/after screenshots render the real Control UI with the recorded real-Gateway RPC results (synthetic local-provider HTTP failure, not live model inference); both comparison assertions pass. Clean and annotated comparisons are shown below.
- Patched real-Gateway replay of the same HTTP 503 scenario returns `unavailable`, preserves the attempt reason, and retains optional ChatGPT sign-in. With the local fixture stopped and no native credentials, the same CLI still returns `needs-sign-in` with no failed attempts. Both CLI calls exit 0.
- Product build and `pnpm ui:build` pass. Focused setup-controller tests: 18/18 pass (5.00 s wall). prs.title: fix(config): reject reserved PostgreSQL schema prefixes
prs.body:
## Summary

### High Level TLDR

OpenClaw could accept a PostgreSQL schema prefix that made a new Gateway fail at startup. Config validation now points to `database.postgres.schemaPrefix` and explains which values to avoid.

## What Problem This Solves

Using `pg` or `pg_openclaw` as the prefix passes config validation on the base commit. A fresh PostgreSQL-backed state store then fails to start because PostgreSQL reserves schema names beginning with `pg_`.

## User Impact

Operators get an actionable error during config validation. Choose a prefix such as `openclaw`. Existing store anchors retain their recorded schema when the configured prefix changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The config schema applies the restriction in its existing regex so CLI validation and the exported JSON Schema share one rule. The field help and PostgreSQL guides explain the restriction.

## Root Cause

The config validator checked characters and length. The store owner adds an underscore after the prefix, so both bare `pg` and prefixes already starting with `pg_` create names PostgreSQL refuses with SQLSTATE `42939`. PostgreSQL documents the reserved names in its `CREATE SCHEMA` reference. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/sql-createschema.html

## Evidence

- Regression on main: two cases failed because config validation returned `ok: true`.
- Candidate: all 35 config tests passed. The exported JSON Schema rejected the same two reserved prefixes and accepted `pgopenclaw`.
- Local autoreview did not produce a report. The isolated reviewer could not initialize through the local Codex launcher.

## Real behavior proof

In a fresh state directory with PostgreSQL 17.12, configure the state family to use PostgreSQL and set `database.postgres.schemaPrefix` to `pg` or `pg_openclaw`. Run `node openclaw.mjs config validate --json`, then `node openclaw.mjs gateway run --bind loopback --port "$PORT"` with a free loopback port.

- Base: validation returned `"valid": true` with exit 0 for both prefixes. Gateway startup exited 1 with `unacceptable schema name "pg_state_<id>"` or `unacceptable schema name "pg_openclaw_state_<id>"`. A direct PostgreSQL check returned SQLSTATE `42939`.
- Candidate: validation exited 1 and Gateway startup exited 78 with the `database.postgres.schemaPrefix` error for both values. No reserved schema was created.
- Valid control: `pgopenclaw` passed config validation and created a real PostgreSQL state schema, and the isolated Gateway returned HTTP 200 from `/ready`.

- Published stable 2026.11.6 accepted all three prefixes. Reading the same config file with the candidate accepted `pgopenclaw` and rejected the two reserved prefixes. Neither CLI rewrote the config during validation. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/releases/tag/v2026.11.6

- Populated-store handoff: started the published 2026.11.6 Gateway with PostgreSQL state and ran `cron add --disabled --name "Prefix compatibility control" --every 24h --session isolated --message "Retained PostgreSQL cron message" --no-deliver --json --port "$PORT"`. After stopping that Gateway, started the candidate over the same config, anchor, and PostgreSQL database. The schema advanced from v36 to v40. `cron list --all --json --port "$PORT"` returned the same disabled job ID and payload. Config bytes, anchor store ID, and recorded namespace matched. Changing the valid configured prefix to `pgother` and restarting the candidate kept the original namespace and row. All three Gateway runs returned HTTP 200 from `/ready`.

The populated-store handoff addresses the advisory review's compatibility proof request. The review found no code defects. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202097#issuecomment-7024547388

## What was not tested

The published-to-candidate handoff used a manual switch between binaries. The installed updater, live services, and paid models were outside this check. Each Gateway used a local mock model and PostgreSQL 17 over a private Unix socket.

## Verification

- `pnpm test src/config/zod-schema.database.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` passed 35/35 (107.57 seconds locally). Main failed both new rejection cases and passed the 33 other cases.
- Candidate runtime build, targeted typecheck and lint, formatter, `pnpm config:docs:check`, `pnpm config:schema:check`, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Exact-head CI and the required gate passed, including four PostgreSQL 17 conformance jobs and the PostgreSQL 16 Gateway smoke. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44629625127

prs.title: fix(x): bound mention polling batches and defer via backfill checkpoints
prs.body:
Closes #198995

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: X mention polling fetches every available page and keeps all posts in memory before delivering any of them, so a large backlog grows the poll without bound.

## User Impact

User impact: a large mention backlog is fetched in bounded batches across polls instead of in one unbounded pass.

## Why This Change Was Made

`pollXMentions()` now stops at a per-poll bound (10 pages, 100 posts or 1,048,576 characters), delivers that batch, stores the existing `backfill` continuation checkpoint without advancing `sinceId`, and reports the deferral through `onStatus`. Later polls continue from the stored pagination token until the backlog is done.

## Evidence

- 3 regression tests added in `extensions/x/src/events.test.ts` (long pagination, empty pages, large retained content).
- `pnpm test extensions/x/src/events.test.ts extensions/x/src/events-budget.test.ts extensions/x/src/monitor.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 3 files, 78 tests passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:extensions`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test` and `npx oxlint` on the changed files: 0 warnings, 0 errors.

Gaps: tests use a mocked fetch; there is no capture against the real X API or a running Gateway. Known trade-off raised by the automated review and not resolved in this revision: X returns newest first, so a backlog that spans several bounded batches is admitted newest batch first, where `main` admits the whole backlog oldest first.

prs.title: fix(mcp): compile tool output validators on first call, not at catalog load (#199327)
prs.body:
Fixes #199327.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: every session that connects to an MCP server with a large tool catalog keeps a compiled output validator for each tool, including the tools it never calls.

## User Impact

User impact: sessions that use large MCP catalogs retain less memory and load the catalog faster. Output validation is unchanged: valid structured results pass and invalid ones are still rejected.

One behavior differs. A tool whose output schema cannot compile now fails when that tool is called, rather than failing the catalog load for the whole server. The other tools on that server stay usable.

## Why This Change Was Made

`normalizeMcpToolCatalog` (`src/agents/mcp-tool-metadata.ts`) compiled an output-schema validator for every included tool as soon as a catalog was listed, and each session MCP runtime normalizes its own catalog.

The catalog now stores each included tool's output schema, and `validatorForCall` compiles it the first time that tool is called. The compiled validator is cached for that catalog's later calls.

- Every caller (`agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.ts`, `native-mcp-runtime-client.ts`, `node-host/mcp.ts`) gets the validator before it sends `tools/call`, so a broken schema still fails before anything reaches the server.
- **Shared schema resources (review P2, head `f992f15609f`):** compiling a schema also registers its `$id` resources so that other tools can `$ref` them. A schema that contains an `$id` key therefore still compiles at catalog load, in catalog order. Schemas without one stay lazy. The check is a key scan, so a property that happens to be named `$id` also compiles early; that costs only the laziness for that one tool.
- Not done: sharing compiled validators across runtimes. Triage noted that client-local schema resources and dialects make a global cache premature, so each catalog still owns its validator provider.

## Evidence

### Regression tests

`mcp-tool-metadata.test.ts` has two:

- Loading a two-tool catalog compiles nothing, the first `validatorForCall` compiles once, and a second call returns the same validator. It fails on `main` ("called 2 times").
- A catalog with tool `base` (`$id: https://example.test/base`) and tool `derived` (`$ref` to it): calling `derived` first validates correctly. It fails on the previous head `f1386727098` with `can't resolve reference https://example.test/base` and passes on `f992f15609f`.

Run on head `f992f15609f`: `mcp-tool-metadata`, `mcp-json-schema-validator`, `agent-bundle-mcp-schema`, `agent-bundle-mcp-runtime`, `native-mcp-runtime`, `native-mcp-runtime.http` and `node-host/mcp.recovery` all pass (7 files, 140 tests). oxlint, oxfmt and `git diff --check` are clean.

### Live Gateway run (head `f992f15609f`)

An isolated Gateway (`node openclaw.mjs gateway run`, own state directory, `OpenClaw 2026.11.3 (f992f15)`) ran three agent turns through `openclaw agent --agent main`. Setup:

- **MCP server:** a hand-written stdio server registered with `openclaw mcp add proof --command node …`. It lists 204 tools, each with an `outputSchema`: 200 bulk tools plus `good`, `bad`, `base` (declares `$id`) and `derived` (`$ref` to `base`). It does no output checking of its own, so only OpenClaw can reject a result.
- **Model:** a scripted loopback OpenAI-compatible provider. For the prompt `CALL <name>` it calls `dispatch_action` with id `proof__<name>` (the catalog sits behind Tool Search), then replies with the tool result it was given.

Neither script is committed. No real model was used, so this shows the Gateway tool path, not model behavior.

MCP server log (what reached the server):

```
11:01:17.687Z initialize
11:01:17.695Z tools/list -> 204 tools
11:01:19.135Z tools/call derived -> {"ok":true}
11:01:20.668Z tools/call good -> {"ok":true}
11:01:21.928Z tools/call bad -> {"ok":"not-a-boolean"}
```

Tool result the Gateway handed back to the model for each turn (external-content wrapper trimmed):

```
CALL derived -> {"tool":{"id":"mcp:proof:proof__derived","name":"proof__derived","source":"mcp"},"result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"structuredContent:\n{\"ok\":true}"}]}}
CALL good    -> {"tool":{"id":"mcp:proof:proof__good","name":"proof__good","source":"mcp"},"result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"structuredContent:\n{\"ok\":true}"}]}}
CALL bad     -> {"status":"error","tool":"dispatch_action","error":"Structured content does not match the tool's output schema: data/ok must be boolean"}
```

- `derived` was the first tool called in the process and `base` was never called, so the shared `$id` schema was registered at catalog load.
- `good` passed validation on its first call, and `bad` was rejected with the schema error after the server had answered.

Not shown live: the same three turns on the previous head. The `derived` failure on `f1386727098` is covered by the regression test above. Retained heap was not measured inside the Gateway; the numbers below come from the session runtime directly.

### Measured: real session runtimes against a real HTTP MCP server

A Node 24 script (`node --expose-gc`, not committed) ran a loopback streamable-HTTP MCP server built on the SDK's low-level `Server`. It advertised 200 tools, each with the same draft-2020-12 `outputSchema`, and its raw `tools/call` handler sends output unchecked, so only OpenClaw's client-side validator can reject it. The script created 25 `createSessionMcpRuntime` runtimes, loaded each catalog, forced GC and measured retained heap. It then called one tool with valid output and one with invalid output. Each run was repeated twice with the same result:

```
### main
node=v24.22.1 tools=200 runtimes=25 catalogLoadMs=345 retainedHeapMB=40.0 perRuntimeMB=1.60
valid call -> {"id":"x","items":[],"meta":{"total":0}}
invalid call -> rejected: Structured content does not match the tool's output schema: must have required properties items, meta, /id must be string
### fix
node=v24.22.1 tools=200 runtimes=25 catalogLoadMs=182 retainedHeapMB=11.0 perRuntimeMB=0.44
valid call -> {"id":"x","items":[],"meta":{"total":0}}
invalid call -> rejected: Structured content does not match the tool's output schema: must have required properties items, meta, /id must be string
```

Retained heap per runtime drops from 1.60 MB to 0.44 MB, and catalog load time roughly halves. Output validation still rejects invalid structured content. The reporter's 15–20 MB per runtime came from larger real-world schemas and tool descriptions. This fixture's schema is small, so only the ratio, not the absolute number, carries over.

These heap numbers were measured on the first revision (`f1386727098`). The fixture's schemas have no `$id`, so the `f992f15609f` change does not affect them, but the run was not repeated on the new head.

prs.title: fix: let Codex 0.170 turns with display instructions finish
prs.body:
Related: openai/codex#60904

## What Problem This Solves

Codex 0.170 can attach a versioned display instruction to an answer (`moderation.display` with mode `show`, `hide` or `block`). The bundled Codex plugin validates app-server messages against the 0.169 schema, so a completed-turn receipt carrying one of these instructions is rejected. The turn's watcher then stays `pending` instead of confirming. A later valid receipt can still settle it; otherwise the run waits until its deadline.

## User Impact

Codex turns whose answers carry a 0.170 display instruction finish normally. The plugin now ships `@openai/codex` 0.170.0.

The Codex ACP adapter's pinned Codex moves to 0.170.0 as well, keeping the repo's rule that both ship the same Codex version.

Answer display does not change. OpenClaw does not read Codex moderation today and still does not: an answer Codex marks `hide` or `block` is shown, as moderated answers are shown on 0.169. Honoring those instructions is a separate follow-up.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Bump `@openai/codex` to 0.170.0 and regenerate the app-server schema and validators. The repo's source-version check requires the pin and the generated protocol to match. `CODEX_APP_SERVER_VERSION` moves with the pin, so the doctor's exact-version check accepts the managed binary, and the `@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp` override in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` moves with it (as in #200784), so the lockfile resolves exactly one `@openai/codex`. The 0.149 compatibility floor is unchanged.
- Validate exactly first. Only when that fails, and only for an `agentMessage` whose `moderation.moderated` is a boolean and whose non-null `display` is unreadable, apply Codex's own restricted read (`display: null`, `moderated: true`, as `StoredModeration` does in openai/codex#60904), then revalidate the whole envelope. No other field is repaired; a non-boolean `moderated` or any unrelated invalid field is still rejected. The fallback covers `turn/completed`, `turn/start`, `thread/start`, `thread/fork` and `thread/resume` (including `initialTurnsPage`).
- The display check uses the generated `AgentMessageDisplay` guard; there is no handwritten copy of the wire union.

## Evidence

Failing before the fix, at red-test commit `c5ed9765` on base `1fbcec10` (`pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/turn-router.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`), the same assertion for show, hide and block:

```text
AssertionError: expected 'pending' to be 'confirmed' // Object.is equality

Expected: "confirmed"
Received: "pending"
Tests  3 failed | 26 passed (29)
```

After the fix (manifest, router and validators, 64 passed):

```text
settles a valid native show receipt after a malformed receipt
settles a valid native hide receipt after a malformed receipt
settles a valid native block receipt after a malformed receipt
settles a Codex 0.170 terminal snapshot without changing answer presentation
```

`keeps managed Codex and the ACP adapter on the same exact bundled version` passes, and both installed entrypoints report `codex-cli 0.170.0`.

Also covered: plain and 0.149-era receipts, v1 instructions with extra fields, legacy `action` and unknown version or mode read as restricted, non-boolean `moderated` and unrelated invalid fields still rejected, and each response path above. Adjacent projector, ephemeral, bounded, catalog, client and doctor suites pass unmodified (439 tests). Scoped `oxlint -c .oxlintrc.json`, `oxfmt`, the line-cap ratchet and `codex-app-server:validators:check` pass.

Protocol generation: the schema was compacted from the exact `rust-v0.170.0` tag's checked-in experimental exports with the repo compactor. All nine resources match the packaged 0.170.0 CLI's `codex app-server generate-json-schema --experimental` output byte for byte, and `validateCodexProtocolSourceVersion` accepts the tag against the pin.

Not established locally:
- The Cargo-backed `codex-app-server:protocol:sync` and `:check` could not build here (a v8 dependency lacks `third_party/abseil-cpp`).
- The typecheck wrapper refuses this checkout because declarations resolve into the shared pnpm store.
- Two tests fail identically on the unmodified base with its own lockfile: the database-alias case in `run-attempt.protocol-validation.test.ts` and the managed-binary absence control.
- A scoped compile of the changed router test is clean apart from one error in untouched `packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-websocket.ts`.
- No live trace: a real turn cannot be made to carry a `hide` or `block` instruction on demand, so the evidence is the router, validator and run-attempt tests plus the schema comparison.

CI runs the full checks.

Independent review: READY at `a6f541a6` (two rounds; the ACP lockstep and router-test findings were fixed). Local ClawSweeper on `11f6ad8f`: patch C, proof F (tests only, no live trace), one test-typing finding fixed in `a6f541a6`.

prs.title: improve: reduce admission CPU for large shared-state reads
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Large shared-state reads spend main-thread CPU counting thousands of ordinary session IDs, paths, and hashes before worker admission. Each printable ASCII string currently pays both UTF-8 byte counting and an escape scan.

## User Impact

Lower admission-accounting CPU for large session, subagent, and workspace requests, with identical byte charges and overload decisions. No configuration, schema, permission, or migration change.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing accounting owner can charge printable ASCII without quotes or backslashes as `length + 2`. Other strings retain the original UTF-8 and JSON-escape calculation. The generic payload traversal still charges every field, including extra fields on nominally payload-free commands.

The large audited requests already carry projected identities or prepared file metadata. Subagent descendant selection combines live and persisted topology in the worker; trimming its live topology on the host can lose descendants. Splitting session cohorts adds transport work and changes snapshot boundaries. This change therefore preserves their payloads and removes redundant byte counting at the admission owner.

Production grows by five lines to retain the proven Unicode path. There is no new payload cache or caller-supplied size. A single JavaScript character loop was slower than this approach. The existing benchmark gains command-shape census and steady-state controls.

## Evidence

Five serial A/A/B triplets through the production `requestBytes` owner, using 5,000 session identities and a 62,000-file prepared workspace. Acceptance required exact charges, CPU gains beyond A/A variation on large ASCII shapes, and no material Unicode/escape regression.

| Synthetic command | Charged input | Baseline CPU µs/call | A/A CPU | Candidate CPU | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `sessionRows.sharedFacts`, 5k rows | 1,716,067 B | 2,845.62 | 2,831.38 | 2,186.96 | −23.1% |
| `subagents.runs`, 5k topology links | 920,590 B | 1,207.73 | 1,201.20 | 965.65 | −20.0% |
| `localWorkspace.manifest`, 62k prepared files | 18,888,453 B | 31,394.97 | 31,737.86 | 25,397.68 | −19.1% |
| `cron.jobNames`, 5k IDs | 230,540 B | 299.35 | 293.24 | 175.14 | −41.5% |
| Unicode control | 140,512 B | 212.07 | 212.66 | 213.17 | +0.5% |
| Escaped-string control | 360,512 B | 338.62 | 343.95 | 342.50 | +1.1% |

All 2,175,105 valid-fixture charge comparisons matched (excluding the superseded configuration fixture). ID lists, plugin lookup keys, session-state selectors and configuration projections also improved. Scalar archive/export requests remain small. Database size and reply bodies do not contribute to this input charge; these are source-derived owner measurements, not a production frequency mix or whole-Gateway latency claim. One-minute host load ranged from 6.08 to 7.72.

Workspace cumulative V8 allocation was identical at 2,260 B/call. Short topology bursts showed tiering allocation, so five additional A/A/B triplets used 1,000 warmup and 1,000 measured calls: median allocation was 630 / 746 / 687 B per call, within A/A variation; CPU was 1,188.53 / 1,194.73 / 954.09 µs. No allocation speedup is claimed. A separate CPU profile confirms the synchronous accounting owner.

The existing exhaustive UTF-16/surrogate test and oversized-request refusal remain; the added seeded differential test checks 2,000 randomized nested payloads against the original JSON-based charge. This is a behavior-preserving performance change, so the oracle passes both versions; the benchmark is the regression proof.

Focused request/worker tests: 27 passed (30.59 seconds including compilation). Final request suite: 4 passed (29.63 seconds including compilation; 83 ms test execution). `pnpm check:changed --staged` completed: its initial fixture type/style errors were corrected, and the failed typecheck/lint/format gates reran green; all other guards, including dead exports, passed. No inherited failures. Independent Codex autoreview: scoped-clean through P2 against base `72a92df06f2e079e698d682e6281cadabdc03305`, no actionable findings. No modified production module is imported by Control UI.

Reproduce after saving the parent request module as `/path/base.ts`:

```sh
node scripts/perf/state-read-request-bytes.ts --baseline /path/base.ts --module /path/base.ts --shape payloads --iterations 100
# Repeat for A/A; omit --module for candidate; run five serial triplets.
node scripts/perf/state-read-request-bytes.ts --baseline /path/base.ts --shape payloads --group 1 --iterations 1000 --warmup 1000
# Repeat the steady-state command in the same A/A/B pattern.
```

prs.title: fix: let managed Windows plugins load the host SDK without a junction
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A plugin can fail to load in the managed Windows Gateway when generation capture tries to create a junction to the host SDK and Windows returns `EPERM`.

## User Impact

Plugins using the packaged SDK can load in this configuration without the generation-root junction. Their ordinary Node workers can import the same SDK modules as the parent.

## Why This Change Was Made

The managed loader already knows the selected host and its SDK aliases. This change uses those aliases when the running host and the selected host have the same filesystem identity. It passes them to workers whose entry points belong to that capture and drops the binding when the capture is released. Copied native dependencies still use the existing native admission path and can have their own junction requirements.

This draft targets `release/2026.11.1`, the affected release line. The capture implementation has since moved on `main`.

## Evidence

A focused Windows fixture on packaged Node 24.22.1 exercised 16 cases and observed all eight worker exits. ESM and CommonJS workers loaded the selected host SDK. The fixture also exercised disposal, overlapping captures, and fallback to ordinary worker creation.

The added Windows regression exercises plugin registration, SDK resolution and release through the inspection loader. The full Windows build and that Vitest test have not run locally. To verify this draft on Windows with the release dependencies installed:

```sh
pnpm build:runtime
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.plugins.config.ts src/plugins/loader.windows-sdk-generation.test.ts
```

prs.title: fix(ci): restore PostgreSQL conformance coverage
prs.body:
## Summary

### High Level TLDR

PostgreSQL conformance could skip a pull request that changed only Gateway database ownership. It also missed three suites with PostgreSQL cases. Route those ownership changes to the existing PostgreSQL jobs and include the mixed-engine suites in the existing shards.

## What Problem This Solves

A change to Gateway startup custody or lock recovery could pass PR CI without running its PostgreSQL tests. CI also missed the PostgreSQL cases for ingress scheduling, GitHub publication recovery, and complete plugin-state views.

## User Impact

Maintainers get PostgreSQL results for those changes before merge. This is a CI coverage fix with no production behavior change.

## Why This Change Was Made

Extend the existing preflight paths and conformance inventory. The same planner applies to all four shards. SQLite-only Gateway lock test edits still skip PostgreSQL conformance.

## Root Cause

The preflight path filter covered Gateway server files and database implementation directories, but omitted the Gateway lock, recovery, and PostgreSQL custody owners under `src/infra`. The shard runner discovers `.postgres.test.ts` files automatically. The three mixed-engine suites use regular test filenames and were absent from its additional targets.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof

On main, the real preflight emitted `run_postgres_conformance=false` for a PR that touched only `src/infra/gateway-postgres-owner.ts`. With the patch, the same command emitted `run_postgres_conformance=true`.

```sh
OPENCLAW_CI_EVENT_NAME=pull_request \
  OPENCLAW_CI_CHANGED_PATHS_JSON='["src/infra/gateway-postgres-owner.ts"]' \
  GITHUB_OUTPUT="$MANIFEST_OUTPUT" node scripts/ci-build-manifest.mjs
node scripts/test-database-conformance.mjs --engine postgres --list
```

The real conformance runner verified the state and agent catalogs and passed 97 cases on a disposable PostgreSQL 17.12 server. The run included all 23 PostgreSQL GitHub publication cases, the PostgreSQL complete plugin-state view case, six ingress cases with PostgreSQL state, and the Gateway lock recovery suite.

node scripts/test-database-conformance.mjs --engine postgres --connection "$LOCAL_DSN" -- \

prs.title: fix(windows): report a Startup-folder login item as itself in gateway status
prs.body:
Closes #202094

## What Problem This Solves

On Windows, a non-elevated `openclaw gateway install` cannot register the S4U Scheduled Task, so it falls back to a Startup-folder login item. On such a host:

- `gateway status` labels the service `Scheduled Task (registered)`.
- `gateway status` and `doctor` report `Service definition inspection could not be completed.` on every run. The service audit asks Task Scheduler for a task definition that does not exist.

## User Impact

User impact: on a login-item install, `gateway status` shows `Service: Startup-folder login item (registered)`, and neither command reports the false inspection failure. Real inspection failures are still reported, such as an unreadable Task Scheduler with no login item installed. Scheduled Task installs are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **New predicate.** `isStartupEntryOnly` (`schtasks-runtime.ts`) names the existing "no registered task, Startup entry installed" check. `shouldControlStartupEntry` now uses it, so the two paths share one predicate.
- **Audit.** `auditGatewayServiceConfig` still audits the Scheduled Task definition first. Only if that read fails and the install is a login item does it treat "no definition" as correct. So Scheduled Task installs spawn nothing extra.
- **Label.**
  - `readScheduledTaskRuntime` already routes a missing task with a Startup entry to `resolveFallbackRuntime`. It now records that as `windowsStartupEntry: true`.
  - `formatServiceLabel`, the label owner for both status paths, renders that fact as `Startup-folder login item`.
  - The new field also appears in `gateway status --json` under `service.runtime`, as an additive field.

Not changed:

- Update-owned service refresh still rejects the Startup fallback by design (`UPDATE_NATIVE_AUTHORITY`).
- In the live run below, both unfixed main and this branch printed `Gateway service definition changed during Doctor` when the CLI and the service came from different installs. That is a separate case, and this change neither causes nor fixes it.

## Evidence

**Regression tests.** I checked both against main by restoring the five source files from `upstream/main` with the new tests in place:

- `schtasks-runtime.test.ts`: a missing task plus a Startup entry yields `windowsStartupEntry: true` and the label `Startup-folder login item`. On main it fails: `expected { status: 'unknown', …(1) } to match object { windowsStartupEntry: true }`.
- `service-audit.definition-facts.test.ts`: a login item with no task produces no `definitionDriftError`. On main it fails: `expected 'Service definition inspection could n…' to be undefined`.
- Control: the existing `reports failed native task inspection independently from legacy issues` test still passes. It covers a failed read with no login item.

**Affected suites.** I ran the daemon lane on Windows over `schtasks-runtime`, `schtasks-runtime.deadline`, `schtasks`, `schtasks-runtime-probe.windows`, `service-audit-schtasks.windows`, `service-audit` and `service-audit.definition-facts`.

- 204 tests passed.
- The 10 failures are systemd cases (KillMode, Delegate, base-unit directives, backup modes) that fail identically on unchanged `upstream/main` on this Windows host.

**Static checks.** `pnpm tsgo:core`, `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint` and `git diff --check` are all clean.

**Live run.**

- Setup: Windows 11 26200, non-elevated. The login item was installed by `openclaw@2026.11.5` for a throwaway profile and removed afterwards.
- Before, with 2026.11.5:

```text
Service: Scheduled Task (registered)
Service definition inspection incomplete: Service definition inspection could not be completed.
Runtime: running (pid <pid>, Startup-folder login item installed; matching gateway process detected for port <port>.)
```

- After, with this branch built and run against the same install:

```text
Service: Startup-folder login item (registered)
Runtime: running (pid <pid>, Startup-folder login item installed; matching gateway process detected for port <port>.)
```

- `gateway status --json` (after): `"label": "Startup-folder login item"`, `"windowsStartupEntry": true`.
- `doctor --non-interactive`, run against the same stopped login item: an unfixed main build (7f059c01cd03; the touched files are unchanged up to this branch's base) prints the `Gateway service definition` box with `Service definition inspection could not be completed.`. This branch does not.

prs.title: fix: keep agent temporary files in owned scratch
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Agent validation commands can leave large temporary trees in host `/tmp`, outside OpenClaw's 24-hour scratch cleanup. On hosts where `/tmp` is tmpfs, that consumes memory and swap until an operator intervenes.

## User Impact

Local agent commands now default `TMPDIR`, `TMP`, and `TEMP` to their workspace's `.openclaw/tmp`. Temporary validation output is disposable under the existing 24-hour rule, even when artifacts reference it. Live and queued agent work remains protected; durable outputs belong outside scratch. After those runs settle, a detached background service alone does not extend the 24-hour lifetime of unchanged workspace scratch. Services needing longer-lived files must place them outside scratch or explicitly select a temp root with their own cleanup.

## Why This Change Was Made

Connect core exec, local CLI execution, and native Codex shell/Code Mode environment preparation to the existing scratch owner. Codex obtains the path through its run-bound host capability and applies it through thread shell policy, preserving shared app-server reuse. Docker/Podman commands use scratch in their writable workspace mount. Read-only workspaces keep writable temporary files in the container-private `/tmp` tmpfs, owned and released by the container lifecycle.

The existing cleanup inventory now includes configured agent and local sandbox workspaces, including sandbox directories left after container retirement. Queued protection uses the production session selector, including attachment grants and immutable skill-library isolation. Sandbox scope resolution and active-command custody reuse their existing owners. No new TTL implementation, configuration option, schema, reference-protection index, or cache. Explicit CLI/command/container environment overrides remain supported. Remote execution keeps its own paths. Programs that explicitly choose `/tmp` can bypass the policy; arbitrary host temp entries are not swept by name. Deep workspace paths can exceed Unix-domain socket limits: those tools need a short workspace or an explicit short-temp override with their own cleanup. The existing test runner already owns that exception.

Related: #193677. The short-lived native socket-path workaround from #196509 remains intact.

## Evidence

A real core exec from a nested working directory creates its temporary file inside checkout scratch. The committed regression fails on base `f685aad5977d707e47ba402b3d072e482a6b091b` at that assertion and passes with this change. Native Codex engine tests cover fresh and cold-resumed shells, login/snapshot variations, and restrictive environment filters. Local CLI tests cover default routing and explicit overrides; the generated sandbox shell creates an actual temporary directory. Hosted review identified a read-only-workspace regression; two real-shell tests reproduced it for Docker and Podman, and all 40 backend tests pass after preserving container-private temp for that mode. Cleanup tests verify expiry, live/queued protection, and queued sandbox protection after its last container registry row retires. Attachment and skill-library isolation regressions fail before the correction; all 17 custody and five managed-custody tests pass afterward. A real Docker read-only bind-mount probe fails before the temp-path correction and succeeds afterward.

Synthetic btrfs workload: 62,000 scratch files / 1.181 GB, beside a physical 37.63 GB synthetic SQLite storage fixture with 5,000 session rows. Five serial A1/A2 pairs per variant (10 observations each), using the same unchanged TTL owner:

| Metric | Inherited temp | Workspace temp |
|---|---:|---:|
| Expired validation scratch reclaimed | 0 | 670.56 MB |
| Total reclaimed, including existing coverage cleanup | 38.10 MB | 708.66 MB |
| Owner wall median / p95 | 2.118 / 3.123 s | 41.630 / 54.049 s |
| Deliberate pacing | 1.5 s | 29.0 s |
| Process CPU median / p95, workers included | 0.559 / 1.616 s | 11.075 / 14.684 s |
| Main-thread CPU median / p95 | 12.475 / 27.676 ms | 171.015 / 265.320 ms |
| Separate sampled main-isolate allocation A1 / A2 | 1.257 / 0.757 MB | 2.325 / 1.936 MB |

Every run preserves fresh/live/outside files and reports zero cleanup errors. This is the added cost of reclaiming previously unowned scratch, not a speedup comparison or a production-stall reproduction. A/A wall variation reached 24% on the shared virtual disk. The SQLite file supplies storage shape; this filesystem benchmark does not query the agent schema or measure whole-Gateway latency. Worker/native allocations are excluded from the heap sample.

Reproduce with `node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/scratch-cleanup-measure.ts --root <new-btrfs-directory> --samples 5 --mode timing --agent-temp`; use `--samples 1 --mode allocation` for the separate allocation pair.

Focused tests, the full package build, targeted typechecks/lint, formatting, line-cap checks, and final `pnpm check:changed` at `8c3d312db0fa258486ab502ad7ad128a83ed8600` pass. An earlier expanded check exposed an inherited SDK surface-budget regression: exact base and candidate both have 3,908 exports / 2,250 callables against limits 3,894 / 2,243. The check passes at `422ff062032e6`; the first expansion at `5795128db2d0c` (#201073) fails at 3,896 / 2,244. This is a main regression, not a budget change in this PR. No standalone SDK export was added. Final snapshot Codex autoreview is clean through P2. Production delta: +197/-49 = +148 lines, required for the missing environment handoffs, run-bound host operation, and root/custody coverage; repeated Codex placement checks and duplicate sandbox active-use logic were consolidated.

prs.title: docs: clarify PostgreSQL storage and backup coverage
prs.body:
## Summary

### High Level TLDR

A PostgreSQL-backed Gateway still keeps Knowledge data on local disk. Third-party plugins can open PostgreSQL stores through the SDK and need their own migration and recovery procedures. The operator and SDK guides now spell out both boundaries.

### What Problem This Solves

Operators planning a move or restore can miss Knowledge’s local database and vault files. Plugin authors following the SDK engine setup can also miss the separate requirements for moving or recovering a private store.

### User Impact

Operators can identify the Knowledge files to keep together and see which PostgreSQL stores the built-in backup and port tools handle.

## Root Cause

The engine registry selects PostgreSQL for five built-in families. Knowledge opens local SQLite databases independently. Knowledge has no managed SQLite backup resource in its manifest, so archive creation treats its included SQLite files as ordinary files. The SDK resolves PostgreSQL input for external stores. Port and PostgreSQL backup and restore use a fixed provider registry. The docs left those limits implicit.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof

The engine selector returned PostgreSQL for state, agent, Workboard, Logbook, and Team Reports with `database.engine: "postgres"`. It kept all three fixed safety journals on SQLite.

A focused docs check read both guides on main and on this patch. Main missed all three assertions. The check looked for the location of Knowledge’s local data, the operator guidance for private plugin PostgreSQL stores, and the SDK port and backup boundary. All three passed on the patch. `pnpm docs:list --headings` showed both pages and the linked section headings.

### What was not tested

Docs validation used no Gateway, PostgreSQL server, or paid model calls. A runtime backup and restore drill was outside this docs patch.

## Verification

- `pnpm docs:list --headings` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- The commit hook formatted both Markdown files. The committed blobs match the reviewed files.
- Autoreview (P0–P3) found no actionable findings on the final two-file diff against `1fbcec108f4`.

prs.title: fix(cli): restore dashboard Gateway start and install recovery
prs.body:
> **AI-assisted: yes**

Closes #202037

## What Problem This Solves

- Fixes an issue where `openclaw dashboard` could never start or install the Gateway when it was stopped or absent: the command printed "Use the owning environment or supervisor to start or repair the selected Gateway." and exited 1, even with `--yes` or after accepting the prompt, so the documented start/install recovery never ran and the usual `gateway start` / `gateway run` hints were suppressed.
- **Related:** #202037 (traced in source at main @ 59ca885df59). The readiness probe forwarded the dashboard's internally resolved URL as a probe override; the daemon status reader classifies any URL override as diagnostic-only, so the native service was never the recovery target and the start/install branch was unreachable.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Intended outcome:** The dashboard readiness check no longer forwards its own resolved URL as a probe override. The daemon status reader resolves the configured local endpoint itself (with config credentials and TLS verification, which URL overrides skip), keeps the native service as the probe target, and the documented start/install prompt, `--yes`, and the post-recovery re-probe become reachable again for an owned local Gateway.
- **Out of scope:** `gateway status --url` keeps classifying explicit URL overrides as diagnostic-only (intended and already tested in `status.gather.test.ts`); externally supervised or non-default-identity targets remain unrecoverable from the dashboard.
- **Highest-risk area:** Readiness probing now targets the daemon-config-resolved local endpoint rather than the dashboard's handoff URL; for default local installs (the recovery-relevant population) these are the same endpoint.
- **How is that risk mitigated?** Dashboard delivery still verifies its own resolved target afterwards (`waitForControlUiDocument`, `hasVerifiedControlUiLoopbackAlias`), and regressions pin the no-override call shape and the recovery decision.

## User Impact

- **Success criteria:** With the Gateway stopped or absent on a default local install, `openclaw dashboard` offers to start or install the background Gateway service (or does so immediately with `--yes`) and prints the `openclaw gateway start` / `openclaw gateway run` hints again instead of the misleading supervisor message; `dashboard --json` still never installs or starts a service.
- **What should reviewers focus on:** `src/commands/dashboard.ts` (`ensureDashboardTargetReady`), the new regressions in `src/commands/gateway-readiness.test.ts` (`probes the configured endpoint without a URL override so the native service stays the recovery target`, `never installs or starts the gateway service for JSON output`), and the updated call-shape assertions in `src/commands/dashboard.test.ts`.

## Evidence

- **Real environment tested:** Linux (EL8) with the real systemd user manager and live port probes; the worktree CLI sources were executed directly (tsx) against the machine's real service discovery and ports — no mocks in the evidence path.
- **Exact steps or commands run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  # Real gatherDaemonStatus comparison, pre-fix call shape vs fixed call shape
  # (profile-isolated unit absent, port 18790 free):
  OPENCLAW_PROFILE=evid202037 OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT=18790 DASHBOARD_PROBE_PORT=18790 \
    node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs evidence-composition.mts
  # Real dashboard command, before (origin/main) and after (this patch), no TTY:
  OPENCLAW_PROFILE=evid202037 OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT=18790 \
    node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs evidence-dashboard-driver.mts
  # Regression tests (RED on main, GREEN with this patch) via validate.sh:
  #   src/commands/gateway-readiness.test.ts, src/commands/dashboard.test.ts
  ```
- **Evidence after fix:**
  ```json
  {
    "before": {
      "callShape": "old: rpc:{url:<dashboard-resolved wsUrl>}",
      "serviceTargetRole": "diagnostic-only",
      "gatewayLooksStopped": true,
      "nativeServiceTargetsGateway": false,
      "canStartService": false,
      "recoveryBranchReachable": false
    },
    "after": {
      "callShape": "fixed: rpc:{}",
      "serviceTargetRole": "target",
      "gatewayLooksStopped": true,
      "nativeServiceTargetsGateway": true,
      "canStartService": true,
      "shouldInstall": true,
      "recoveryBranchReachable": true
    }
  }
  ```
- **Observed result after fix:** The real `dashboard` command (no TTY, no `--yes`) in the same environment now prints `Gateway is not running.` followed by `Run "openclaw gateway start" to start a managed gateway.` and `Run "openclaw gateway run" for a foreground gateway.`, and the install/start recovery branch is reachable (`canStartService: true`, `shouldInstall: true`). On main @ 73a53a58eba the identical run printed `Use the owning environment or supervisor to start or repair the selected Gateway.` (exit 1) with the recovery branch unreachable.
- **Before evidence:** main @ 73a53a58eba, same environment and driver: `Gateway is not running.` / `Run "openclaw gateway status --deep" for details.` / `Use the owning environment or supervisor to start or repair the selected Gateway.` — exactly the reported symptom, including the suppressed `gateway start` / `gateway run` hints.
- **What was not tested:** A full end-to-end service install/start lifecycle (`--yes` proceeding through `runDaemonInstall` / `runDaemonStart` to dashboard delivery) in an isolated environment; this machine's desktop-owned Gateway service could not be stopped or replaced. The install/start actions are unchanged pre-existing code paths covered by the `gateway-readiness.test.ts` recovery tests; this fix restores their reachability.
- **Proof tier:** L2
- **Proof limitations:** none
- **Review state:** Awaiting CI + maintainer review (CI lanes pending)

prs.title: fix: let PostgreSQL agents start turns with plugin tools
prs.body:
## Summary

### High Level TLDR

A healthy PostgreSQL Gateway can reject an agent turn with the full tool profile before contacting the model. Load missing plugin tools through the existing asynchronous loader so their readiness read runs in a worker.

## What Problem This Solves

A plugin needed by the turn may not yet be registered in its runtime generation. Cold tool construction then reports `PostgreSQL connections must run in a worker`, even though Gateway readiness succeeds.

## User Impact

Agent turns can load those plugin tools and complete. Synchronous compatibility entry points remain synchronous. This changes no configuration, schema, permissions, retention, or durability.

## Why This Change Was Made

Async tool construction now carries its execution mode through the existing tool-resolution generator, including callers without workspace-readiness state. Plugin selection, registry reuse, factories, and tool policy keep their existing owners. The synchronous API selects the existing synchronous loader.

Existing consumer test doubles follow that same generator contract. The database regression reuses the existing forked plugin inspection suite and its fixture. An explicit conformance target keeps both PostgreSQL cases in database CI. One unchanged diagnostic helper moves into the existing tool inspection module to satisfy the source-file size limit.

## Root Cause

On the base, `resolvePluginToolsFromRegistry` calls `loadPluginRegistryHandle` for missing owners. That synchronous loader skips the readiness worker step and falls back to `readPluginStateMigrationReadiness` on the Gateway thread. Opening the PostgreSQL connection there is correctly refused. The asynchronous agent adapter also previously selected the synchronous resolver when no workspace-readiness context existed.

The regression runs with the actual Gateway process role on thread zero, prepares metadata as startup does, and loads and invokes a synthetic cold tool. Both PostgreSQL cases fail on the base at `readDeferredPluginMigrations` / `readPluginStateMigrationReadiness`; both SQLite controls pass. Each case uses an independent store and plugin cache.

## Real behavior proof

RAN on Linux, Node 26.13.1, PostgreSQL 17.12, with a disposable Unix-socket-only server and isolated foreground Gateways. The model endpoint is the repository's loopback OpenAI mock fixture. Configuration uses `tools.profile: "full"` and disables memory search.

The turn command was:

```sh
openclaw agent --agent main --session-id <isolated-session> \
  --message 'Return marker <marker>' --thinking off --json
```

Temporary session and marker values are placeholders above. On the base, readiness returned `ready: true`, the command exited 1 with the worker-only connection error, and the mock received zero requests. With the fix, eight turns completed with `status: "ok"`, `summary: "completed"`, and the requested marker in the reply. The SQLite control also completed eight turns.

## What was not tested

No paid or external model calls, live channels, production state, TLS deployment, other server majors, or database port/upgrade workflow. The mock-backed turns prove tool construction and model reachability, not the functionality of every registered tool. PostgreSQL successful-turn latency has no baseline comparison because the base fails before model dispatch.

## Verification

- RAN: exact regression on the base: two PostgreSQL failures at the readiness read; two SQLite passes. With the fix: four passes.
- RAN: full `pnpm build`, focused consumer tests including prompt-prefix stability, core and changed-test typechecks, targeted lint/format, mock-export ratchet, and `git diff --check`.
- RAN: 198 focused consumer tests passed, plus four real-database regression cases. The consolidated registry suite passed 16 cases in 39.52 s including collection (about 4 s test time); its wrapper took 41.06 s. CI conformance shard 3/4 also passed all 16 cases, with 6.439 s summed per-case execution time.
- RAN: same SQLite full-profile mock workload on the base and final source, three warmup turns then five measured fresh-session turns. CLI-to-reply median: 949 ms before, 877 ms after; ranges 863-982 ms and 801-1048 ms. This small shared-host sample is a control, not a throughput or tail-latency guarantee.
- Simplification: reuse the existing async loader and generator. No new worker, registry, cache, or state owner. Production delta: 41 added / 29 removed lines; test, fixture, and conformance-routing delta: 128 added / 17 removed lines. The diagnostic helper move is included in those counts.

## Evidence

Local autoreview of the production repair, P0-P2, reports `scoped-clean`. The complete option-construction and loader owners were supplied. Local autoreview of the CI inventory repair also reports `scoped-clean`. The current-head diagnostic only adds refusal details to an existing assertion; it changes no expected response, request, wait, retry, or production behavior.

### CI inventory repair

The first CI run found 78 jobs against the scheduled 77-job cap. The regression now reuses the existing forked inspection suite. No extra host-worker inventory entry or increased limit remains. RAN the four scheduled-capacity cases and eleven conformance-routing cases: all passed.

### Repeated Bun failure investigation

Both failed CI attempts tested the same merge commit. Their avatar-subscription test received `ok: false`:

- https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44545665684/job/135637036420
- https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44545665684/job/135658712659

RAN the actual `scripts/ci-run-node-test-shard.mts` entry with its three-file `agentic-gateway-server-isolated-hosted-3` selection, Node 24.22.1 and the checksum-verified repository Bun pin, `1.4.4-canary.1+191755ec1`. On base `3587df70a23`, the avatar case passed three of three runs. On PR head `271b8a34a6d`, it also passed three of three. The full shard had a separate terminal-subagent timeout once on each ref; these are separate outcomes, not avatar failures.

Three runs each on CI's exact main parent and tested merge ref also passed the avatar case. A further clean-home, four-CPU run reproduced the exact avatar refusal on the PR head, while its base control passed. Thus the repeated CI failure remains unclassified. No inherited-failure claim is made.

A verified main-branch snapshot contains the same test and passed it:
https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44598233217/job/135823119335

The diagnostic commit retains `ok: true` and the same subscribed-session payload assertion while reporting the RPC error code and message when that assertion fails. This is diagnostic evidence collection, not a claimed fix for the CI refusal. Focused lint, formatting and the gateway test typecheck pass. Equivalent temporary assertion diagnostics passed three head and three base Bun shard runs with fresh homes and four CPUs.

Current head: [649f80c3e072](https://github.com/VACInc/openclaw/commit/649f80c3e072be27bcfb52808d2c7f9843c95322). Production source remains unchanged.

### Current diagnostic CI result

The original avatar case passed in the same three-file Bun group, taking 2.943 s:
https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44616678138/job/135888545902

CI also advanced its main base. The pass does not establish that the assertion diagnostic repaired the historical refusal; that cause remains unclassified.

The current run is red on a different test: `session-message-events.history-worker.test.ts > delivers selected-session count updates after worker overload` times out:
https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44616678138/job/135888546116

The CI classifier labels this **unknown** with no matching job on main. RAN that exact two-file Bun group three times on base and three times on this head: all six local runs passed. These replays do not classify the CI timeout as inherited or fix it. No timeout, retry, expected response, or gate was relaxed. Merge readiness is not claimed. No merge or auto-merge was requested.

prs.title: fix(gateway): record role assignments in change history
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an administrator changes a person's role with `users.setRole`, nothing records who changed it or what it was before. Configuration edits already show up in the Gateway's change history (`openclaw.changes.list`, the **Recent changes** list on the Ask OpenClaw page), but role assignments, which grant or remove access, leave no trace.

## User Impact

Administrators can now see each committed role assignment in the existing change history: which profile changed, its previous role, its new role (or that it was cleared), who made the change, and when. Refused requests and requests that leave the role unchanged are not recorded. Authorization, the wire protocol and the Control UI do not change.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The profile write already knows the exact before and after rows of the committed transaction. `setCanonicalUserProfileRole` now reports a role transition from that commit receipt, and only when the role actually changed. A refused or rolled-back write never produces a receipt, so it never produces a record.
- `users.setRole` writes that transition through the existing `appendSystemAgentAuditEntry` writer. That writer feeds the store `openclaw.changes.list` already reads: the `system-agent-audit` scope of the shared state database, which keeps the latest 50,000 rows and is readable only with `operator.admin`. These rows are listed as `kind: "operation"` with the existing `config-rpc` source, which the Control UI shows as "settings", rather than as system-agent operations. An existing source keeps responses valid for strict v4 clients. There is no new RPC, store, protocol value or config option.
- The reply waits for the record. A role that committed but whose result failed to deliver is still recorded. Recording is best effort: if the append fails, the committed role change still succeeds and the Gateway logs a warning. The docs say that a missing entry therefore does not prove the role is unchanged.
- Recorded identity is limited to what attribution needs: the target profile id and one requester identifier. That is the requester's profile id (the shared owner shows as `gateway-owner`), or its device id when the connection has no profile, or the client id as a last resort. Profile and device ids are never stored together. No emails or names are recorded. Role names are JSON-quoted.
- Approval: on 2026-11-19 the requester (@fuller-stack-dev) approved the Team roles design. Its PR plan item 1: "record role assignments (`users.setRole`) in change history (actor, profile, before → after) so `openclaw.changes.list` shows them." This PR stays within that. It uses the existing admin-only history and its 50,000-row bound, and adds no new readers or retention.

Coordination: #201610 also edits `users-role.ts` and `user-profile-writes.ts`. This diff keeps away from its hunks; `git merge-tree` of this branch with #201610's head (`ca0a209b`) merges cleanly in either order. Related: #195408 (read-only People view) does not overlap this change.

## Evidence

**Isolated Gateway, real RPCs, before and after.** This used a temporary state directory and config (not Odin's), with token auth on loopback port 19447 and named roles `administrator` and `reader`. One synthetic person profile was seeded in the temporary state DB. Calls went through `openclaw gateway call` against `openclaw gateway run` built from each revision.

Before (base `4eb3541d`): assign `administrator`, change to `reader`, and clear all succeed, then `openclaw.changes.list {limit: 10}` returns:

```json
{ "entries": [] }
```

After (head `d55a7314`; the config also defines a role named `night "ops"` to show quoting), the requests and results were:

1. Assign `administrator`: ok.
2. Repeat `administrator` (unchanged): ok.
3. `role: "ghost"`: `INVALID_REQUEST: unknown operator role "ghost"; define it under gateway.roles.definitions before assigning it`
4. `profileId: "gateway-owner"`: `INVALID_REQUEST: the shared owner profile is not governed by operator roles`
5. Change to `night "ops"`: ok.
6. Clear: ok.
7. Clear again (unchanged): ok.

`openclaw.changes.list {limit: 10}` then returns exactly the three committed transitions:

```text
system-agent-audit:3  operation  config-rpc  Role for profile e0d681a5-e175-46ab-9fba-f1c4fd760219 cleared (was "night \"ops\"") by profile gateway-owner
system-agent-audit:2  operation  config-rpc  Role for profile e0d681a5-e175-46ab-9fba-f1c4fd760219 changed from "administrator" to "night \"ops\"" by profile gateway-owner
system-agent-audit:1  operation  config-rpc  Role for profile e0d681a5-e175-46ab-9fba-f1c4fd760219 changed from no role to "administrator" by profile gateway-owner
```
(`id  kind  source  summary` from the JSON response.)

Stored row `details` (read from a copy of the stopped Gateway's DB) keep one requester identifier, e.g. `{"profileId":"e0d681a5-…","previousRole":"administrator","role":"night \"ops\"","actor":{"kind":"profile","id":"gateway-owner"}}`.

The unchanged repeats and both refused requests added no entries.

**Regression tests (red on base, green here).** `src/gateway/server-methods/users-role.worker.test.ts` runs the real users and change-history handlers against an isolated state DB:
- New: "lists committed role assignments, not refused or unchanged ones, in change history" covers assign (with a quoted role name), unchanged repeat, unknown role, owner refusal, and clear, then reads them through `openclaw.changes.list` and checks the exact before, after, and actor.
- Extended: the existing "failed delivery" and "self downgrade" cases now also check that the committed role is in history, including when the RPC result could not be delivered.
- With the production change reverted, the 3 affected tests fail (`expected [] to deeply equal [...]`). With the change applied, all pass.

Also passing: `users.test.ts`, `system-changes.test.ts`, `linked-owner-authority.test.ts`, `user-profile-writes.owner.test.ts` and `custodian-history.test.ts` (on `a6db2ddd`); `users-role.worker` and `system-changes` again on `d55a7314` (whose change is limited to the history writer); `server.config-patch.test.ts` on the first head. Type-aware oxlint, tsrs typecheck (changed files), `format:check` and `format:docs:check` are clean.

No state schema or stored payload shape changes: the rows use the existing `SystemAgentAuditEntry` shape in an existing scope, so upgrade and Doctor behavior are unaffected.

<details>
<summary>Touched test file audit</summary>

- `users-role.worker.test.ts` (read in full): every case runs the real dispatcher and state worker. The only mock is the boundary hook that injects a result-delivery failure. Added one behavior test and history assertions to the two existing commit cases. There are no tautologies and no dead or duplicate tests.
- `users.test.ts` (read in full): a mock-isolated admission suite. The "sets role … before responding" case pinned the writer's exact options.
